Thus if $f\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $n\geq 3$ is NCC, then $f$ depends on at least 3 variables after any affine linear transformation; we will see in §4.4 that related “nondegeneracy” conditions are also useful when proving upper bounds for affine thin sets of type II as in [BPW25].

If the leading form of $f$ is absolutely irreducible, then $f$ must be NCC. For suppose $f$ is cylindrical over the curve $C=\{g(x,y)=0\}$ , so that $f=g(L_{1}(\mathbf{x}),L_{2}(\mathbf{x}))$ . Let $g_{0}$ denote the leading form of $g$ , which cannot be absolutely irreducible since it is a binary form (see e.g. [BP24, Remark 5.3]). Thus the leading form of $f$ , namely $g_{0}(L_{1}(\mathbf{x}),L_{2}(\mathbf{x}))$ is never absolutely irreducible when $f$ is cylindrical over a curve. On the other hand, there are many polynomials whose leading forms are not absolutely irreducible that are also not cylindrical over curves.

Now consider the class of hypersurfaces $H$ that are NCC. Additionally, assume that $H\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ is defined as the vanishing set of a polynomial $f\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ of degree $d\geq 4$ such that $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ and has leading form $f_{d}$ with no linear factors over $\mathbb{Q}$ (in which case $f_{d}$ is said to be 1-irreducible). For this class, [CDH+23, Thm. 1.5] shows (3.15) with $C(n,d)\ll_{n}d^{7}$ and small factor $s(B)\leq(\log B)^{\gamma(n)}$ . If the hypothesis is strengthened to assume the leading form $f_{d}$ of $f$ has no factors of degree $\leq 2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ (in which case $f_{d}$ is said to be 2-irreducible), this can be strengthened to $s(B)\leq 1$ for $d\geq 5$ . Under hypotheses such as these, it remains an open problem to achieve (3.15) for degree $d=3$ . So far, [CDH+23, Thm. 1.5] has achieved the bound (3.16) if $H$ is a hypersurface that is NCC and $f$ is of degree $3$ with 1-irreducible leading form $f_{3}$ .

Regarding lower bounds, by [CCDN20, §6], for every $d\geq 1$ there exists a hypersurface $H\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ defined as the vanishing set of an absolutely irreducible degree $d$ polynomial $f\in\mathbb{Q}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ such that $N_{\mathrm{aff}}(H,B)\gg_{n}d^{2}B^{n-2}$ , so that in general one cannot expect to prove smaller than quadratic growth in $d$ .

In contrast, if $f\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is cylindrical over a curve and we consider the hypersurface $H\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ defined as the vanishing locus of $f$ , then

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(H,B)\ll_{n}B^{n-2}N_{\mathrm{aff}}(C,B) $$

for a curve $C\subset\mathbb{A}^{2}(\mathbb{Q})$ [CDH+23, Remark 1.6]. The resulting curve $C$ could contain many points; for example $C:x_{1}=x_{2}^{d}$ contains $\gg B^{1/d}$ points $(x_{1},x_{2})\in[-B,B]^{2}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ , in which case one could not expect to improve on the exponent in Pila’s bound (3.7). This shows that the NCC condition cannot in general be removed from the above results. But a conjectural approach in [CDH+23, Thm. 1.9] suggests that $N_{\mathrm{aff}}(H,B)\ll_{n,d,\varepsilon}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}H-1+\varepsilon}$ may be true for all affine hypersurfaces $H\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ defined as the vanishing set of a polynomial $f\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ of degree $d\geq 2$ and $n\geq 2$ such that the leading form $f_{d}$ of $f$ has no linear factors over $\mathbb{Q}$ .

#### 3.4.2. Varieties

We now return to the question of proving (3.15), for more general varieties than hypersurfaces. Here Vermeulen has generalized the notion of NCC. Let $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ be an affine variety of dimension $m$ . Then $V$ is said to be cylindrical over a curve if there exists a $\mathbb{Q}$ -linear map $L:\mathbb{A}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n-m+1}$ such that $L(V)$ is a curve; otherwise, $V$ is said to be NCC. Under the hypothesis that $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ is NCC of degree $d\geq 4$ , [Ver24, Thm. 1.2] has proved (3.15) with small factor $s(B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ (and unspecified $C(n,d)$ ). It remains an open question to achieve this for degree $d=3$ . So far, in this setting, (3.16) is obtained with a $B^{\varepsilon}$ factor, if $d=3$ .

On the other hand, if $V$ is cylindrical over a curve, and so there is a $\mathbb{Q}$ -linear map $L:\mathbb{A}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n-m+1}$ such that $L(V)$ is a curve, then

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)\leq B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V-1}N_{\mathrm{aff}}(L(V),B) $$

so that consideration reduces to counting points on the curve $L(V)$ , leading to similar considerations as in (3.17).

It remains an open question to characterize the largest “allowable” class of affine varieties for which the main exponent in (3.15) is achievable. This concludes our discussion of Dimension Growth results, relevant to thin sets of type I in both the projective and affine settings.

## 4. Survey of type II thin sets

We now shift focus to thin sets of type II. Our path will follow a similar pattern to that above: studying the main conjecture in the projective setting will require results from the affine setting; we must restrict attention to special cases in the affine setting in order to obtain suitably strong results to attain the central conjecture in the projective setting; and finally we can ask for the largest “allowable” class in the affine setting for which strong results (analogous to the main conjecture in the projective setting) can be obtained.

### 4.1. Type II, projective

By definition, if $M$ is of type II then there is an irreducible projective algebraic variety $Z$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{P}}Z=\dim_{\mathbb{P}}(\mathbb{P}^{n-1})$ , and a dominant morphism $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ with generically finite fibres, of degree $d\geq 2$ , with $M\subset\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q}))$ . In this setting, the central conjecture is:

#### Conjecture 4.1 (Projective type II, nonuniform).

Let $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ be a thin set of type II. Then

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)\leq C(M)B^{n-1}s(B), $$

in which $C(M)$ is a constant depending on $M$ , and $s(B)$ is a “small factor,” which could take the form $s(B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}$ (for any $\varepsilon>0$ ); or $s(B)\leq(\log B)^{\gamma(M)}$ for some $\gamma(M)>0$ ; or $s(B)\leq 1$ .

This is stated in [Ser97, Ch. 13, p. 178] as a reasonable expectation, with small factor $s(B)\ll(\log B)^{\gamma(M)}$ , and no discussion of how $C(M)$ depends on $M$ . To say that $C(M)$ depends on $M$ is to say it depends on the morphism $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ , and we will study this dependence in detail later in §5-7.

Serre proved this for $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ , namely showing that $N_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(M,B)\ll B$ ; see [Ser97, §9.7. Thm. page 133]. Broberg [Bro03a] again proved Conjecture 4.1 for $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ , in the stronger form that $N_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(M,B)\ll_{M,\varepsilon}B^{2/d+\varepsilon}$ , in which $d$ denotes the degree of $\pi$ . Broberg also proved the conjecture for $\mathbb{P}^{2}$ when $d\geq 3$ , with small factor $s(B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}$ and unspecified dependence $C(M)\ll_{M}1$ . For $\mathbb{P}^{2}$ and $d=2$ , Broberg proved $N_{\mathbb{P}^{2}}(M,B)\ll_{M,\varepsilon}B^{9/4+\varepsilon}$ .

In the case where $\pi$ is a smooth cyclic cover, the conjecture was proved by Heath-Brown and Pierce [HBP12] for all $n\geq 10$ , with mildly weaker bounds for $3\leq n\leq 9$ .

Historically, the first general improvement on the trivial bound $N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)\ll_{n}B^{n}$ , valid for any projective thin set of type II, was Theorem 1.3, which yields the baseline upper bound

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)\leq C(M)B^{n-1/2}(\log B)^{\gamma(M)}. $$

This theorem is stated for any thin set in [Ser97, Ch. 13 Thm. 3], but it is only nontrivial for thin sets of type II, by recalling the trivial bound (3.2) for type I. By an application of Lemma 1.4, proving (4.1) can be reduced to considering affine thin sets of type II, which we turn to next in §4.2.

We defer discussing works that improved the baseline bound (4.1) (namely [Mun09], [Bon21], [BP24], [BPW25]), and the recent resolution of Conjecture 4.1 by [BCS+25] in nearly all cases, to §4.3, as all these results rely on progress in the analogous affine setting.

#### Remark 4.2 (Deduction of (3.4)).

Serre made the following observation to prove (3.4), as in [Ser97, p. 178 Thms. 3,4]. Suppose an irreducible variety $V\subsetneq\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ has $\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V=m\leq n-2$ and degree $d\geq 2$ . Select coordinates for $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ so that projection onto the first $m+1$ coordinates induces a finite morphism $\pi:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{m}$ of degree $d$ . The image $\pi(V(\mathbb{Q}))$ is then a projective thin set in $\mathbb{P}^{m}$ (arguing as in Lemma 2.6). Applying (4.1) then shows

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{m}}(\pi(V(\mathbb{Q})),B)\ll C(V)B^{(m+1)-1/2}(\log B)^{\gamma(V)}=C(V)B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V+1/2}(\log B)^{\gamma(V)}. $$

Each fibre of $\pi$ has a finite number of points, so this implies

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\leq C(V)B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V+1/2}(\log B)^{\gamma(V)}. $$

We end this section with a technical lemma, which shows that in order to prove Serre’s Conjecture 4.1 for a type II thin set $M$ defined according to a suitable morphism $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ , it is enough to prove it when $\pi$ is quasi-finite. (We will later assume this in Proposition 4.5.) We recall from Dfn. 29.20.1 part (3) and the equivalence in Lemma 29.20.10 of [Sta26, Section 01TC] that for schemes $X,Y$ , a morphism $f:X\rightarrow Y$ is quasi-finite precisely when $f$ is locally of finite type, quasi-compact, and has finite fibres.

#### Lemma 4.3.

Let $Z\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ be an irreducible projective variety of dimension $n-1$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ . Let $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ with generically finite fibres, be a dominant morphism of degree $d\geq 2$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ , so that $\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q}))$ is a thin set of type II in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ . Then there exists an open dense subset $U\subset Z$ such that $\left.\pi\right|_{U}:U\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ is a quasi-finite morphism, and

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q})),B)\leq N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(\left.\pi\right|_{U}(U(\mathbb{Q})),B)+O_{\pi}(B^{n-1}). $$

#### Proof.

Let $Z$ and $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ , a generically-finite dominant morphism, be as given. As recalled in §2.1, $\pi$ is locally of finite type. Since $\pi$ has generically finite fibres, we can find $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ and $U\subset Z$ open affine, dense subsets such that $\pi_{U}:=\left.\pi\right|_{U}:U\rightarrow V$ is finite. In particular, $\#\pi_{U}^{-1}(v)<\infty$ for every $v\in V$ . By Lemma 20.15.2 of [Sta26, Section 01T0], since $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ is locally of finite type, then for any open sets $U\subset Z$ and $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ , $\pi_{U}:U\rightarrow V$ is locally of finite type. By the remark immediately before the lemma, to conclude that $\pi_{U}$ is quasi-finite, it suffices to show that $\pi_{U}$ is quasi-compact: Since $U\subset Z$ is an affine subset and $Z$ is noetherian then $U$ is noetherian and hence $\pi_{U}$ is quasi compact thanks to [Sta26, Lemma $28.5.8$ ]. We may conclude that $\pi_{U}:U\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ is quasi-finite.

Now let $Z_{0}=Z\setminus U$ , and consider the image $\pi(Z_{0})$ . Since $Z_{0}$ does not contain the generic point of $Z$ , it follows that for some proper closed subset $W\subsetneq\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ , $\overline{\pi(Z_{0})}\subset W$ (arguing as in Lemma 2.6). Consequently,

$$ \begin{split}N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q})),B)&=N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(\pi(U(\mathbb{Q})),B)+N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(\pi(Z_{0}(\mathbb{Q})),B)\\
&\leq N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(\pi_{U}(U(\mathbb{Q})),B)+N_{\mathrm{proj}}(W,B)\\
&=N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(\pi(U(\mathbb{Q})),B)+O_{N,\deg W,\dim_{\mathbb{P}}W}(B^{n-1}),\end{split} $$

where in the last line we used the trivial bound of Lemma 3.1. Since $\deg W$ is inexplicit, we write the last term as $O_{\pi}(B^{n-1}).$ ∎

### 4.2. Type II, affine

By Lemma 1.4, the baseline upper bound (4.1) is implied by the result that for any affine thin set $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ ,

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M,B)\leq C(M)B^{n-1/2}(\log B)^{\gamma(M)}. $$

This appears as [Ser97, Ch. 13 Thm. 1]. Recall from Lemma 1.2 that if $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ is an affine thin set of type II with corresponding dominant morphism $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}$ , with $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}Z=n$ and $\pi$ of degree $d\geq 2$ , such that $M\subset(\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q}))\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n})$ , there exists a proper closed subset $V\subsetneq Z$ and an irreducible polynomial $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ that is monic in $Y$ and has $\deg_{Y}F=d$ , such that

$$ M\subset\left(\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)\cup\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{$F(Y,\mathbf{x})=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$}\}\right). $$

Since $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V<n$ , it follows that $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)\leq n-1$ (arguing as in Lemma 2.6), so applying the trivial bound from Lemma 3.9 shows:

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V),B)\ll_{\deg\left.\pi\right|_{V},\dim_{\mathbb{A}}\left.\pi\right|_{V}}B^{n-1}\ll_{\pi}B^{n-1}. $$

(Here the dependence on $\pi$ is inexplicit since the degree of $V$ is inexplicit.) Consequently, the counting function

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B):=\{\bfx\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{$F(Y,\bfx)=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$}\} $$

is the essential object to prove (4.2) and to study $N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M,B)$ further.

The following example (for $d=2$ ) shows that (4.2) cannot essentially be improved (analogous to Example 3.11 in the affine type I case).

#### Example 4.4.

For a given integer $d\geq 2$ , let $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=Y^{d}-(X_{1}+\cdots+X_{n}).$ Then $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\gg_{n}B^{n-1/d}$ , since

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq z\leq nB\\
\text{$z$ a $d$th power}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n}=z\\
\mathbf{x}\in[-B,B]^{n}\end{subarray}}1\gg_{n}B^{1/d}\cdot B^{n-1}. $$

Thus, if the route to bounding $N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)$ is via the simplistic construction of a corresponding affine thin set $M^{\prime}$ via Lemma 1.4, in general no further progress below the baseline bound (4.1) can be made. Fortunately, a different passage from projective thin sets of type II to affine thin sets of type II can be devised (playing a role analogous to Proposition 3.12 in the type I setting).

#### Proposition 4.5.

Let $Z\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ be an irreducible projective variety of dimension $n-1$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ . Let $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ be a quasi-finite dominant morphism of degree $d\geq 2$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ , so that $\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q}))$ is a thin set of type II in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ . Then there exists a proper closed subset $V\subsetneq Z$ , a positive integer $e$ , and an irreducible polynomial $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ of the form

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{d}+Y^{d-1}f_{1}(\mathbf{X})+\cdots+f_{d}(\mathbf{X}), $$

in which each $f_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is homogeneous of degree $e\cdot i$ , such that

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q})),B)\leq N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)+N_{\mathrm{proj}}(\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V(\mathbb{Q})),B). $$

Thus

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q})),B)\leq N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)+O_{\pi}(B^{n-1}). $$

We will call $F$ the polynomial associated to the thin set $\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q}))$ .

This is [BCS+25, Lemma 2.4], which builds on ideas of [Bro03a, Lemma 3]. (Compare to the affine analogue in Lemma 1.2.) The last conclusion follows similarly to the argument of Lemma 2.6: since $V\subsetneq Z$ is a proper closed subset and $Z$ is irreducible so $\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V<\dim_{\mathbb{P}}Z$ , the trivial bound of Lemma 3.1 for counting points in a projective variety implies:

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V),B)\ll_{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V),\deg\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)+1}\ll_{\pi}B^{(n-2)+1}\ll_{\pi}B^{n-1}. $$

Since $\deg\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)$ is inexplicit, the dependence on $\pi$ is inexplicit.

To use Proposition 4.5 to prove Conjecture 4.1, it suffices to consider $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)$ in the special case that $F$ is absolutely irreducible, by the following lemma (analogous to Lemma 3.7 for type I thin sets).

#### Lemma 4.6.

Let $F(Y,\bfX)=Y^{d}+f_{1}(\bfX)Y^{d-1}+\cdots+f_{d}(\bfX)\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]$ . Suppose $F$ is irreducible but not absolutely irreducible. Then $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F}B^{n-1}$ .

A special case of this result (in which each $f_{i}$ is assumed to be homogeneous of degree $e\cdot i$ , for a fixed positive integer $e$ ) is stated in [BCS+25, Lemma 2.5] without proof; for clarity we provide a proof.

#### Proof.

For such $F$ , we can define a polynomial $\Delta_{F}(\bfX)\in\mathbb{Q}[\bfX]$ such that for every $\bfx\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ , $\Delta_{F}(\bfx)=\text{disc}(F(Y,\bfx))$ . Hence,

$$ F(Y,\bfx)\text{ is squarefree}\Longleftrightarrow\Delta_{F}(\bfx)\neq 0. $$

(Precisely $\Delta_{F}$ is the discriminant of $F$ over $\mathbb{Q}(\bfX)$ , i.e. $\text{Res}\left(F,\frac{\partial F}{\partial Y}\right)$ over $\mathbb{Q}(\bfX)$ , and $\deg\Delta_{F}(\mathbf{X})\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ as in [GKZ08, Ch. 13 Prop. 1.1].) Under the hypothesis that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , we claim $\Delta_{F}(\bfX)\not\equiv 0$ . By the Hilbert Irreducibility Theorem (see e.g. [Lan83, Ch. 9]), one can find $\bfx\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ such that $F(Y,\bfx)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , hence separable, and thus squarefree. For such $\bfx$ , $\Delta_{F}(\mathbf{x})\neq 0$ , and hence $\Delta_{F}(\bfX)\not\equiv 0$ , as claimed.

Assume furthermore $F$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ but not over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ we can write

$$ F(Y,\bfX)=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}G_{i}(Y,\bfX), $$

with $\ell\geq 2$ , where for every $i=1,...,\ell$ we have that $G_{i}(Y,\bfX)\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[Y,\bfX]\setminus\mathbb{Q}[Y,\bfX]$ , and $G_{i}$ irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Now assume $\bfx$ is such that $F(Y,\bfx)$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$ , so there exists $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $F(n,\bfx)=0$ . Since

$$ 0=F(n,\bfx)=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}G_{i}(n,\bfx), $$

there exists $k\in\{1,...,\ell\}$ such that $G_{k}(n,\bfx)=0$ . Since $G_{k}\not\in\mathbb{Q}[Y,\bfX]$ , we can find $\tau\in\text{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ such that $\tau(G_{k})\neq G_{k}$ . On the other hand, since $\tau(F(Y,\bfX))=F(Y,\bfX)$ it follows that $\tau(G_{k})=G_{j}$ for some $j\in\{1,...,\ell\}\setminus\{k\}$ . Hence, we have that

$$ 0=\tau(G_{k}(n,\bfx))=G_{j}(n,\bfx). $$

Since $n$ is a root of $G_{k}(Y,\bfx)$ and a root of $G_{j}(Y,\bfx)$ , it follows that $n$ is a double root of $F(Y,\bfx)$ , so that $\Delta_{F}(\bfx)=0$ . This shows that for every $\bfx\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ :

$$ F(Y,\bfx)=0\text{ is solvable over }\mathbb{Z}\Rightarrow\Delta_{F}(\bfx)=0. $$

Hence by the Schwartz-Zippel bound (Lemma 3.8),

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\leq\#\{\bfx\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\|\bfx\|\leq B,\quad\Delta_{F}(\bfx)=0\}\ll_{n,\deg F}B^{n-1}, $$

as claimed. ∎

#### 4.2.1. Progress via sieve methods

Several works have proved bounds, for polynomials $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ of special shape, which approach $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{F,\varepsilon}B^{n-1+\varepsilon}$ asymptotically as $n\rightarrow\infty$ . All of these works are united by the attribute that they used sieve methods: the power sieve, various types of polynomial sieve, and more complicated variants. For the special shape

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{r}-G(\mathbf{X}) $$

with $r\geq 2$ and $G$ a nonsingular homogeneous form with $\deg G=mr$ for some $m\geq 1$ , Munshi proved $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{F,\varepsilon}B^{n-1+1/n}(\log B)^{\frac{n-1}{n}}$ [Mun09]. (See [Bon21, Remark 1.1], which improved the main exponent to $n-1+1/(n+1)$ , and work of analogous strength over function fields by Bucur, Cojocaru, Lalín and Pierce [BCLP23].) Heath-Brown and Pierce [HBP12] improved this, showing that for $G(\mathbf{X})$ any polynomial $d\geq 3$ with nonsingular leading form,

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\leq C(F)\begin{cases}B^{n-1+\frac{n(8-n)+4}{6n+4}}(\log B)^{2},&2\leq n\leq 8\\
B^{n-1+\frac{1}{2n+10}}(\log B)^{2},&n=9\\
B^{n-1-\frac{(n-10)}{2n+10}}(\log B)^{2},&n\geq 10.\end{cases} $$

Note that for $n\geq 10$ , this upper bound takes the form $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\leq C(F)B^{n-1-\Delta_{n}}(\log B)^{2}$ for $\Delta_{n}\rightarrow 1/2$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ . Consider next the shape

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=g(Y)+G(\mathbf{X}) $$

for $g$ any polynomial of degree $r\geq 2$ in $\mathbb{Z}[Y]$ and any irreducible form $G\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ of degree $e\geq 2$ such that the projective hypersurface $V(F)$ defined by $F=0$ is nonsingular over $\mathbb{C}$ . For such $F$ , Bonolis obtained $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}}(\log B)^{\frac{n}{n+1}}$ [Bon21]. Consider a yet more general setting that does not separate the variables $Y$ and $\mathbf{X}$ : fix an integer $m\geq 2$ and integers $d,e\geq 1$ , and let

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{md}+Y^{m(d-1)}f_{1}(\mathbf{X})+\ldots+Y^{m}f_{d-1}(\mathbf{X})+f_{d}(\mathbf{X}), $$

in which for each $1\leq i\leq d$ , $f_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is a homogeneous form with $\deg f_{i}=m\cdot e\cdot i$ , and $f_{d}\not\equiv 0$ . Under the hypothesis that the weighted hypersurface $V(F(Y,\mathbf{X}))\subset\mathbb{P}(e,1,\ldots,1)$ defined by $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=0$ is nonsingular over $\mathbb{C}$ , Bonolis and Pierce proved

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{n,m,d,e}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{e(n)}B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}}(\log B)^{\frac{n}{n+1}} $$

for some integer $e(n)\geq 1$ [BP24]. If $m=1$ , that work obtained the same result, conditional on GRH. (For clarity, note that [BP24] stated this result with an implicit constant depending only on $n,m,d,e$ but independent of the maximum coefficient $\|F\|$ , but this was corrected in [BP26] to state that the implicit constant may depend (at most) polylogarithmically on $\|F\|$ ; thus (4.9) corrects [BP24, Thm. 1.1].) Most recently, in [BPW25] the authors of the present paper improved this result by removing the nonsingularity hypothesis: instead, the polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ need only be absolutely irreducible and satisfy an appropriate “nondegeneracy hypothesis” that assures that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ depends nontrivially on each of $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ after any linear change of variables; we provide details in §4.4.

As a consequence of Proposition 4.5, each of the results $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll B^{\alpha(n)}s(B)$ listed above implies a corresponding result $N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)\leq C(M)[B^{n-1}+B^{\alpha(n)}s(B)]$ for any projective thin set $M$ of type II whose associated polynomial $F$ , in the sense of Proposition 4.5, is of the relevant shape (4.5), (4.7), or (4.8).

#### 4.2.2. Affine result to resolve Conjecture 4.1

Buggenhout, Cluckers, Salberger, Santens and Vermeulen [BCS+25] have recently announced the resolution of Serre’s Conjecture 4.1 in nearly all cases. This is deduced by passing to the affine setting via Proposition 4.5, and considering any polynomial of the following form. For integers $n\geq 1$ , $d\geq 2$ , $e\geq 1$ , let

$$ F_{\mathrm{top}}(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{d}+Y^{d-1}f_{1}(\mathbf{X})+\cdots+Yf_{d-1}(\mathbf{X})+f_{d}(\mathbf{X}) $$

be an absolutely irreducible polynomial, in which each $f_{i}$ is homogeneous of degree $e\cdot i$ , so that $F_{\mathrm{top}}(Y^{e},\mathbf{X})$ is homogeneous of degree $de$ . Then consider any polynomial of the form

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=F_{\mathrm{top}}(Y,\mathbf{X})+F_{0}(Y,\mathbf{X}) $$

in which $F_{0}(Y^{e},\mathbf{X})$ has total degree strictly smaller than $de$ . For any polynomial $F$ of type (4.10), [BCS+25, Thm. 1.2] proves that for some absolute constant $\gamma$ , and for some $\kappa(n,d)$ ,

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{n,d}\|F\|^{\kappa(n,d)}\begin{cases}B^{n-1}&\text{if $d\geq 5$}\\
B^{n-1}(\log B)^{\gamma}&\text{if $d=4$}\\
B^{n-1+(2/\sqrt{d}-1)}(\log B)^{\gamma}&\text{if $d=2,3$.}\end{cases} $$

### 4.3. Type II, revisiting the projective setting

The work of Buggenhout, Cluckers, Salberger, Santens and Vermeulen [BCS+25, Thm. 1.1] resolves Serre’s question on counting points in projective thin sets of type II (Conjecture 4.1), in nearly all cases:

#### Theorem 4.7 (BCSSV).

Let $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ be a thin set of type II, with corresponding integral variety $X$ and morphism $\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ that is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ , quasi-finite, dominant and of degree $d\geq 2$ . Then for some absolute constant $\gamma$ ,

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)\ll_{\pi}\begin{cases}B^{n-1}&\text{if $d\geq 5$}\\
B^{n-1}(\log B)^{\gamma}&\text{if $d=4$}\\
B^{n-1+(2/\sqrt{d}-1)}(\log B)^{\gamma}&\text{if $d=2,3$.}\end{cases} $$

This is deduced by passing to the affine setting via Proposition 4.5, and finally applying (4.11). By Lemma 4.3, it suffices to consider the quasi-finite setting, and so the bound in Theorem 4.7 holds for any thin set of type II. It remains an open question to achieve the exponent of Conjecture 4.1 for $d=2,3$ , and further understand the dependence of the implicit constant on $\pi$ .

#### Remark 4.8 (Inexplicit bounds).

The $O_{\pi}(B^{n-1})$ term in the conclusion of Lemma 4.3 has inexplicit dependence on $\pi$ . This arises because the construction of the proper closed subset $W\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ in the proof of that lemma has inexplicit degree. (See also [BCS+25, Thm. 1.1], which alternatively uses Zariski’s Main Theorem in order to reduce to consideration of finite covers, also leading to an inexplicit conclusion.) Similarly, the degree of $V$ in Proposition 4.5 is inexplicit, leading to an $O_{\pi}(B^{n-1})$ term in that conclusion. Thus, even though the affine result (4.11) explicitly controls dependence on $\|F\|$ , the application in Theorem 4.7 has inexplicit dependence on $\pi$ .

### 4.4. Type II, revisiting the affine setting

By Example 4.4, in general the baseline affine upper bound (4.2) cannot be essentially improved in general. However, parallel to the type I setting of §3.4, it is reasonable to ask for the largest class of affine thin sets of type II for which the baseline upper bound can be improved to exponent $n-1$ , or analogously, the largest class of “allowable” polynomials $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ for which one can show

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\leq C(F)B^{n-1}s(B) $$

for a constant $C(F)$ and small factor $s(B)$ . By (4.11), any polynomial of the shape (4.10) belongs to this class, for $d\geq 4$ . Moreover, the results in (4.6) suggest it is an interesting question to characterize affine thin sets of type II for which an even better upper bound holds. Finally, it is also interesting to study uniformity questions related to the factor $C(F)$ .

Our recent work [BPW25] advanced the first line of inquiry. There, we described a large class of polynomials $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ , for which

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{\varepsilon}C(F)B^{n-1+\delta_{n}+\varepsilon}, $$

for $\delta_{n}=1/(n+1)$ , so that this result approaches (4.12) as $n\rightarrow\infty$ . Let us state what makes a polynomial “allowable” more precisely, using the terminology of [BPW25]. First, consider absolutely irreducible polynomials of the form

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{md}+Y^{m(d-1)}f_{1}(\mathbf{X})+\cdots+Y^{m}f_{d-1}(\mathbf{X})+f_{d}(\mathbf{X}), $$

for some integers $m,d\geq 1$ with $md\geq 2$ . No homogeneity condition or degree condition is placed on the polynomials $f_{j}$ , so that this class is larger than the class (4.10).

Let $L$ be a finite (nontrivial) extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ . We say $L$ is an $n$ -genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ if for every $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ such that $L=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X})),$ $G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ has nonzero degree in each of $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ . We say an absolutely irreducible polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ that is monic in $Y$ and has $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ is $(1,n)$ -allowable if for every linear change of variables $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ , the polynomial $F_{\sigma}(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}):=F(Y,\sigma(\mathbf{X}))$ has the property that $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is an $n$ -genuine extension. For every polynomial $F$ in the class (4.14) for $m\geq 2$ that is $(1,n)$ -allowable, [BPW25, Thm. 1.2] proves (4.13) with $C(F)\ll_{n,m,\deg F}\|F\|^{\kappa(n)}$ depending at most polynomially on $\|F\|$ . (If $m=1$ , the same result holds if GRH is assumed.) For each fixed $m\geq 1$ , $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials are generic among polynomials of the form (4.14), by [BPW25, Cor. 3.2].

The dependence on $\|F\|$ can be reduced if a stronger nondegeneracy assumption is made. Precisely, we say that a finite (nontrivial) extension $L$ of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ if for all subextensions $L^{\prime}$ satisfying $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq L^{\prime}\subset L,$ $L^{\prime}$ is an $n$ -genuine extension. We say that an absolutely irreducible polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ that is monic in $Y$ and has $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable if for every linear change of variables $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ , the polynomial $F_{\sigma}(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}):=F(Y,\sigma(\mathbf{X}))$ has the property that $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension. For $F$ in the class (4.14) for $m\geq 2$ that is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable, [BPW25, Thm. 1.3] proves (4.13) with $C(F)\ll_{n,m,\deg F}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{\kappa(n)}$ . (If $m=1$ , the same result holds if GRH is assumed.) This relies on uniformity results for trace functions recently obtained in [BKW25]. For each fixed $m\geq 1$ , strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials are generic among polynomials of the form (4.14), by [BPW25, Cor. 3.2].

By different methods, for any polynomial $F$ that is $(1,n)$ -allowable but not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable, [BPW25, Thm. 1.4] attains the stronger bound (4.12), but now with $C(F)$ depending on $\|F\|$ in an unspecified way. It remains an interesting open problem to characterize those polynomials for which (4.12) holds.

#### Remark 4.9.

We remark on an underlying similarity between the notion of nondegeneracy encapsulated by $(1,n)$ -allowability here, and the notion in §3.4 of NCC (not cylindrical over a curve) for a polynomial $f$ . Here, requiring a polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ to be $(1,n)$ -allowable excludes the possibility that a $\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ change of variables reduces the number of variables; compare to Remark 3.18.

This completes our survey of recent results on counting points in thin sets.

## 5. Revisiting Serre’s large sieve argument

In the remainder of the paper, we focus on questions of dependence and uniformity, in the setting of affine thin sets of type II. In this section, we show that Serre’s original large sieve argument to prove the baseline bound in Theorem 1.3, in particular for affine thin sets of type II, can be refined to control the dependence of $C(M)$ , in some cases. Additionally, we clarify the role of Dedekind zeta functions and GRH, building on [Ser97, §3.2]. Our main result in this section is:

#### Theorem 5.1.

Let $n\geq 2$ be fixed. Let $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ of total degree $D$ be absolutely irreducible and of the form

$$ F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})=Y^{md}+Y^{m(d-1)}f_{1}(\mathbf{X})+\cdots+Y^{m}f_{d-1}(\mathbf{X})+f_{d}(\mathbf{X}), $$

for a given integer $m\geq 2$ . Then for some $c(n)\geq 1$ ,

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{c(n)}B^{n-1/2}\log(B+2)\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$.} $$

If $m=1$ and $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ , the same result holds, conditional on GRH for a single Dedekind zeta function.

Serre’s original argument does not specify the dependence on $\|F\|$ , but it improves the $\log B$ factor to $(\log B)^{\gamma(F)}$ for some $\gamma(F)<1$ . Including those additional steps from Serre’s argument with our presentation of the $m=1$ case will lead to this same log factor in Theorem 5.1 (see §5.2 and Remark 5.5).

The proof relies on both the large sieve and the Lang-Weil bound, which we recall in the affine form stated in [BPW25, Lemma 2.4]:

#### Lemma 5.2.

Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{k}]$ have degree $d$ (not necessarily homogeneous) and let $p$ be a prime such that the affine variety $\{F(\mathbf{X})=0\}\subset\mathbb{A}^{k}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ of dimension $k-1$ is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ . Then

$$ \#\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k}:F(\mathbf{x})=0\}=p^{k-1}+O_{k,d}(p^{k-1-1/2}). $$

We also require a standard consequence of Noether’s Lemma, which we quote from [BPW25, Lemma 2.9].

#### Lemma 5.3.

Let $F(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ have degree $D\geq 1$ . If $F$ is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , then there exists a finite set $\mathcal{E}$ of exceptional primes with $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ such that for $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ , the reduction of $F$ modulo $p$ is again of degree $D$ and is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ .

Now we turn to the proof of Theorem 5.1. Initially, let $m\geq 1$ be fixed. For simplicity, we assume $\|F\|\geq 3$ , $B\geq 3$ in what follows. As Serre states, a formulation of the large sieve in [Ser97, §12.1] (specialized to the case $K=\mathbb{Q}$ ) shows that

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\leq 2^{n}(B^{n}+Q^{2n})/L(Q) $$

where $L(Q)$ is a sum over squarefree integers defined by

$$ L(Q)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq Q,\\
\text{squarefree}\end{subarray}}\prod_{p\mid q}\frac{\omega_{p}}{1-\omega_{p}}, $$

in which $\omega_{p}$ is defined by

$$ 1-\omega_{p}=\frac{|N_{p}(F)|}{p^{n}}, $$

and

$$ N_{p}(F):=\#\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}:\exists y\in\mathbb{F}_{p},F(y,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0\;\text{in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$}\}. $$

Choose $Q=B^{1/2}$ to balance the two main terms in (5.2); to prove the proposition, it suffices to show that $L(Q)\gg Q/\log Q$ , and to quantify any dependence on $\|F\|$ . By positivity, we may bound $L(Q)$ below by restricting the sum over $q\leq Q$ to any convenient nonempty set of primes $p\in[Q/2,Q]$ ; the task is then to produce a lower bound for $\omega_{p}$ for each prime in this set.

We make a preliminary observation. For any prime $p$ , define

$$ M_{p}(F):=\#\{(y,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n+1}:F(y,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0\;\text{in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$}\}. $$

By Lemma 5.3, aside from a set $\mathcal{E}$ of at most $\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ exceptional primes, the reduction of $F$ modulo $p$ is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ . For each $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ , the Lang-Weil bound (Lemma 5.2) implies $M_{p}(F)=p^{n}+O_{n,D}(p^{n-1/2}).$ In particular, for all $p\gg_{n,D}1$ with $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ , $M_{p}(F)\geq 1$ , so that $N_{p}(F)\geq 1$ and hence $\frac{\omega_{p}}{1-\omega_{p}}$ is finite. In the main arguments that follow, we will only consider $B$ sufficiently large so that this lower bound holds for a positive proportion of primes $p\in[Q/2,Q]$ , when $Q=B^{1/2}$ .

### 5.1. The case $m\geq 2$

We first restrict our attention to the case in which $m\geq 2$ in the assumed shape (5.1) of the polynomial $F$ . We can prove a lower bound for $L(Q)$ by only considering primes $p\in[Q/2,Q]$ such that $p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;m)$ . For each such prime, we now focus on proving a lower bound for $\omega_{p}$ . Write $N_{p}(F)=N_{p}^{\prime}(F)+N_{p}^{\prime\prime}(F)$ where the first term is the contribution from those $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ such that $f_{d}(\mathbf{x})=0$ , and the second term is those such that $f_{d}(\mathbf{x})\neq 0$ , in which case any solution $y$ to $F(Y,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0$ must have $y\neq 0$ . By the trivial bound (Lemma 3.8 over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ ), $N_{p}^{\prime}(F)\ll_{D}p^{n-1}$ . On the other hand, if $f_{d}(\mathbf{x})\neq 0$ , $y$ is a nonzero solution in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ to $F(Y,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0$ and $\gamma$ is a primitive $m$ -th root of unity in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , then $y,\gamma y,\ldots,\gamma^{m-1}y$ provide $m$ distinct solutions to the equation. This yields the essential relation $M_{p}(F)\geq mN_{p}^{\prime\prime}(F)$ , with $M_{p}(F)$ as defined above. With the exceptional set $\mathcal{E}$ as defined above, for each $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ with $p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;m)$ ,

$$ N_{p}^{\prime\prime}(F)\leq\frac{1}{m}M_{p}(F)=\frac{1}{m}(p^{n}+O_{n,D}(p^{n-1/2})). $$

For such $p$ , by construction

$$ \omega_{p}=1-\frac{|N_{p}^{\prime}(F)|}{p^{n}}-\frac{|N_{p}^{\prime\prime}(F)|}{p^{n}}\geq 1-\frac{1}{m}+O_{D}(p^{-1})+O_{n,m,D}(p^{-1/2})\gg_{m}1, $$

as long as $p\gg_{n,m,D}1$ . By the Siegel-Walfisz theorem for primes in arithmetic progressions, for all $Q\gg_{m}1$ sufficiently large, $\#\{p\in[Q/2,Q]:p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;m)\}\gg_{m}Q/\log Q$ . We can guarantee that at least half, say, of these lie outside the finite exceptional set $\mathcal{E}$ as long as $Q\gg_{n,m,D}(\log\|F\|)(\log\log\|F\|)$ . Consequently, by positivity, for such $Q$ ,

$$ \displaystyle L(Q) \displaystyle\geq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\leq Q\;\text{prime}\\
p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;m)\end{subarray}}\frac{\omega_{p}}{1-\omega_{p}}\gg_{m}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in[Q/2,Q]\setminus\mathcal{E}\\
p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;m)\end{subarray}}\omega_{p} \displaystyle\gg_{m}\#\{p\in[Q/2,Q]\setminus\mathcal{E}:p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;m)\}\gg_{m}Q/\log Q. $$

This proves the claimed lower bound for $L(Q)$ for all $Q\gg_{n,D}(\log\|F\|)(\log\log\|F\|)$ , and hence $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{n,D}B^{n-1/2}\log B$ has been proved if $B\gg_{n,D}(\log\|F\|)^{2}(\log\log\|F\|)^{2}$ , and so certainly for $B\gg_{n,D}(\log\|F\|)^{3}$ , say. On the other hand, for $B\ll(\log\|F\|)^{3}$ , we may apply the trivial bound $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{n}B^{n}\ll(\log\|F\|)^{3n}.$ In total,

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{n,D}(\log\|F\|)^{c(n)}B^{n-1/2}\log B\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$,} $$

in which $c(n)=3n$ suffices, and the theorem is proved in the case $m=2$ .

### 5.2. The case $m=1$

In the case that $m=1$ we must impose that $d\geq 2$ in (5.1), so the morphism $\pi:V(F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}))\rightarrow(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ has degree at least 2. Now if $m=1$ the relation (5.5) no longer suffices to imply $\omega_{p}\gg_{m}1$ . Instead, the argument of Serre in [Ser97, §13.3] proceeds via [Ser97, §13.1 Thm. 5], which we record with additional attention to uniformity:

#### Lemma 5.4.

Let $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be an absolutely irreducible polynomial of total degree $D>1$ . There is a constant $c=c(n,D)$ with $0<c<1$ , an exceptional set $\mathcal{E}$ with $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ , and a finite Galois extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$ such that if $p$ splits completely in $K$ and $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ , then

$$ |N_{p}(F)|=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}:\exists y\in\mathbb{F}_{p},F(y,\mathbf{x})=0\}\leq cp^{n}+O_{n,D}(p^{n-1/2}). $$

Moreover, $2\leq[K:\mathbb{Q}]\ll_{n,D}1$ and $\log|\mathrm{Disc}K/\mathbb{Q}|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|$ .

#### Remark 5.5.

In fact, Serre shows one may take $c=1-1/r!$ where $2\leq r\leq[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ . (In the notation of the argument presented below, $r=[K(Z):K(X_{1},...,X_{n})]\leq[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ .) Let $c^{*}=1/c-1$ . Serre presents an argument to improve the factor $\log B$ in Theorem 5.1 to $(\log B)^{\gamma(F)}$ for $\gamma(F)=1-\lambda(F)$ , in which $\lambda(F):=c^{*}/[K:\mathbb{Q}]>0$ ; see [Ser97, p. 182-183].

#### Proof.

We elaborate on Serre’s proof in order to quantify dependence on $\|F\|$ . Let $Z=V(F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}))$ denote the vanishing set of $F$ , and let $D$ denote the total degree of $F$ . Then define $K(Z)$ to be the function field of $Z$ ; this a finite field extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})$ of degree $\ll_{n,D}1$ . Take $\Omega$ to be the Galois closure of $K(Z)$ over $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ . Define $K$ to be the integral closure of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\Omega$ and $Z_{\Omega}$ the normalization of $Z$ in $\Omega$ . In particular, $2\leq[K:\mathbb{Q}]\ll_{n,D}1$ since $\deg F\geq 2.$

Now, we want to take an open subscheme $U\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ such that $U_{Z}/U$ and $U_{Z_{\Omega}}/U$ are finite and étale. We write $U_{Z_{\Omega}}$ as $U_{\Omega}$ for simplicity. In particular, viewing $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})$ as a polynomial in $Y$ , we have that $U=\{\disc(F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}))\neq 0\}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}.$ Now we note that the defining polynomial equations of $U$ will have degree bounded by $n$ and $D$ . As a result, $U_{Z}$ and $U_{\Omega}$ will also be defined by polynomials of degree bounded by $n$ and $D$ . Additionally, the field of constants of $U_{\Omega}$ is $K$ , so $U_{\Omega}$ is absolutely irreducible over $K$ .

Let $p$ be a prime; by Noether’s Lemma 5.3, apart from an exceptional set $\mathcal{E}$ with $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ , $U_{\Omega,p}=U_{\Omega}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ will be absolutely irreducible. As a consequence of Lang-Weil (Lemma 5.2),

$$ |U_{\Omega}(\mathbb{F}_{p})|=p^{n}+O_{n,D}(p^{n-1/2}), $$

where furthermore the explicit dependencies on $n$ and $D$ can be described by

$$ |U_{\Omega}(\mathbb{F}_{p})|=\sum_{i}\pm\lambda_{i}(p). $$

Here $\lambda_{i}(p)$ are the eigenvalues of the Frobenius map at $p$ acting on $\ell$ -adic cohomology with compact support, $\lambda_{i}(p)=\pm p^{n}$ for exactly one value of $i$ , $|\lambda_{i}(p)|\leq p^{n-1/2}$ for all other values of $i$ , and the number of such eigenvalues is $\leq C(n,D)$ ; the constant $C(n,D)$ is described in [Bom78, Theorem 1]. Now, following identically the rest of the proof given by Serre,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}:\exists y\in\mathbb{F}_{p},F(y,\mathbf{x})=0\}\leq(1-\frac{1}{[K:\mathbb{Q}]!})p^{n}+O_{n,D}(p^{n-1/2}). $$

Finally, we claim that $\log|\textrm{Disc}(K/\mathbb{Q})|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|.$ To see this, consider the discriminant $\textrm{Disc}(\Omega/\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n}))$ as an algebraic function in $X_{1},...,X_{n}.$ If $\alpha_{1}(X_{1},...,X_{n}),...,\alpha_{D}(X_{1},...,X_{n})$ are the roots of $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})$ , then $\Omega=\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})(\alpha_{1}(X_{1},...,X_{n}),...,\alpha_{D}(X_{1},...,X_{n})).$ Consequently $\textrm{Disc}(\Omega/\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n}))$ is a polynomial of degree $\ll_{n,D}1$ in terms of the $\alpha_{i}(X_{1},...,X_{n})$ . Additionally, these algebraic functions $\alpha_{i}(X_{1},...,X_{n})$ satisfy that for any choice of $(x_{1},...,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}$ such that $\alpha_{i}(x_{1},...,x_{n})$ is a well-defined value in $\mathbb{C}$ , we have that

$$ \log\|\alpha_{i}(x_{1},...,x_{n})\|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|+\log\|(x_{1},...,x_{n})\|. $$

(This follows from the fact that the coefficients of the polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})$ will be symmetric polynomials of the roots $\alpha_{i}(X_{1},...,X_{n})$ .) Thus for any $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}$ ,

$$ \log|\textrm{Disc}(\Omega/\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n}))(x_{1},...,x_{n})|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|+\log\|(x_{1},...,x_{n})\|. $$

Since $K$ is the integral closure of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\Omega$ , this implies that $\log|\textrm{Disc}(K/\mathbb{Q})|\leq_{n,D}\log\|F\|.$

∎

As a consequence of the lemma, for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ , the quantity $\omega_{p}$ defined in (5.4) satisfies

$$ \omega_{p}\geq 1-c+O_{n,D}(p^{-1/2})\geq c^{\prime}>0 $$

where $c^{\prime}=c^{\prime}(n,D)$ , as long as $p\gg_{n,D}1$ . Then in the expression (5.3) for $L(Q)$ , by restricting the sum to such primes, as long as $Q\gg_{n,D}1$ ,

$$ L(Q)\geq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in[Q/2,Q]\setminus\mathcal{E}\\
\text{p splits completely in $K$}\end{subarray}}\frac{\omega_{p}}{1-\omega_{p}}\geq c^{\prime}\#\{p\in[Q/2,Q]\setminus\mathcal{E},\text{$p$ splits completely in $K$}\}. $$

Let $G=\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$ (in the notation of Lemma 5.4). By the Chebotarev density theorem in the form of [LO77, Thm. 1.1.] as refined in [Ser81, Thm. 4], if the Dedekind zeta function $\zeta_{K}(s)$ of the finite Galois extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$ constructed in Lemma 5.4 satisfies the Riemann Hypothesis, then for every $Q\geq 2$ ,

$$ |\#\{p\leq Q:\text{$p$ splits completely in $K$}\}-\frac{1}{|G|}\frac{Q}{\log Q}|\ll_{n,|G|}Q^{1/2}(\log Q+\log|\mathrm{Disc}(K/\mathbb{Q})|). $$

By Lemma 5.4, $|G|\ll_{n,D}1$ and $\log|\mathrm{Disc}(K/\mathbb{Q})|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|.$ Thus as long as $Q\gg_{n,D}(\log\|F\|)^{2+\varepsilon_{0}}$ for some $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ , both $|\mathcal{E}|$ and the remainder term above can be made at most $(1/4)|G|^{-1}Q/\log Q$ in absolute value. Applying this in (5.6) shows that $L(Q)\gg_{n,D}Q/\log Q$ for $Q\gg_{n,D}(\log\|F\|)^{2+\varepsilon_{0}}$ . Inserting this in (5.2) and recalling $Q=B^{1/2}$ shows that

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{n,D}B^{n-1/2}\log B $$

for $B\gg_{n,D}(\log\|F\|)^{5}$ , say. As before in the case $m\geq 2$ , this estimate can be rephrased as the conclusion of Theorem 5.1 by including a factor of $(\log\|F\|)^{5n}$ , say.

### 5.3. The role of GRH

Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ be as in (5.1) for a given integer $m\geq 1$ . Both Serre’s large sieve approach to bounding $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)$ and the polynomial sieve approach that we have developed in [BP24] and [BPW25], depend on counting solutions to $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , and therefore depend on finding sufficiently many primes with a certain property. When $m=1$ (so that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is simply monic in $Y$ ), this introduces a role for GRH in both proofs, but in somewhat different ways.

The case of $m=1$ in Theorem 5.1, as argued here, only requires assuming GRH for one Dedekind zeta function (of the Galois extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$ constructed in Lemma 5.4). Instead of the full strength of GRH in (5.7) it would suffice to know the weaker property that the right-hand side of (5.7) can be replaced by $c_{|G|}Q/\log Q$ for a sufficiently small effective constant $c_{|G|}$ . (This is equivalent to proving effective control of the possible Siegel zero of the Dedekind zeta function $\zeta_{K}(s)$ in the error term of the Chebotarev density theorem in this case; see e.g. [BP24, Eqn. (3.6)]. It would even be sufficient to prove this in some average sense, over primes $p\in[Q/2,Q]$ .)

In comparison, the conditional version of the polynomial sieve stated in [BPW25, Lemma 6.1] when $m=1$ assumes that GRH holds for a large collection of Dedekind zeta functions (each associated to some $\bfk\in[-2B,2B]^{n}$ , in the proof provided in [BP24, §3.2]). As $B\rightarrow\infty$ , this formulation of the polynomial sieve assumes GRH for the Dedekind zeta functions of potentially infinitely many fields. See [BPW25, Remark 7.3] for an alternative formulation of the conditional polynomial sieve (when $m=1$ ) that replaces the assumption of GRH with an average statement, also still unknown.

## 6. An unconditional polylog estimate

In this section, we consider polynomials that have constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ . That is to say,

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=c_{D}Y^{D}+Y^{D-1}f_{1}(\mathbf{X})+\cdots+f_{D}(\mathbf{X}), $$

for an integer $c_{D}\neq 0$ ; this of course includes all polynomials that are monic in $Y$ . We now describe an unconditional method to bound $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)$ as in the baseline bound (1.9), with at most polylog dependence on $\|F\|$ .

#### Theorem 6.1.

Fix an integer $n\geq 1$ . Let $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]$ be irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]$ of total degree $D$ , with $\deg_{Y}(F)\geq 2$ , and assume that $F$ has constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ . Then for some $e(n)\geq 1$ ,

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{e(n)}B^{n-\frac{1}{2}}(\log(B+2))^{e(n)}\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$.} $$

Note that to prove the theorem, we may assume that $\deg_{X_{i}}F(Y,\mathbf{X})\geq 1$ for some $i=1,\ldots,n$ . For indeed, suppose $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\deg_{Y}(F)\geq 2$ while $\deg_{X_{i}}F=0$ for all $i=1,\ldots,n$ . Then $F(Y,\mathbf{x})=F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ for every $\bfx\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ , so that $F(Y,\bfx)$ is never solvable over $\ZZ$ since by hypothesis $F$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , and consequently $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)=0$ .

The proof of the theorem originates in [BPW25, Thm. 2.13], but we report it here to clarify how it inherits (at most) polylogarithmic dependence on $\|F\|$ from a recent result of Cluckers et al, on effective Hilbert’s Irreducibility Theorem, obtained via the determinant method.

#### Theorem 6.2 ([CDH+23, Theorem 1.10]).

Let $F(T,X_{1},...,X_{m})\in\mathbb{Z}[T,X_{1},...,X_{m}]$ be irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[T,X_{1},...,X_{m}]$ with $d=\deg_{\mathbf{X}}(F)\geq 1$ . For each integer $B\geq 1$ define

$$ R_{T}(F,B)=\{t\in\mathbb{Z}\cap[-B,B]:\text{$F(t,X_{1},\ldots,X_{m})$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{m}]$}\}. $$

Then there is a constant $h(m)>0$ depending only on $m$ such that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ R_{T}(F,B)\ll_{m}2^{h(m)d}d^{h(m)}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{h(m)}B^{1/2}. $$

Note that if $\deg_{T}(F)=0$ , then the hypothesis that $F(T,X_{1},\ldots,X_{m})=F(X_{1},\ldots,X_{m})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ is independent of specializing $T=t$ to any value $t$ . In this case the set $R_{T}(F,B)$ is empty for all $B$ , and the theorem is vacuously true. Note also that the theorem does not require $F$ to be monic, or even constant-leading-coefficient, in $T$ .

To deduce Theorem 6.1, we start by observing that, since $\deg_{Y}(F)\geq 2$ ,

$$ \#\{\bfx\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{$F(Y,\bfx)=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$}\}\\
\leq\#\{\bfx\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{$F(Y,\bfx)=0$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$}\}. $$

It thus suffices to prove:

#### Proposition 6.3.

Fix an integer $n\geq 1$ . Let $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]$ be irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]$ of total degree $D$ , with degree $\deg_{Y}(F)\geq 1$ , and assume that $F$ has constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ . Then for some $e(n)\geq 1$ ,

$$ \#\{\bfx\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{$F(Y,\bfx)=0$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$}\}\\
\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{e(n)}B^{n-1/2}(\log B)^{e(n)}. $$

Similar to various remarks above, for each $n\geq 1$ it suffices to prove this when $\deg_{\mathbf{X}}F\geq 1$ , since if $F$ is independent of $\mathbf{X}$ the set on the left-hand side must be empty.

If $n=1$ , then we may apply Theorem 6.2 to $F(Y,X_{1})$ with $t$ playing the role of $x_{1}$ . (Since $F$ is constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ , observe that $\deg_{Y}F\geq 1$ , as required.) Consequently,

$$ \#\{x_{1}\in[-B,B]\cap\mathbb{Z}:\text{$F(Y,x_{1})=0$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$}\}\ll_{D}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{h(1)}B^{1/2}. $$

From now on, let $n\geq 2$ , and we proceed by induction on the number $n$ of variables. Let us now assume that for any polynomial $G\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1}]$ that is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1}]$ and of $\deg_{Y}(G)\geq 1$ with constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ , the following inductive hypothesis holds:

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in[-B,B]^{n-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}:\text{$G(Y,\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$}\}\\
\ll_{n,\deg G}(\log(\|G\|+2))^{e(n-1)}B^{(n-1)-1/2}, $$

for some $e(n-1)$ .

Suppose $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ satisfies the hypotheses of the proposition. We split up the count according to those $x_{n}$ such that $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is reducible/irreducible, and in the first case we apply Theorem 6.2 with $t$ playing the role of $x_{n}$ . (It may be that $\deg_{X_{n}}F=0$ , but recall that Theorem 6.2 is also applicable in this case.) This leads to:

$$ \#\{x_{n}\in[-B,B]\cap\mathbb{Z}:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}]$}\}\\
\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{h(n)}B^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Now if $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}]$ , then $F(Y,x_{1},...,x_{n-1},x_{n})$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$ for any choice of $x_{1},...,x_{n-1}$ , so we count these trivially. Hence the overall contribution to (6.1) of the $x_{n}\in[-B,B]\cap\mathbb{Z}$ such that $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is reducible is bounded by

$$ \ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{h(n)}B^{(n-1)+\frac{1}{2}}\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{h(n)}B^{n-\frac{1}{2}}, $$

which is acceptable.

On the other hand, suppose $x_{n}\in[-B,B]\cap\mathbb{Z}$ is fixed and $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}]$ . To apply the inductive step, observe that $\deg_{Y}F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})\geq 1,$ since $F$ has constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ . Then by the inductive hypothesis,

$$ \#\{\bfx^{\prime}\in[-B,B]^{n-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}:\text{$F(Y,\bfx^{\prime},x_{n})$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$}\}\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F_{x_{n}}\|+2))^{e(n-1)}B^{n-1-\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Here $\|F_{x_{n}}\|$ denotes the norm of the polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ and satisfies the relation

$$ \log(\|F_{x_{n}}\|+2)\ll_{n,D}\log(\|F\|+2)+\log B. $$

The number of $x_{n}$ which lead to this case is trivially at most $\ll B$ , so the overall contribution from all $x_{n}$ for which $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}]$ is $\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2)+\log B)^{e(n-1)}B^{n-\frac{1}{2}}$ .

In total, this argument has proved that for all $B\geq 1$ , the conclusion of the proposition holds, with $e(n)=\max\{h(n),e(n-1)\}.$ This completes the proof of the proposition, and hence of Theorem 6.1.

## 7. A question about uniformity

Recall from §3 that a distinctive achievement in the study of thin sets of type I is that many results are uniform; see Theorems 3.15 and 3.16. In light of this, it is tempting to ask whether a similar phenomenon holds for thin sets of type II. That is, should a uniform version of Conjecture 4.1 be true for projective thin sets of type II? Or, in the affine setting, should a uniform bound $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll_{n,D}B^{n-1}s(B)$ hold for all $F$ in some suitable class of polynomials, and an appropriate choice of “small factor” $s(B)?$ In this section, we demonstrate that the latter question appears to be subtle, and to have different features from known results in the type I setting.

### 7.1. A restricted counting function

First, it is illuminating to introduce temporarily a restricted counting function that avoids an essential feature of the type II setting. Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ be a polynomial of the form (4.8) or (4.10), so that it is weighted homogeneous with weights $(e,1,\ldots,1)$ , or has top degree polynomial $F_{\mathrm{top}}$ that is weighted homogeneous with weights $(e,1,\ldots,1)$ . Recall the counting function $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)$ for the associated affine thin set of type II, as in (4.3). Define now the restricted count

$$ [N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}]_{\mathrm{res}}(F;B^{e},B):=\{y\in[-B^{e},B^{e}]\cap\mathbb{Z},\bfx\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:F(y,\bfx)=0\}. $$

Thus this restricts to solutions with $|y|\leq B^{e}$ , in contrast to the count $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)$ , which a priori allows $|y|\ll\|F\|B^{e}$ . In this sense, the restricted count attempts to mimic the type I setting, in which all variables are governed only by the parameter $B$ .

The methods of [BP24] can be applied to prove

$$ [N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}]_{\mathrm{res}}(F;B^{e},B)\ll_{n,m,d,e}B^{n-1+1/(n+1)}(\log B)^{n/(n+1)}, $$

with implicit constant independent of $\|F\|$ . But for the original count $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)$ , polylogarithmic dependence on $\|F\|$ cannot be ruled out by those methods; this is explained in the correction [BP26].

The restricted count can nevertheless be a useful tool for studying the original count, but at the cost of introducing polynomial dependence on $\|F\|$ . Indeed, for any polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ of the class (4.10), [BCS+25, Thm. 1.3] proved that for some absolute constant $\gamma$ ,

$$ [N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}]_{\mathrm{res}}(F;B^{e},B)\ll_{n,d}\begin{cases}B^{n-1}&\text{if $d\geq 5$}\\
B^{n-1}(\log B)^{\gamma}&\text{if $d=4$}\\
B^{n-1+(2/\sqrt{d}-1)}(\log B)^{\gamma}&\text{if $d=2,3$,}\end{cases} $$

with implicit constant independent of $\|F\|$ . There exists a combinatorial constant $c_{n,d,e}$ such that

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll[N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}]_{\mathrm{res}}(F;c_{n,d,e}\|F\|B^{e},B). $$

Therefore, the uniform bound for the restricted count immediately implies the bound (4.11) for the original count, with polynomial dependence on $\|F\|$ . To achieve at most polylogarithmic dependence on $\|F\|$ in a bound for $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)$ , different methods must be employed, such as in [BPW25].

### 7.2. Examples that fail certain uniform upper bounds

We now demonstrate via counterexamples that a particular shape of conjectural uniform bound for $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)$ for affine thin sets of type II can be false; this requires specifying the small factor $s(B)$ as well. (For clarity, we note that [Ser97] did not address uniformity questions, and there is no contradiction to statements there.)

#### Example 7.1 (Sums of two squares).

Consider the affine thin set $M_{k}$ defined for a given integer $k$ by

$$ M_{k}=\{x_{1}\in\mathbb{Z}:\exists y\in\mathbb{Z}:y^{2}+x_{1}^{2}-k=0\}\subset\mathbb{A}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}). $$

For $B\geq k^{1/2}$ ,

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}(M_{k},B)=\tfrac{1}{2}r(k), $$

where $r(k)$ is the number of representations of $k$ as the sum of two squares. If $k$ is squarefree, we can compute $r(k)$ explicitly as

$$ r(k)=4\cdot 2^{\omega(k)}, $$

if every prime divisor $p|k$ has $p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;4)$ , and $r(k)=0$ otherwise; see for example [MW06, Theorem 2.5]. In particular, if we define

$$ k=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\leq\log B\\
p\equiv 1\bmod 4\end{subarray}}p, $$

then note that $k\sim B^{1/2}$ as $B\rightarrow\infty$ , and $\omega(k)\sim\tfrac{1}{2}\log B/\log\log B$ , by the Siegel-Walfisz theorem. Consequently we can calculate that as $B\rightarrow\infty,$

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}(M_{k},B)=2^{\frac{\log B}{\log\log B}(1/2+o(1))}. $$

A uniform version of Conjecture 4.1 for thin sets of type II in $\mathbb{A}^{1}$ with polylogarithmic small factor, say $s(B)\ll(\log B)^{c}$ , would ask whether for some constant $c$ ,

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}(M_{k},B)=O((\log B)^{c}) $$

holds independent of the choice of $k$ . This fails as $B\rightarrow\infty$ , by (7.4). However, we observe that a putative uniform bound of the form

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}(M_{k},B)=O_{\varepsilon}(B^{\varepsilon}) $$

is not violated by this example.

#### Example 7.2 (A multi-dimensional generalization).

Define for a given integer $k$ the affine thin set

$$ M_{k}=\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}:y^{2}+x_{1}^{2}-k(x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n})=0\}. $$

(Note that in the terminology of [BPW25], while $F_{k}(y,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}):=y^{2}+x_{1}^{2}-k(x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n})$ is a polynomial in $n+1$ variables, it is not a $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomial.) For $B\gg k$ , we see that

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M_{k},B)\gg\sum_{(x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\in[-B,B]^{n-1}}r(k(x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n}))\gg B^{n-2}\sum_{|z|\ll B}r(kz). $$

Here $r(k)$ again denotes the number of representations of $k$ as the sum of two squares. Now, $r(k)$ is not a totally multiplicative function, but it does satisfy that

$$ r(m_{1}m_{2})=\sum_{d\mid\gcd(m_{1},m_{2})}\mu(d)\chi(d)r(m_{1}/d)r(m_{2}/d), $$

where $\chi$ is the nontrivial quadratic character mod 4 (see [HB03, Section 6]; this is also an instance of a Busche-Ramanujan identity). Thus,

$$ \sum_{|z|\ll B}r(kz)=\sum_{d\mid k}\mu(d)\chi(d)r(k/d)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|z|\ll B\\
d\mid z\end{subarray}}r(z/d). $$

By counting the number of lattice points in a circle of radius $X^{1/2}$ ,

$$ \sum_{x\leq X}r(x)=\pi X+O(X^{1/2}). $$

Plugging the above into (7.5), we have that

$$ \sum_{|z|\ll B}r(kz)=\pi B\sum_{d\mid k}\frac{\mu(d)\chi(d)r(k/d)}{d}+O(B^{1/2}\sum_{d\mid k}r(k/d)d^{-1/2}). $$

Now define $k$ to be

$$ k=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\equiv 1\bmod 4\\
\log B/2\leq p\leq\log B\end{subarray}}p. $$

Then $k\sim B^{1/4}$ and $\omega(k)\sim\tfrac{1}{4}\log B/\log\log B$ , by the Siegel-Walfisz theorem. Moreover, (7.3) shows that $r(k/d)\leq r(k)$ for each $d|k$ . We also observe for future reference that $\sum_{p|k}1/p\ll(\log B)^{-1}\omega(k)\ll(\log\log B)^{-1}$ .

We may rewrite (7.6) as

$$ \sum_{|z|\ll B}r(kz)=\pi Br(k)+E_{1}+E_{2} $$

in which

$$ \displaystyle|E_{1}| \displaystyle\ll B\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid k\\
d>1\end{subarray}}\frac{r(k/d)}{d}, \displaystyle|E_{2}| \displaystyle\ll r(k)B^{1/2}\sum_{d\mid k}d^{-1/2}\ll r(k)d(k)B^{1/2}, $$

denoting the divisor function by $d(k)$ . By our previous observation,

$$ \displaystyle|E_{1}| \displaystyle\ll Br(k)\left(\sum_{p\mid k}\frac{1}{p}+\sum_{p_{1}p_{2}\mid k}\frac{1}{p_{1}p_{2}}+\ldots\right) \displaystyle\ll Br(k)\left(\frac{1}{\log\log B}+\frac{1}{(\log\log B)^{2}}+\ldots\right)\ll Br(k)\left(\frac{1}{\log\log B-1}\right). $$

Additionally, since $k$ is squarefree so that $d(k)\ll 2^{\omega(k)}\ll B^{1/\log\log B}\ll B^{1/4}$ , say, we can write $|E_{2}|\ll Br(k)\cdot B^{-1/4}$ . Consequently,

$$ \sum_{|z|\ll B}r(kz)=\pi Br(k)(1+O((\log\log B)^{-1})) $$

as $B\rightarrow\infty$ . This shows that

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M_{k},B)\gg B^{n-1}r(k)(\pi+o(1))\gg 2^{\frac{\log B}{\log\log B}(1/4+o(1))}B^{n-1}. $$

This example demonstrates that for any $c$ , a bound of the form

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M_{k},B)=O_{n,\deg(M_{k})}(B^{n-1}(\log B)^{c}) $$

that is independent of $k$ , fails as $B\rightarrow\infty$ . It does not violate a putative bound of the form

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M_{k},B)=O_{n,\deg(M_{k}),\varepsilon}(B^{n-1+\varepsilon}). $$

These counterexamples have demonstrated Theorem 1.6.

# Sums of Hecke eigenvalues along polynomial sequences and base change for $\text{GL}(2)$

**Authors:** Katharine Woo Address: Department of Mathematics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305 Email address: katywoo@stanford.edu

## Abstract

We study sums of absolute values of Hecke eigenvalues of $\textrm{GL}(2)$ representations that are tempered at all finite places. We show that these sums exhibit logarithmic savings over the trivial bound if and only if the representation is cuspidal. Further, we connect the problem of studying the sums of Hecke eigenvalues along polynomial values to the base change problem for $\textrm{GL}(2).$

## 1. Introduction

Let $\pi$ be a cuspidal automorphic representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ that satisfies the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture; let $\lambda_{\pi}$ denote the normalized Hecke eigenvalues of $\pi$ . Fix an irreducible nonconstant solvable polynomial $P(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ . In this paper, we focus on the following correlation sum:

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(n)|)|. $$

In particular, we connect the above sum to the base change of $\pi$ to the splitting field of $P(x)$ , denoted as $K$ . In the following theorem, we give a sufficient condition for (1.1) to exhibit extra savings over the trivial bound obtained using the bound $|\lambda_{\pi}(p)|\leq 2$ .

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $\pi$ be a cuspidal automorphic representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ that satisfies the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture. Let $P(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be irreducible and solvable, and let $K$ denote the splitting field of $P(x)$ . Assume that the base change $\pi_{K}$ to $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{K})$ is cuspidal, then the following bound holds:

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(n)|)|\ll_{\pi,P}X\log(X)^{-0.066}. $$

Observe that Theorem 1.1 applies to those $\pi$ ’s corresponding to holomorphic cusp forms ([10, 9]). One may expect that there should be further, even power-saving, cancellation on the sum

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}\lambda_{\pi}(|P(n)|). $$

Indeed, when $P(x)$ is a linear polynomial, this stronger bound exists. Blomer [2] analyzes sums of the above form when $P(x)$ is quadratic and $\pi$ corresponds to a holomorphic cusp form of weight $k\geq 4$ , and determines when the sum exhibits power-saving cancellation; these sums were further studied in [32, 31] by Templier and Tsimerman. However, when $P(x)$ is of higher degree, it is not clear how to successfully approach these sums (as discussed by Sarnak in [27]). When $\pi$ is no longer cuspidal, asymptotics are known for certain variants of this problem – Greaves [15] and Daniel [6] derive asymptotics for this expression when $\lambda_{\pi}$ is replaced by the divisor function, which is the Fourier coefficient of an Eisenstein series, along binary cubic and binary quartic forms respectively; most recently, Leung and Pandey proved an asymptotic with a power-saving error term in the case the divisor function along binary quartic forms [22].

By instead considering (1.1), which has absolute values around the Hecke eigenvalues, we gain flexibility in the polynomial arguments that we can study; the caveat of this approach is that one should expect a limit of a logarithmic power saving. Consider, for example, when $P(x)=x$ : if $\pi$ satisfies the Sato-Tate distribution (see [5, 30]), then the following asymptotic for the absolute values of the Hecke eigenvalues holds (see the concluding remarks of [11] by Elliot, Moreno, and Shahidi):

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(n)|\sim\frac{cX}{\log(X)^{1-\frac{8}{3\pi}}}. $$

There have been many successful upper bounds for cases of (1.1). Elliot, Moreno, and Shahidi [11] considered the case of the Ramanujan $\tau$ -function and their method forms the basis for our proof. Holowinsky [17] studied the case of (1.1) for the polynomials $x(x+\ell)$ ; Nelson [25] later studies the case when the polynomial is a irreducible quadratic. For general polynomial entries, Chiriac and Yang [4] considered when $\pi$ is defined by a non-CM holomorphic newform with trivial character along arbitrary polynomials.

We also briefly remark that sums of the form (1.1) have numerous applications in number theory. They played a critical role in the resolution of the holomorphic analogue of QUE by Holowinsky and Soundararajan [18, 16], i.e. mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms; notably the bounds achieved by Holowinsky depended logarithmically on the coefficients of the polynomial arguments $x(x+\ell)$ and hence summing over $\ell$ is well-controlled. These sums appear in the recent proof of the mixing conjecture conditional on GRH by Blomer, Brumley, and Khayutin [1]. The author began studying these correlation sums while working on Manin’s conjecture for Châtelet surfaces [33], where nontrivial upper bounds on these sums are applied in the indefinite case.

#### Remark 1.2.

In Theorem 1.1, we focus on the case where $P(x)$ is an irreducible polynomial. However, for applications of this bound, one may desire for $P(x)$ to be a squarefree polynomial. The sieve used (Theorem 2.1) has been generalized to squarefree polynomials and from these generalizations the following can be deduced:

Let $P(x)=P_{1}(x)\ldots P_{r}(x)$ be a squarefree polynomial and $P_{i}(x)$ irreducible factors. Let $K_{i}$ be the splitting field of $P_{i}(x)$ . Assume that the base change $\pi_{K_{i}}$ is cuspidal for all $i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}$ . Then there exists a positive $c_{r}>0$ such that

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(n)|)|\ll_{\pi,P}X\log(X)^{-c_{r}}. $$

In §4, we establish the connection between (1.1) and the base change of $\pi$ to the splitting field of $P(x)$ . In doing so, the problem reduces to the linear case over number fields. After introducing a new argument exploiting the structure of dihedral representations, we establish the following classification for the $L^{1}$ -norm:

#### Theorem 1.3.

Let $K$ be a number field and $\pi$ an automorphic representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{K})$ that is tempered at all finite places of $K$ . Then there exists a positive constant $c_{\pi}>0$ such that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
N(\mathfrak{a})\leq X\end{subarray}}|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{a})|\ll_{\pi}X\log(X)^{-c_{\pi}} $$

if and only if $\pi$ is cuspidal. Moreover, if $\pi$ is cuspidal, then there is a universal lower bound $c_{\pi}>0.066$ .

The work of Rankin [26] and Selberg [28] for the $L^{2}$ -norm of cuspidal representations tells us that there is also a power of $\log(X)$ difference depending on the cuspidality of $\pi$ in that story – in particular, that the asymptotic

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(n)|^{2}=c_{\pi}X+O(X^{1-2/5}) $$

holds if and only if $\pi$ is a cuspidal automorphic representations of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ . If $\pi$ is not cuspidal, then the $L^{2}$ -norm is of size $\asymp X\log(X)^{m}$ for $m\geq 1$ . Observe that by Cauchy-Schwarz, this implies that the $L^{1}$ -norm, i.e. the sum studied in Theorem 1.3, is bounded by $O_{\pi}(X)$ when $\pi$ is cuspidal. We will use analysis on the higher symmetric powers to establish our upper bound.

#### Remark 1.4.

We remark that we assume that $\pi$ is tempered at all finite places in order to apply our sieves (Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 2.3). In [34], Yang studies upper and lower bounds for this $L^{1}$ -norm when $\pi$ is a cuspidal representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ that is nonmonomial and unitary, without the assumption that $\pi$ satisfies the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture. For the nonlinear case of Theorem 1.1, we currently need this temperedness assumption to apply an appropriate sieve.

Finally, we hope to understand (1.1) when $\pi_{K}$ is not a cuspidal representation. The work on the base change of $\text{GL}_{2}$ representations by Langlands [21] classifies exactly when this phenomenon occurs for $P(x)$ a solvable polynomial; we use this to establish lower bounds for (1.1).

#### Theorem 1.5.

Let $\pi$ be a cuspidal automorphic representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ that satisfies the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture. Let $P(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be irreducible and $K$ be the splitting field of $P(x)$ be solvable. Assume that the base change $\pi_{K}$ is not cuspidal; hence, it has the form

$$ \pi=\text{Ind}_{W_{F}}^{W_{\mathbb{Q}}}\theta $$

for some quadratic subfield $F\subset K$ and unitary Hecke character $\theta$ of $F$ . If $\theta$ has finite order, let $L_{\theta}$ denote the ray class field of $\theta$ .

- (1) If $\theta$ is of infinite order or if $\text{Gal}(L_{\theta}/L_{\theta}\cap K)\not\subset\ker(\theta^{2})$ , then

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(n)|)|\ll_{\pi,P}X\log(X)^{1/2}. $$

- (2) Otherwise, the following lower bound holds:

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(n)|)|\geq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\leq X\\ P(n)\text{ squarefree}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_{F}\\ N(\mathfrak{a})=|P(n)|\end{subarray}}1. $$

#### Remark 1.6.

A necessary requirement for $\pi_{K}$ to be noncuspidal is that $F\subset K$ ; this correspondingly increases the size of our “trivial” bound – the one induced by the trivial representation. Specifically, let $\Psi=\text{Ind}_{W_{F}}^{W_{\mathbb{Q}}}1$ . If $F\subset K$ , then we have that

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\Psi}(|P(n)|)|\ll_{\Psi,P}X\log(X). $$

In comparison, if $F\not\subset K$ , then the trivial bound gives:

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\Psi}(|P(n)|)|\ll_{\Psi,P}X. $$

When $F\subset K$ , this extra power of $\log(X)$ is a consequence of the Dedekind zeta function $\zeta_{K}(s)$ twisted by the quadratic character generating $F$ having a pole at $s=1$ of order one. Hence Theorem 1.5 (1) can also be viewed as a polylogarithmic savings over the trivial bound.

Finally, we remark on a natural generalization of this problem – when $P(x)$ is replaced by an absolutely irreducible multivariate polynomial:

$$ \sum_{x_{i}\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}|)|. $$

First, if $P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ is a homogeneous binary form, then we achieve the same theorems as the single variable case (see the remarks after Theorem 2.1). In particular, if $K$ is the splitting field of $P(\mathbf{x})$ and if the base change $\pi_{K}$ is cuspidal, then

$$ \sum_{x,y\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(x,y)|)|\ll X^{2}\log(X)^{-0.066}. $$

For $n\geq 3$ or for nonhomogeneous polynomials with $n=2$ , after an appropriate sieve for nonnegative multiplicative functions along polynomial values (as derived by Chiriac and Yang in [4, Proposition 2.2]), this problem reduces to questions about the Sato-Tate distribution of $\pi$ and the number of local solutions of $P(\mathbf{x})\bmod p$ . Under the assumption of a wide range of conjectures (including those connecting the Hasse-Weil $L$ -function of the variety $\{P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0\}$ to automorphic representations), one can achieve conditional polylogarithmic savings over the trivial bound by using second and fourth moment calculations.

### 1.1. Notation

Let us first set some notation:

- • $p$ , $\mathfrak{p}$ , or $\mathfrak{P}$ will denote primes or prime ideals,

- • sums over $p$ , $\mathfrak{p}$ , or $\mathfrak{P}$ are sums over primes or prime ideals,

- • $\varrho(p)=\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:P(x)=0\}$ will denote the local count of the polynomial $P(x)$ ,

- • $\pi$ , $\Xi$ will denote $\text{GL}_{2}$ representations,

- • $\psi$ , $\xi$ , $\theta$ will denote $\text{GL}_{1}$ representations, i.e. Hecke characters,

- • Let $\Pi(G)$ denote the irreducible admissible automorphic representations of $G$ . The base change map sends

$$ \Pi(\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}}))\rightarrow\Pi(\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{K})) $$

and is analyzed for solvable extensions by Langlands in [21].

We end this section by outlining the rest of the paper. In §2, we establish the necessary background on sieve theory. In §3, we establish Theorem 1.3. In §4, we first prove Theorem 1.1 by reducing it to the setting of Theorem 1.3; second, we consider non-cuspidal base change and establish Theorem 1.5.
