## 2. Sieve methods

### 2.1. Upper bound sieves

We begin with a classical upper bound. Let $f(n)$ be a nonnegative multiplicative function supported on squarefree numbers. Then if $f(n)$ satisfies the following condition for the sum over primes:

$$ \sum_{w\leq p<X}\frac{f(p)\log(p)}{p}\leq a\log(X/w)+b, $$

for all $w$ with $2\leq w<X$ and $a\geq 0,b\geq 1$ constants, then one can derive that11 1 See [12, Theorem A.1] for further details

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}f(n)\ll X\prod_{p\leq X}\left(1+\frac{f(p)-1}{p}\right). $$

Now, let $P(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be a polynomial – we would like a similar upper bound along values of $P$ . The following sieve was deduced by Nair [24] for nonnegative multiplicative functions along polynomial values. It was later generalized by de la Bretéche and Browning [7] and de la Bretéche and Tenenbaum [8] for binary forms; by Browning and Sofos [3] for sums over prime ideals.

#### Theorem 2.1 (Nair, [24]).

Let $f(n)$ be a nonnegative multiplicative function such that there exist constants $A,B\geq 0$ such that for any natural number $v$ , $f(p^{v})\leq A^{v}$ , and in general, $f(n)\leq Bn^{\epsilon}$ . Then the following bound holds for any irreducible polynomial $P(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ :

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}f(|P(n)|)\ll_{P,A,B}X\exp\left(\sum_{p\leq X}\frac{\varrho(p)(f(p)-1)}{p}\right), $$

where $\varrho(p)=\#\{a\bmod p:P(a)=0\}.$

#### Remark 2.2.

Later, Nair and Tenenbaum [23] generalized the above result for multiplicative functions in several variables. A consequence of their work is that if $P_{1}(x),\ldots,P_{k}(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ are distinct irreducible polynomials and $f_{1},\ldots,f_{k}$ are nonnegative multiplicative functions that are bounded on prime values, then

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}f_{1}(|P_{1}(n)|)\ldots f_{k}(|P_{k}(n)|)\ll_{P_{1},\ldots,P_{k},f_{1},\ldots,f_{k}}X\exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{p_{i}\leq X}\frac{\varrho_{P_{i}}(p_{i})(f_{i}(p_{i})-1)}{p_{i}}\right), $$

where $\varrho_{P_{i}}(p)=\#\{a\bmod p:P_{i}(a)=0\}.$ A consequence of the work of de la Bretéche and Tenenbaum [8] for binary forms is that a similar bound holds for $g_{1},\ldots,g_{k}$ nonnegative multiplicative functions bounded on prime values and $F_{1},\ldots,F_{k}$ distinct irreducible binary forms:

$$ \sum_{x,y\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}g_{i}(|F_{i}(x,y)|)\ll_{g_{1},\ldots,g_{k},F_{1},\ldots,F_{k}}X^{2}\exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{p_{i}\leq X}\frac{\varrho_{F_{i}}(p_{i})(g_{i}(p_{i})-1)}{p_{i}^{2}}\right), $$

where $\varrho_{F_{i}}(p)=\#\{(a,b)\bmod p:F(a,b)=0\}.$ For this paper, we will stick however to the case of one irreducible polynomial, $P(\mathbf{x})$ , and the particular nonnegative multiplicative functions $|\lambda_{\pi}(n)|$ .

### 2.2. Lower bound sieves

In Theorem 1.3, we also want to consider lower bounds. To do so, we use a corresponding lower bound sieve.

#### Theorem 2.3 ([12, Theorem A.4]).

Let $f(n)$ be a multiplicative nonnegative function and satisfy that:

$$ \sum_{y<p\leq x}\frac{f(p)\log(p)}{p}\leq a\log(x/y)+b, $$

$$ \sum_{p\leq y}f(p)\log(p)\gg y. $$

Then $f(n)$ satisfies that

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}f(n)\gg X\prod_{p\leq X}\left(1+\frac{f(p)-1}{p}\right). $$

#### Remark 2.4.

If $f(n)$ is bounded on prime values, then the first condition is always satisfied.

#### Corollary 2.5.

Let $K$ be a number field and $g:I_{K}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be a nonnegative multiplicative function on the ideals of $K$ that is bounded on prime ideals. If

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
N(\mathfrak{p})\leq y\end{subarray}}g(\mathfrak{p})\log(N(\mathfrak{p}))\gg y, $$

then the following bound is satisfied:

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
N(\mathfrak{a})\leq X\end{subarray}}g(\mathfrak{a})\gg_{K}X\prod_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\left(1+\frac{g(\mathfrak{p})-1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}\right). $$

#### Proof.

Apply Theorem 2.3 with the nonnegative multiplicative function

$$ f(n)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
N(\mathfrak{a})=n\end{subarray}}g(\mathfrak{a}). $$

∎

#### Remark 2.6 (Non-existence of a lower bound sieve for polynomial values).

One might expect, given Theorem 2.3, that a similar bound would hold for the sum:

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}f(|P(n)|). $$

However, this can not happen; for instance, take $f(p)=\mathbf{1}_{p\equiv 3\bmod 4}$ and $P(x)=x^{2}+1$ . Then it is clear that

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}f(|P(n)|)=0. $$

However, if we consider what the analogous lower bound to Theorem 2.3 would produce,

$$ X\prod_{p\leq X}\left(1+\frac{\varrho(p)(f(p)-1)}{p}\right)=X\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\leq X\\
p\equiv 1\bmod 4\end{subarray}}\left(1-\frac{2}{p}\right)\gg X\log(X)^{-1}, $$

this causes immediate issues.

## 3. Linear polynomials

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.3. Recall that $K$ is a number field and $\pi$ is an automorphic representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{K})$ that is tempered at all finite places of $K$ . Consequently, we know that the normalized Hecke eigenvalues satisfy that

$$ |\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})|\leq 2, $$

for all prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}$ .

To prove the theorem, we split the study into different cases. In the first two subsection, we prove that the upper bound holds whenever $\pi$ is cuspidal. In the final subsection (in §3.3), we will show that when $\pi$ is not cuspidal, a sufficient lower bound holds.

For the upper bound, we first apply Theorem 2.1, as the assumptions are satisfied:

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{a})|\ll_{K}X\exp\left(\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})|-1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}\right). $$

In order to study the sum

$$ S_{\pi}(X):=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})|-1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}, $$

we relate $|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})|$ to the Hecke eigenvalues of $\text{sym}^{2}(\pi)$ , the automorphic representation on $\text{GL}_{3}(\mathbb{A}_{K})$ . This causes us to need to break the proof into two cases: when $\pi$ is dihedral and when $\pi$ is non-dihedral.

### 3.1. Galois representations

First, we tackle the case when $\pi$ is a Galois representation, and hence has finite image. There is a Galois extension $L/K$ such that

$$ \pi:\text{Gal}(L/K)\rightarrow\textrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}). $$

Additionally, the Hecke eigenvalues are of the form

$$ \lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})=\text{Tr}(\pi(\textrm{Frob}_{\mathfrak{p}}))=\chi_{\pi}(\textrm{Frob}_{\mathfrak{p}}), $$

where $\chi_{\pi}$ denotes the character of the representation $\pi$ . In this case, we can see that

$$ S_{\pi}(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in\text{Gal}(L/K)}|\chi_{\pi}(\sigma)|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X\\
\textrm{Frob}_{\mathfrak{p}}=\sigma\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}-\log\log(X)+O_{K}(1). $$

Recall that $\chi_{\pi}$ is invariant under conjugation and hence we can apply the Chebotarev density theorem to determine that

$$ S_{\pi}(X)=\left(\frac{1}{|\text{Gal}(L/K)|}\sum_{\sigma\in\text{Gal}(L/K)}|\chi_{\pi}(\sigma)|-1\right)\cdot\log\log(X)+O_{K}(1). $$

In order to establish Theorem 1.3 in this case, we need to prove that

$$ \frac{1}{|\text{Gal}(L/K)|}\sum_{\sigma\in\text{Gal}(L/K)}|\chi_{\pi}(\sigma)|<1. $$

To do so, we apply Cauchy-Schwarz:

$$ \frac{1}{|\text{Gal}(L/K)|}\sum_{\sigma\in\text{Gal}(L/K)}|\chi_{\pi}(\sigma)|\leq\left(\frac{1}{|\text{Gal}(L/K)|}\sum_{\sigma\in\text{Gal}(L/K)}|\chi_{\pi}(\sigma)|^{2}\right)^{1/2}. $$

Since $\pi$ is an irreducible representation, we know that

$$ \frac{1}{|\text{Gal}(L/K)|}\sum_{\sigma\in\text{Gal}(L/K)}|\chi_{\pi}(\sigma)|^{2}=1. $$

Observe that the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is in fact a strict inequality unless $|\chi(\sigma)|$ is equal for every $\sigma\in\text{Gal}(L/K)$ . On the other hand, since $\pi$ is cuspidal, it is a nontrivial irreducible representation and hence $\chi(1)=\dim(\pi)\geq 2$ . Thus, in this case, Cauchy-Schwarz is a strict inequality.

Furthermore, since $|\chi_{\pi}(\sigma)|\in\mathbb{Z}$ for each $\sigma$ , we can see that

$$ S_{\pi}(X)\leq-|\text{Gal}(L/K)|^{-1}\cdot\log\log(X)+O_{K}(1), $$

and thus we have that

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{a})|\ll_{K}X\log(X)^{-|\text{Gal}(L/K)|^{-1}}. $$

.

#### Remark 3.1.

For a fixed Galois representation, we can understand completely the $L^{1}$ -norm of $\pi$ , since we can compute all of the moments of $\pi$ . Indeed, the asymptotic holds:

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{a})|\sim c_{\pi}X\log(X)^{\beta_{\pi}} $$

where $\beta_{\pi}$ is one fewer than the $L^{1}$ -norm of the trace function of $\pi$ .

#### Remark 3.2.

One can instead look at cuspidal representations of the Weil group $W_{K}$ with finite image and derive a similar logarithmic savings over the trivial bound for the $L^{1}$ -norm of $\pi$ .

### 3.2. Using the second and fourth moment

Now, let us assume that $\pi$ is any cuspidal automorphic representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{K})$ satisfying the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture; we will use information about the $L^{2}$ -norm and $L^{4}$ -norm of $\pi$ to derive nontrivial savings on the $L^{1}$ -norm of $\pi$ . We follow the proof of Elliott, Moreno, and Shahidi [11] regarding the Ramanujan $\tau$ -function. Similar proofs also appear in the work of Chiriac and Yang [4], and Holowinsky [17].

Let us define

$$ \delta:=\inf_{-1\leq y\leq 2}y^{-2}(1+y/2-(1+y)^{1/2})\approx 0.067. $$

We remark that the definition of $\delta$ is strictly positive and independent of $\pi$ . By the definition of $\delta$ , the following relation holds for any prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ :

$$ \displaystyle|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})|-1 \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}(\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})\lambda_{\overline{\pi}}(\mathfrak{p})-1)-\delta\left(\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})\lambda_{\overline{\pi}}(\mathfrak{p})-1\right)^{2} \displaystyle\leq-\delta+\left(\frac{1}{2}+2\delta\right)\left(\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})\lambda_{\overline{\pi}}(\mathfrak{p})-1\right)-\delta\left(\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})^{2}\lambda_{\overline{\pi}}(\mathfrak{p})^{2}-2\right). $$

(Observe that we use that the eigenvalues of the Hecke operators are real.) Let $\pi\boxtimes\pi^{\prime}$ denote the Rankin-Selberg convolution of $\pi$ and $\pi^{\prime}.$ From the above inequality, we know

$$ S_{\pi}(X)\leq-\delta\log\log(X)+\left(1/2+2\delta\right)\cdot T_{\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}}(X)-\delta\cdot T_{\pi\boxtimes\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}\boxtimes\overline{\pi}}(X)+O_{K}(1), $$

where we define

$$ T_{\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}}(X)=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{\lambda_{\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}}(\mathfrak{p})-1}{N(\mathfrak{p})},\hskip 14.22636ptT_{\pi\boxtimes\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}\boxtimes\overline{\pi}}(X)=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{\lambda_{\pi\boxtimes\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}\boxtimes\overline{\pi}}(\mathfrak{p})-2}{N(\mathfrak{p})}. $$

In other words, $T_{\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}}$ measures the second moment of $\pi$ and $T_{\pi\boxtimes\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}\boxtimes\overline{\pi}}$ measures the fourth moment. At this point, we split into the case when $\pi$ is dihedral and non-dihedral.

If $\pi$ is a dihedral representation, then it must also be a representation of the Weil group $W_{K}$ (see [19] for a classification of representations with a noncuspidal symmetric power.) Moreover, since $\pi$ is dihedral, it will be a representation of $D_{2n}$ for some $n\in[3,\infty]$ , where we include the infinite dihedral group and exclude $D_{2}$ and $D_{4}$ which have no two-dimensional irreducible representations.

Now if $\pi$ is dihedral Galois representation with $\text{Gal}(L/K)\cong D_{2n}$ , then §3.1 shows that

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{a})|\ll X\log(X)^{-1/2n}. $$

However, this exponent is not uniform in the choice of cuspidal representation $\pi$ . So, let us present a separate argument to give the uniform lower bound on $c_{\pi}$ in the case when $\pi$ is dihedral.

If $\pi$ is a dihedral representation, then there must exist a quadratic extension $L/K$ such that $\pi=\text{Ind}_{W_{L}}^{W_{K}}\theta$ , where $\theta$ denotes a Hecke character. We can further assume that $\text{ord}(\theta)>2$ , as otherwise $\pi$ would be a two-dimensional irreducible representation of $D_{4}$ which do not exist. Since $\pi$ is an induced representation, when a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ splits in $L$ , say as $\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{P}\overline{\mathfrak{P}}$ , we have that

$$ \lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})=\theta(\mathfrak{P})+\overline{\theta(\mathfrak{P})}. $$

Further, for all but finitely many primes $\mathfrak{p}$ such that $\mathfrak{p}$ does not split, $\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})=0$ . Since $\pi$ is tempered at all finite places, for each prime $\mathfrak{p}$ that splits in $L$ , we can assign an angle $\alpha_{\mathfrak{p}}\in[0,1]$ such that

$$ \lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})=|e^{2\pi i\alpha_{\mathfrak{p}}}+e^{-2\pi i\alpha_{\mathfrak{p}}}|=2|\cos(2\pi\alpha_{\mathfrak{p}})|. $$

Now, we can write that

$$ S_{\pi}(X)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X\\
\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{P}\overline{\mathfrak{P}}\end{subarray}}\frac{2|\cos(2\pi\alpha_{\mathfrak{p}})|-1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}-\frac{1}{2}\log\log(X)+O_{\pi,K}(1). $$

The cosine identity gives us the following useful fact:

$$ 2|\cos(2\pi\alpha_{\mathfrak{p}})|\leq\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\cos(4\pi\alpha_{\mathfrak{p}}). $$

Thus,

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X\\
\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{P}\overline{\mathfrak{P}}\end{subarray}}\frac{2|\cos(2\pi\alpha_{\mathfrak{p}})|-1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X\\
\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{P}\overline{\mathfrak{P}}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{2N(\mathfrak{p})}+\frac{\cos(2\pi\alpha_{\mathfrak{p}})}{2N(\mathfrak{p})}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X\\
\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{P}\overline{\mathfrak{P}}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{2N(\mathfrak{p})}+\frac{\theta(\mathfrak{P})^{2}+\theta(\overline{\mathfrak{P}})^{2}}{2N(\mathfrak{p})}. $$

Evaluating the first of these summands, we can rearrange to see that

$$ S_{\pi}(X)\leq\frac{1}{4}\log\log(X)-\frac{1}{2}\log\log(X)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{N_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})\leq X}\frac{\theta(\mathfrak{P})^{2}}{N_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})}+O_{\pi,K}(1). $$

Since $\text{ord}(\theta)>2$ , $\theta^{2}$ will be a nontrivial Hecke character of $L$ . Hence,

$$ \sum_{N_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})\leq X}\frac{\theta(\mathfrak{P})^{2}}{N_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})}=O_{\pi,K}(1). $$

With this in mind, we can see that when $\pi$ is dihedral,

$$ S_{\pi}(X)\leq-\frac{1}{4}\log\log(X)+O_{\pi,K}(1), $$

and in this case, we can take $c_{\pi}>1/4.$ Take $\delta^{\prime}=1/5$ for our future comparison, as the non-dihedral case will give the eventual lower bound on $c_{\pi}$ stated in Theorem 1.3.

So, it remains to analyze when $\pi$ is not dihedral. We claim that in this case:

$$ T_{\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}}(X)=O_{\pi}(1),\qquad T_{\pi\boxtimes\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}\boxtimes\overline{\pi}}(X)=O_{\pi}(1). $$

Before we prove the above claim, we make the observation that both sums converge if and only if the following limits exist:

$$ \lim_{s\rightarrow 1^{+}}\zeta_{K}(s)^{-1}L(s,\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}), $$

$$ \lim_{s\rightarrow 1^{+}}\zeta_{K}(s)^{-2}L(s,\pi\boxtimes\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}\boxtimes\overline{\pi}). $$

Let us start with the $T_{\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}}(X)$ and the $L$ -function $L(s,\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi})$ . Since $\pi$ is cuspidal, we know that $L(s,\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi})$ has a simple pole at $s=1$ ; consequently, the limit (3.23) exists and hence the first part of (3.22) is true. Another way of viewing this statement is that $L(s,\pi,\text{Ad})$ is analytic at $s=1$ , where $\text{Ad}(\pi)$ is the Gelbart-Jacquet lift of [13].

Next, we can decompose $\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}=1\boxplus\text{Ad}^{2}(\pi)$ ; here we use $\boxplus$ to denote the isobaric sum (see [20]). If $\pi$ is non-dihedral, we know that $\text{Ad}^{2}(\pi)$ is cuspidal. Now we consider $T_{\pi\boxtimes\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}\boxtimes\overline{\pi}}(X)$ and (3.24). From our decomposition of $\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}$ , we know that $L(s,\pi\boxtimes\pi\boxtimes\overline{\pi}\boxtimes\overline{\pi})$ has the same analytic behavior at $s=1$ as the product $\zeta_{K}(s)L(s,\pi,\text{Ad}^{2})^{2}L(s,\text{Ad}^{2}(\pi)\boxtimes\text{Ad}^{2}(\overline{\pi}))$ – we know that $L(s,\pi,\text{Ad}^{2})$ is entire at $s=1$ since $\text{Ad}^{2}(\pi)$ is a cuspidal automorphic representation of $\text{GL}_{3}(\mathbb{A}_{K})$ . Similarly, we know that since $\text{Ad}^{2}(\pi)$ is cuspidal, $L(s,\text{Ad}^{2}(\pi)\boxtimes\text{Ad}^{2}(\overline{\pi}))$ has a pole of order one at $s=1$ ; here $\text{Ad}^{2}(\pi)\boxtimes\text{Ad}^{2}(\overline{\pi})$ is a $\text{GL}_{3}\times\text{GL}_{3}$ Rankin-Selberg convolution. Hence, this $L$ -function has a pole of order two at $s=1$ . Thus, the limit (3.24) exists and this establishes the second half of claim (3.22).

Hence, in the case when $\pi$ is non-dihedral, we know that

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{a})|\ll_{\pi}X\log(X)^{-\delta}. $$

Now, taking $c=\min(\delta,\delta^{\prime})$ , this completes the cuspidal case of Theorem 1.3.

### 3.3. Lower bounds when $\pi$ is not cuspidal

Let $\pi$ be a non-cuspidal representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{K})$ , so $\pi$ has the isobaric decomposition (see [20])

$$ \pi=\psi_{1}\boxplus\psi_{2}, $$

where $\psi_{1},\psi_{2}$ are $\text{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{A}_{K})$ -representations, i.e. quasi-characters. Since $\pi$ is tempered at each finite place, we take $\psi_{1}$ and $\psi_{2}$ to be unitary.

Let us assume that $|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})|$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem 2.3 for now (we will check this at the end). This would then imply that

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{a})|\gg_{K}X\exp\left(\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})|-1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}\right). $$

Now, since $\pi=\psi_{1}\boxplus\psi_{2}$ , we know that

$$ \lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})=\psi_{1}(\mathfrak{p})+\psi_{2}(\mathfrak{p}). $$

Hence, we can estimate:

$$ S_{\pi}(X)=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{|\psi_{1}(\mathfrak{p})+\psi_{2}(\mathfrak{p})|-1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{|1+\psi_{1}^{-1}\psi_{2}(\mathfrak{p})|-1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}. $$

Define the character $\psi:=\psi_{1}^{-1}\psi_{2}$ and define for each prime $\mathfrak{p}$ , the angle $\theta_{\mathfrak{p}}\in[0,1]$ such that $\psi(\mathfrak{p})=e(2\pi i\theta_{\mathfrak{p}}).$ We have that

$$ S_{\pi}(X)=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{\sqrt{2+2\cos(2\pi\theta_{\mathfrak{p}})}-1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}. $$

We split our analysis into two cases: when $\psi=1$ and when $\psi$ is nontrivial. First, if $\psi=1$ , then $\theta_{\mathfrak{p}}=0$ for all primes $\mathfrak{p}$ . So, we have that

$$ S_{\pi}(X)=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}=\log\log(X)+O_{K}(1), $$

and thus

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{a})|\gg_{K}X\log(X). $$

This completes the lower bound in this case.

Now, if $\psi\neq 1$ , then we know that for any $A>0$ :

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\cos(2\pi\theta_{\mathfrak{p}})=O_{\psi}(X\log(X)^{-A}). $$

Consequently, the following hold:

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}2+2\cos(2\pi\theta_{p})=\frac{2X}{\log(X)}+O_{\psi}(X(\log X)^{-A}). $$

Observing that $\max_{\theta\in[0,1]}\sqrt{2+2\cos(2\pi\theta_{p})}=2$ , we establish that

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\sqrt{2+2\cos(2\pi\theta_{p})}\geq\frac{X}{\log(X)}+O_{\psi}(X(\log X)^{-A}). $$

Hence, through partial summation, we have that

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{\sqrt{2+2\cos(2\pi\theta_{\mathfrak{p}})}}{N(\mathfrak{p})}\geq\log\log(X)+O_{\pi,K}(1). $$

Consequently, from the equation above in combination with (3.29), we know

$$ S_{\pi}(X)\ll_{\pi,K}1. $$

As such, there can not exist any positive constant $c_{\pi}>0$ such that $S_{\pi}(X)\leq-c_{\pi}\log\log(X)+o_{\pi,K}(\log\log(X))$ , as would be necessary for the upper bound in Theorem 1.3 to exist. Thus, in order to complete the proof of Theorem 1.3, it suffices to prove that the multiplicative function $|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})|$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem 2.3.

Finally, let us check that when $\pi=\psi_{1}\boxplus\psi_{2}$

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq y}|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})|\log(N(\mathfrak{p}))\gg y. $$

Again, let $\psi=\psi_{1}^{-1}\psi_{2}$ and $\psi(\mathfrak{p})=e(2\pi i\theta_{\mathfrak{p}}).$ Then we can write

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq y}|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})|\log(N(\mathfrak{p}))=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq y}|1+\psi(\mathfrak{p})|\log(N(\mathfrak{p}))=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq y}\sqrt{2+2\cos(2\pi\theta_{\mathfrak{p}})}\cdot\log(N(\mathfrak{p})). $$

By partial summation in combination with (3.34), we see that:

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq y}\sqrt{2+2\cos(2\pi\theta_{\mathfrak{p}})}\cdot\log(N(\mathfrak{p}))\gg y $$

as desired. Thus $|\lambda_{\pi}(\mathfrak{p})|$ satisfies the conditions of Theorem 2.3. ∎

## 4. Higher degree polynomials

In the following section, we prove Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.5. Before doing so, we will review base change for $\text{GL}_{1}$ and $\text{GL}_{2}$ automorphic representations, as this theory will be critical in both sections. For a more comprehensive discussion of base change, see [14, 21].

Let us recall the following notation:

- • $F$ is a fixed number field; in our applications it will always be $F=\mathbb{Q}$ ,

- • $G=\text{GL}_{1}$ or $\text{GL}_{2}$ defined over $F$ ,

- • For a number field extension $E/F$ , $G_{E/F}$ is the restriction of scalars of $G$ over $E$ , i.e. $G_{E/F}(\mathbb{A}_{F})=G(\mathbb{A}_{E})$ ,

- • The Weil group of a number field $F$ is given by a tuple $(W_{F},\varphi,\{r_{E}\}_{E/F})$ such that $W_{F}$ is a topological group with a continuous homomorphism:

$$ \varphi:W_{F}\rightarrow\text{Gal}(\overline{F}/F) $$

with dense image that satisfies: – For any finite extension $E/F$ with $E\subset\overline{F}$ , define $W_{E}=\varphi^{-1}(\text{Gal}(\overline{F}/E))$ . Since $\varphi$ is continuous, $W_{E}$ is open in $W_{F}$ ; additionally, it induces a bijection

$$ W_{F}/W_{E}\xrightarrow{\sim}\text{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)/\text{Gal}(\overline{F}/E)\cong\text{Gal}(E/F), $$

where the last isomorphism holds when $E/F$ is Galois. – For each finite extension $E/F$ , the map $r_{E}$ gives an isomorphism of topological groups

$$ r_{E}:\mathbb{A}_{E}^{\times}/E^{\times}\xrightarrow{\sim}W_{E}^{\text{ab}}, $$

where $W_{E}^{\text{ab}}$ is the maximal abelian Hausdorff quotient of $W_{E}$ . Furthermore, these maps $r_{E}$ satisfy four conditions that are described explicitly in [29, (W1),(W2),(W3),(W4)].

- • For a one-dimensional representation $\theta$ of $W_{E}$ , $\text{Ind}_{W_{E}}^{W_{F}}\theta$ denotes automorphic induction to the extension $E/F$ .

We also set $\Pi(G)$ to denote the set of irreducible admissible automorphic representations of $G(\mathbb{A}_{F})$ . The base change map sends:

$$ \Pi(G)\rightarrow\Pi(G_{E/F}) $$

$$ \pi\mapsto\pi_{E/F}. $$

Let us assume that $E/F$ is a solvable number field extension; hence there exists a chain of subfields

$$ F=E_{0}\subsetneq E_{1}\subsetneq E_{2}\subsetneq\ldots\subsetneq E_{n-1}\subsetneq E_{n}=E $$

where $E_{i+1}/E_{i}$ is a cylic extension of prime order. Base change on $L$ -groups gives us a map

$$ \Pi(G)\rightarrow\Pi(G_{E_{1}/F})\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow\Pi(G_{E_{n-1}/F})\rightarrow\Pi(G_{E/F}) $$

that is compatible with local data; when $G=\text{GL}_{2}$ , this map was constructed and proved by Langlands in [21].

#### 4.0.1. The $\text{GL}_{1}$ base change problem

First, we review the case of $\text{GL}_{1}$ -base change. Let $\theta$ be a one-dimensional representation of $W_{F}$ , i.e. a quasicharacter of $\mathbb{A}_{F}^{\times}/F^{\times}$ . Let $E/F$ denote a cyclic extension. The base change lift

$$ \Pi(\text{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{A}_{F}))\rightarrow\Pi(\text{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{A}_{E})) $$

is given explicitly by the map

$$ \theta\mapsto\theta\circ N_{E/F}=:\theta_{E}. $$

In particular, for an ideal $I\subset E$ ,

$$ \lambda_{\theta_{E}}(I)=\theta(N_{E/F}(I))=\lambda_{\theta_{F}}(N_{E/F}(I)). $$

Next, observe that $\widehat{\text{Gal}(E/F)}$ are themselves quasi-characters that are trivial on $N_{E/F}(\mathbb{A}_{E}^{\times}/E^{\times})$ and hence will be trivial after base change to $E.$

#### Proposition 4.1 ([14, Proposition 1]).

Let $E/F$ be a cyclic extension. The lifting $\theta_{E}$ will be cuspidal if and only if there exists $\zeta\in\widehat{\text{Gal}(E/F)}$ such that $\theta=\zeta.$

#### 4.0.2. The $\text{GL}_{2}$ base change problem

Now, we discuss the more complicated case of $\text{GL}_{2}$ -base change. The base change for global fields is discussed in [14, Theorem 2]. We recall the relevant parts of the theorem:

#### Theorem 4.2 ([14, Theorem 2 (a),(b)]).

Let $\pi\in\Pi(G)$ be a cuspidal representation. Then there exists a unique lifting $\pi_{E/F}\in\Pi(G_{E/F})$ . Since $E/F$ is solvable, denote the chain of cyclic extension:

$$ F=E_{0}\subsetneq E_{1}\subsetneq\ldots\subsetneq E_{n-1}\subsetneq E_{n}=E. $$

Then, $\pi_{E/F}$ is not cuspidal if and only if there exists $E_{i+1}/E_{i}$ a quadratic extension and $\theta$ a quasicharacter of $\mathbb{A}_{E_{i+1}}^{\times}/E_{i+1}^{\times}$ such that

$$ \pi_{E_{i}}=\text{Ind}_{W_{E_{i+1}}}^{W_{E_{i}}}\theta. $$

In this case, $\pi_{E_{i+1}}$ is a principal series given by quasicharacter $\theta$ , i.e. $\pi(\theta,^{\sigma}\theta).$

We further make the observation that for $\pi$ an automorphic representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{F})$ , the Fourier coefficients of $\pi_{E/F}$ at prime ideals $\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{E}$ satisfying that $N_{E/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})$ is prime will be given by the relation

$$ \lambda_{\pi_{E/F}}(\mathfrak{P})=\lambda_{\pi}(N_{E/F}(\mathfrak{P})). $$

This connection between the Hecke eigenvalues of $\pi$ and $\pi_{E/F}$ will be the key relationship between the correlation sum of Theorem 1.1 and this automorphic picture.

### 4.1. Cuspidal base change

In this subsection, we prove Theorem 1.1, i.e. when the base change of $\pi$ to the splitting field $K$ of $P(x)$ is cuspidal.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1.

We will reduce Theorem 1.1 to the estimates in Theorem 1.3, where $K$ is the splitting field of $P(x)$ . Again, let us start by applying the sieve (Theorem 2.1):

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(n)|)|\ll_{P}X\exp\left(\sum_{p\leq X}\frac{\varrho(p)(|\lambda_{\pi}(p)|-1)}{p}\right). $$

We observe that since $\varrho(p)=\#\{x\bmod p:P(x)=0\}$ , at all but finitely many primes,

$$ \varrho(p)=\#\{\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}:N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p\}. $$

Since $P(x)$ is irreducible, we have

$$ \sum_{p\leq X}\frac{\varrho(p)|\lambda_{\pi}(p)|}{p}-\frac{\varrho(p)}{p}=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{|\lambda_{\pi}(N(\mathfrak{p}))|-1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}+O_{K}(1). $$

Now by (4.1), we know that this gives the relationship

$$ \sum_{p\leq X}\frac{\varrho(p)(|\lambda_{\pi}(p)|-1)}{p}=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{|\lambda_{\pi_{K}}(\mathfrak{p})|-1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}+O_{K}(1)=S_{\pi_{K}}(X)+O_{K}(1), $$

using the notation of §3. Since we have assumed that $\pi_{K}$ is a cuspidal automorphic representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{K})$ , by the proof of Theorem 1.3, for some $c\geq 0.066,$

$$ S_{\pi_{K}}(X)\leq-c\log\log(X)+O_{\pi,K}(1). $$

Thus, we establish the desired estimate

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(n)|)|\ll_{\pi,P}X\log(X)^{-0.066}. $$

∎

### 4.2. Non-cuspidal base change

Let $K$ again denote the splitting field of $P(x)$ and assume that it is solvable. Additionally, assume that $\pi_{K}$ is not cuspidal and want to determine the size of

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(n)|)|. $$

#### Proof of Theorem 1.5.

First, let us determine some structure on these $\pi$ such that $\pi_{K}$ is not cuspidal. Since $K$ is solvable, there exists a chain of subfields:

$$ \mathbb{Q}=E_{0}\subsetneq E_{1}\subsetneq\ldots\subsetneq E_{n-1}\subsetneq E_{n}=K $$

with $E_{i+1}/E_{i}$ cyclic extensions of prime order. Since $\pi_{K}$ is not cuspidal, by Theorem 4.2, we know that there exists some index $i$ such that $[E_{i+1}:E_{i}]=2$ and

$$ \pi_{E_{i}}=\text{Ind}_{W_{E_{i+1}}}^{W_{E_{i}}}\theta, $$

where $\theta$ is a quasi-character of $\mathbb{A}_{E_{i+1}}^{\times}/E_{i+1}^{\times}.$ Furthermore, this fact tells us that

$$ \pi=\text{Ind}_{W_{E_{i+1}}}^{W_{\mathbb{Q}}}\theta. $$

Since $\pi$ is a two-dimensional representation, we claim that we must have that $E_{i}=\mathbb{Q}$ and $E_{i+1}$ a quadratic extension. Assume not – then $[E_{i+1}:\mathbb{Q}]>2$ . Since $\theta$ denotes a one-dimensional representation, $\dim(\pi)=[E_{i+1}:\mathbb{Q}]>2$ , immediately giving us a contradiction to our assumption that $\pi$ is a two-dimensional representation. Finally, since $E_{i+1}$ must be a quadratic extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ and $E_{i}\subsetneq E_{i+1}$ , we must have that $E_{i}=\mathbb{Q}.$

Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{F}$ sitting over $p$ . Then we know that

$$ \lambda_{\pi}(p)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p\end{subarray}}\theta(\mathfrak{p}). $$

Furthermore, for $\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}$ be a prime ideal sitting above $\mathfrak{p}$ , we also can see that

$$ \lambda_{\pi_{K}}(\mathfrak{P})=\lambda_{\pi}(N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P}))=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{F}\\
N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})=N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})\end{subarray}}\theta(\mathfrak{p}). $$

We return to the focus of Theorem 1.5:

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(P(n))|\ll_{P}X\exp\left(\sum_{p\leq X}\frac{\varrho(p)(|\lambda_{\pi}(p)|-1)}{p}\right). $$

Here we have again applied Theorem 2.1. Since we know that

$$ \sum_{p\leq X}\frac{\varrho(p)(|\lambda_{\pi}(p)|-1)}{p}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})\leq X\end{subarray}}\frac{|\lambda_{\pi_{K}}(\mathfrak{P})|-1}{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})}+O_{K,\pi}(1), $$

we find that we want to determine the size of

$$ \displaystyle S_{\pi_{K}}(X) \displaystyle:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})\leq X\end{subarray}}\frac{|\lambda_{\pi_{K}}(\mathfrak{P})|-1}{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})\leq X\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})}\Bigg(\Big|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{F}\\
N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})=N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})\end{subarray}}\hskip-14.22636pt\theta(\mathfrak{p})\Big|-1\Bigg)+O_{K,\pi}(1). $$

Since $\lambda_{\pi_{K}}(\mathfrak{P})$ only depends on the value of $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})=p$ , we group the summand by the prime ideals sitting above $p$ . It is worth observing as well that since we sum over prime ideals, only those primes satisfying that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})$ is prime will contribute to the growth of the summand; the other primes can be grouped into the $O_{K,\pi}(1)$ term. Thus, we achieve that

$$ S_{\pi_{K}}(X)=\sum_{p\leq X}\frac{\#\{\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}:N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})=p\}}{p}\left(\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{F}\\
N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p\end{subarray}}\theta(\mathfrak{p})\right|-1\right)+O_{K}(1). $$

Since $\theta$ is a unitary character of $F$ and $\lambda_{\pi}(p)\in\mathbb{R}$ , we have a stronger replacement for (3.10) that only utilizes the second moment (rather than both the second and fourth moment):

$$ \left|\sum_{N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p}\theta(\mathfrak{p})\right|\leq\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\left(\sum_{N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p}\theta^{2}(\mathfrak{p})\right). $$

Furthermore, if $p$ is a prime such that there does not exists $\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{F}$ with $N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p$ , then $\lambda_{\pi}(p)=0$ . Thus, we have the upper bound

$$ S_{\pi_{K}}(X)\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\leq X\\
\exists\mathfrak{p}:N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p\end{subarray}}\frac{\#\{\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}:N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})=p\}}{p}\\
-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\leq X\\
\not\exists\mathfrak{p}:N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p\end{subarray}}\frac{\#\{\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}:N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})=p\}}{p}\\
+\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\leq X\\
\exists\mathfrak{p}:N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p\end{subarray}}\frac{\#\{\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}:N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})=p\}}{p}\times\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{F}\\
N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p\end{subarray}}\theta^{2}(\mathfrak{p})\right). $$

We make the following comments about these sums: (1) for the first sum, this is equivalent to counting

$$ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})\leq X}\frac{\#\{\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}:N_{K/F}(\mathfrak{P})=\mathfrak{p}\}}{N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})}+O_{K}(1)=\frac{1}{2}\log\log(X)+O_{K}(1), $$

(2) the second sum is empty since $F\subset K$ , (3) after counting the number of ideals with $N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p$ , the third sum becomes

$$ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})\leq X\end{subarray}}\frac{\#\{\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}:N_{K/F}(\mathfrak{P})=\mathfrak{p}\}}{N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})}\cdot\theta^{2}(\mathfrak{p})+O_{K}(1)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})\leq X}\frac{\theta^{2}(N_{K/F}(\mathfrak{P}))}{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})}+O_{K}(1). $$

Thus, we know that

$$ S_{\pi_{K}}(X)\leq\frac{1}{2}\log\log(X)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})\leq X}\frac{\theta^{2}(N_{K/F}(\mathfrak{P}))}{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})}+O_{K}(1), $$

the upper bound of Theorem 1.5 (1) holds so long as $\theta^{2}\circ N_{K/F}$ is not a trivial character; in other words, we need to understand the $\text{GL}_{1}$ -base change of $\theta^{2}$ to the extension $K/E_{i}$ . Observe that if $\theta$ has infinite order, we never have that $\theta^{2}\circ N_{K/F}$ is trivial and Theorem 1.5 (1) falls.

#### 4.2.1. Return to the $\text{GL}_{1}$ -base change problem

By Proposition 4.1, we know that $\theta^{2}_{K}$ is trivial, i.e. noncuspidal, if and only if $\theta^{2}\in\widehat{G}$ for $G=\text{Gal}(K/F).$ Let us denote $\psi=\theta^{2}$ . We want to find another interpretation of our condition for when $\psi_{K}\equiv 1$ . Consider the following diagram, where $L_{\psi}$ (resp. $L_{\theta}$ ) denotes the ray class field of $\psi$ (resp. $\theta$ ). Since $\ker(\theta)\subset\ker(\psi)$ , we can take $L_{\psi}\subset L_{\theta}$ .

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{L_{\theta}K}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{L_{\theta}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{L_{\theta}\cap K}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{L_{\psi}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{L_{\psi}\cap K}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbb{Q}}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P(x)} $$

Let $G_{\psi}$ denote the Galois group of $L_{\psi}\cap F$ . We know that $\psi_{K}=1$ if and only if $\psi\in\widehat{G}$ ; we claim this can occur if and only if $\psi\in\widehat{G_{\psi}}$ , i.e. if and only if $\psi_{L_{\psi}\cap K}=1$ . This is clear since $\psi$ is a character of $\text{Gal}(L_{\psi}/F)$ , and hence the interpretation of $\psi$ as an element of $\widehat{G}$ must be as a character on $G_{\psi}$ extended trivially to $G$ . Now by definition of the ray class field of $L_{\psi}$ , this in fact tells us that $L_{\psi}=L_{\psi}\cap K$ , and hence we have that $L_{\psi}\subset K$ .

#### Lemma 4.3.

Let $\psi$ be a quasi-character of $F$ . Then $\psi_{K}=1$ if and only if $L_{\psi}\subset K$ , where $L_{\psi}$ denotes the kernel field of $\psi$ .

Now we recall that in our set up $\psi=\theta^{2}$ ; we want to determine when $L_{\theta^{2}}\subset K$ in order to determine when $\theta^{2}_{K}=1$ . Instead of analyzing the extension $L_{\psi}$ , we can instead work with $L_{\theta}$ . We can view $\theta^{2}$ as a character of the Galois group $\text{Gal}(L_{\theta}/F)$ and see that $\theta^{2}_{K}=1$ if and only if $\theta^{2}_{L_{\theta}\cap K}=1$ , and thus, if and only if $\theta^{2}\in\widehat{G_{\theta}}$ (where $G_{\theta}=\text{Gal}(L_{\theta}\cap K/F)$ ). In turn, this occurs if and only if $\text{Gal}(L_{\theta}/L_{\theta}\cap K)\subset\ker(\theta^{2}),$ where $\ker(\theta^{2})$ is considered as a subgroup of $\text{Gal}(L_{\theta}/F)$ . This completes Theorem 1.5 (1).

#### Remark 4.4.

We note that $\ker(\theta)=\{1\}\subset\text{Gal}(L_{\theta}/F)$ , but we can have that $\{1\}\subsetneq\ker(\theta^{2})$ . So, this condition does not necessarily imply that $L_{\theta}\subset K$ .

It remains to prove the second part of the theorem when $\text{Gal}(L_{\theta}/L_{\theta}\cap K)\subset\ker(\theta^{2}).$ We return to our original sum:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(n)|)| \displaystyle\geq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\leq X\\
P(n)\text{ squarefree}\end{subarray}}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(n)|)| \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\leq X\\
P(n)\text{ squarefree}\end{subarray}}\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_{F}\\
N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{a})=|P(n)|\end{subarray}}\theta(\mathfrak{a})\right| \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\leq X\\
P(n)\text{ squarefree}\end{subarray}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\mid P(n)\\
\exists\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{F}:N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p\end{subarray}}|1+\theta^{2}(\mathfrak{p})|. $$

Above, $\mathfrak{p}$ denotes a choice of prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{F}$ such that $N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p$ . Since $p\mid P(n)$ , there exists a $\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}$ such that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})=p$ and that $N_{K/F}(\mathfrak{P})=\mathfrak{p}$ ; let $\mathfrak{P}^{\prime}=N_{K/L_{\theta}\cap K}(\mathfrak{P})$ . Since $\text{Gal}(L_{\theta}/L_{\theta}\cap K)\subset\ker(\theta^{2})$ and hence $\theta_{L_{\theta}\cap K}^{2}=1$ , we know that

$$ \theta^{2}(\mathfrak{p})=\theta^{2}(N_{L_{\theta}\cap K/F}(\mathfrak{P}^{\prime}))=\theta^{2}_{L_{\theta}\cap K}(\mathfrak{P}^{\prime})=1. $$

Consequently,

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}|\lambda_{\pi}(|P(n)|)|\geq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\leq X\\
P(n)\text{ squarefree}\end{subarray}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\mid P(n)\\
\exists\mathfrak{p}:N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{p})=p\end{subarray}}2=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\leq X\\
P(n)\text{ squarefree}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_{F}\\
N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{a})=|P(n)|\end{subarray}}1. $$

This completes the proof of Theorem 1.5 (2). ∎

# Genuine and strongly genuine polynomials: With an application to the persistence of Galois groups under specialization

**Authors:** Dante Bonolis Address: Duke University, 120 Science Drive, Durham NC 27708 Email address: dante.bonolis@duke.edu , Lillian B. Pierce Address: Duke University, 120 Science Drive, Durham NC 27708 Email address: lillian.pierce@duke.edu and Katharine Woo Address: 450 Serra Mall, Building 380, Stanford CA 94305 Email address: khwoo98@stanford.edu

## Abstract

We develop the theory of strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , which have the property that the number of specializations $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ with $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=(x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ (respectively $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}$ ) such that $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (respectively over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ ) can be well-controlled quantitatively. We also develop the theory of a larger class of $n$ -genuine polynomials $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , which have the property that the number of specializations $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ with $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ (respectively $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}$ ) such that $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ splits completely over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (respectively over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ ) into factors that are linear in $Y$ can be well-controlled quantitatively. For each of these classes, we prove that there are four equivalent characterizations. As an application, we demonstrate that $n$ -genuine and strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials can be used to prove, for any polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , an upper bound for the number of specializations $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ with $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ such that the Galois group of the splitting field of $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is not isomorphic to the Galois group of the splitting field of $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ over $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ . We simultaneously prove analogous results over any number field.

#### Key words and phrases:

#### 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification

## 1. Introduction

Consider a polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ . If $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , then Hilbert’s Irreducibility Theorem supplies a dense set $V\subset\mathbb{Q}^{n}$ such that for all $\mathbf{x}\in V$ , $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ . A quantitative version would ask for an upper bound on the number of points of bounded height for which $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ is reducible. Analogously, if $G$ is the Galois group of the splitting field of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ over $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , one can ask a qualitative question—is it generically true that for $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}$ the Galois group $G(\mathbf{x})$ of the splitting field of $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is isomorphic to $G$ ?—or a quantitative version: an upper bound on the number of $\mathbf{x}$ of bounded height such that the Galois group $G(\mathbf{x})$ is not isomorphic to $G$ .

Both of these questions can be formulated in terms of counting points of bounded height in a thin set, a notion described in a lecture course of J.-P. Serre at the Collège de France in 1980-1981, which we cite in the form [Ser97]. To be precise, a subset $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ is thin if there is an algebraic variety $X$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ and a morphism $\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}$ such that

(i) $M\subset\pi(X(\mathbb{Q}))$ , and

(ii) the fibre of $\pi$ over the generic point is finite and $\pi$ has no rational section over $\mathbb{Q}$ .

Serre noted a qualitative statement (see §2.3 or [Ser97, §9.2-9.3]):

#### Lemma 1.1.

Let $K$ be a number field. Let $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathcal{O}_{K}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be irreducible over $K(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ .

- (i) There is a thin set $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ such that for $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\not\in M$ , $F(Y,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ is irreducible over $K$ .

- (ii) There is a thin set $M^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ such that for $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\not\in M^{\prime}$ , the Galois group of the splitting field of $F(Y,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ over $K$ is isomorphic to the Galois group of the splitting field of $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ over $K(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ .

These facts motivate a general quantitative question: how many points of bounded height can lie in a thin set? This was famously asked by Serre, and has stimulated research ever since (see §2.2). In the present paper, we focus on quantitative questions related to the persistence of Galois groups under specialization, working over an arbitrary number field. To set notation, let $K$ be a number field of degree $h$ with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . Fix an integral basis $w_{1},\dots,w_{h}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . For $x\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ with the unique representation $x=a_{1}w_{1}+\dots+a_{h}w_{h}$ , let $H_{K}(x)=(\max_{i}|a_{i}|)^{h}$ . For a vector $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n}$ , let $\|\mathbf{x}\|=\max_{i=1,\dots,n}H_{K}(x_{i}).$ Given a polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})$ with coefficients in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , let $\|F\|$ denote the maximum absolute norm of any coefficient of $F$ , namely for $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=\sum_{\vec{e}}b_{\vec{e}}Y^{e_{0}}X_{1}^{e_{1}}\dots X_{n}^{e_{n}}$ , set $\|F\|:=\max_{\vec{e}}|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_{\vec{e}})|.$ One of our aims is to prove the main claim of Cohen [Coh81, Theorem 2.1], for any polynomial (not required to be irreducible):

#### Theorem 1.2.

Let $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})\in\mathcal{O}_{K}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ have total degree at most $D$ and Galois group $G$ over $K(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ . For each $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n}$ , let $G(\mathbf{x})$ denote the Galois group of the splitting field of $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ over $K$ . There exists a constant $c$ depending only on $n,D,K$ such that for all $N\geq 3$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n},\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq N:\text{$G(\mathbf{x})\not\simeq G$}\}\ll_{n,D,K}\|F\|^{c}N^{n-\frac{1}{2}}\log N. $$

This bound has long stood as a baseline upper bound for the number of points in any thin set, and is also frequently cited in the context of persistence of Galois groups under specialization. The proof we describe here fills a subtle gap in the original proof when $n\geq 2$ by applying the theory of $n$ -genuine and strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials, which are generic classes of polynomials recently introduced in our work [BPW25]. Stronger quantitative results than Theorem 1.2 are now known (see §2.1), but we believe it is valuable to clarify the proof method reported in [Coh81, Theorem 2.1], and we expect the natural features of $n$ -genuine and strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials characterized in the present manuscript will be broadly useful. These features also pertain to persistence of a given factorization property under specialization of some of the variables, but now factoring over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , or over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ for varying primes $p$ . (The latter type of consideration plays an important role in applications of a sieve method, such as the large sieve or the polynomial sieve.)

More precisely, the class of $n$ -genuine polynomials $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is designed to provide good quantitative control for the number of $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=(x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ such that $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ splits completely (into linear factors with respect to $Y$ ) over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , as well as for the number of $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}$ such that $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ splits completely over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ (for all but finitely many $p$ ). The class of strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is designed to provide good quantitative control for the number of $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ such that $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , as well as for the number of $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}$ such that $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ (for all but finitely many $p$ ). We will in fact develop this theory more generally over any number field.

### 1.1. Introducing $n$ -genuine and strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials

Let $K$ be a number field.

#### Definition 1.3.

We say that a finite (nontrivial) extension $M$ of $K(\mathbf{X})=K(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is an $n$ -genuine extension if for every $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\in K[Y,\mathbf{X}]=K[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ such that

$$ M=K(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X})), $$

$G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ has nonzero degree in each of $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ . We say that $M$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension of $K(\mathbf{X})$ if for all subextensions $M^{\prime}$ satisfying

$$ K(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq M^{\prime}\subset M, $$

$M^{\prime}$ is an $n$ -genuine extension of $K(\mathbf{X})$ .

#### Definition 1.4.

A polynomial $G(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in K[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ that is monic in $Y$ and irreducible over $K(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is an $n$ -genuine polynomial if $K(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is an $n$ -genuine extension of $K(\mathbf{X}).$ A polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\in K[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ that is monic in $Y$ and irreducible over $K(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial if $K(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension of $K(\mathbf{X}).$

We will later also define a natural generalization of these classes, which specifies when a polynomial $G(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ or an extension of $K(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is $\ell$ -genuine, for some $1\leq\ell\leq n$ ; see Definition 5.3. The definitions above remain valid over an arbitrary field; see Remark 1.9.

Different characterizations of these classes can be more convenient, based on the application of interest, so we provide four equivalent characterizations in Theorem 4.2 (strongly $n$ -genuine case) and Theorem 6.7 ( $n$ -genuine case). Here, we summarize the natural consequences for each class; these consequences played an essential role in [BPW25] and will play an essential role in the recovery of Theorem 1.2 in this paper.

To set terminology, for an arbitrary field $\mathcal{K}$ , and a given algebraic closure $\overline{\mathcal{K}}$ , we say a monic polynomial $f(Y,Z)\in\mathcal{K}[Y,Z]$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathcal{K}}$ if we can write

$$ f(Y,Z)=f_{1}(Y,Z)f_{2}(Y,Z) $$

with $f_{1},f_{2}\in\overline{\mathcal{K}}[Y,Z]$ and $1\leq\deg f_{1}<\deg f$ . We say $f(Y,Z)$ splits completely over $\overline{\mathcal{K}}$ if we can write

$$ f(Y,Z)=\prod_{j}(Y-Q_{j}(Z)) $$

with $Q_{j}(Z)\in\overline{\mathcal{K}}[Z]$ for all $j$ .

For example, the property of being $n$ -genuine over $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ allows us to control quantitatively how many specializations of a polynomial split completely over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}.$ (We also prove versions of the following results over any number field; see Theorem 6.11 and Theorem 4.7, respectively.)

#### Theorem 1.5 (Genuine).

Let $n\geq 2$ . Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be an $n$ -genuine polynomial of total degree $D$ . Then for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}\cap[-B,B]^{n-1}:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ splits completely over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$}\}\ll_{n,D}B^{n-2}. $$

Also, there exists a finite set $\mathcal{E}$ of exceptional primes, with $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ , such that for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ splits completely over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$}\}\ll_{n,D}p^{n-2}. $$

The property of being strongly $n$ -genuine allows us to control, just as effectively, how many specializations are reducible, even though this is (in general) potentially a much larger class than those specializations that split completely:

#### Theorem 1.6 (Strongly genuine).

Let $n\geq 2$ . Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial of total degree $D$ . Then for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}\cap[-B,B]^{n-1}:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$}\}\ll_{n,D}B^{n-2}. $$

Also, there exists a finite set $\mathcal{E}$ of exceptional primes, with $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ , such that for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$}\}\ll_{n,D}p^{n-2}. $$

#### Remark 1.7 (Generic).

The classes of $n$ -genuine and strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials are generic, which enhances their utility. Any strongly $n$ -genuine extension is $n$ -genuine; thus any strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial is $n$ -genuine. Let $\mathcal{M}(D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})$ denote the moduli space of polynomials in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ comprised of polynomials that are monic in $Y$ and satisfy $\deg_{Y}(F)=D$ and $\deg_{X_{i}}(F)\leq k_{i}$ ; this is a closed irreducible subset of the moduli space of polynomials. Strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials are generic in $\mathcal{M}(D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})$ ; hence $n$ -genuine polynomials are also generic in this sense. This is a consequence of [BPW25, Cor. 3.2, 3.3]; in fact those results confirm that an even smaller family, the strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials, a subset of the strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials, are generic in this sense.

### 1.2. The strategy

To see how these classes of polynomials assist in proving Theorem 1.2, we set the following notation. Let us denote by $\Omega_{F}$ the splitting field of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ over $K(\bfX)$ . Define the number field $L_{F}=\Omega_{F}\cap\overline{K}$ , so there is an intermediate extension $K(\bfX)\subset L_{F}(\bfX)\subset\Omega_{F}$ . We will let $M_{F}(Y,\bfX)\in L_{F}(\bfX)[Y]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\Omega_{F}$ over $L_{F}(\bfX)$ ; we may assume that $M_{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is monic in $Y$ and irreducible over $L_{F}(\mathbf{X})$ . Using the properties of strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials, we will prove:

#### Theorem 1.8 (Special case of Theorem 1.2).

Let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be a number field with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . Let $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})\in\mathcal{O}_{K}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ have total degree at most $D$ and Galois group $G$ over $K(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ . Suppose that

$$ M_{F}(Y,\mathbf{X}) n $$

For each $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n}$ , let $G(\mathbf{x})$ denote the Galois group of the splitting field of $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ over $K$ . There exists a constant $c$ depending only on $n,D,K$ such that for all $N\geq 3$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n},\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq N:\text{$G(\mathbf{x})\not\simeq G$}\}\ll_{n,D,K}\|F\|^{c}N^{n-\frac{1}{2}}\log N. $$

Indeed, with the additional hypothesis (1.1), the original proof given in [Coh81, Thm. 2.1] can proceed. Moreover, we will show that a weaker alternative hypothesis can replace the extra hypothesis (1.1) and still yield the conclusion. The weaker alternative hypothesis is ultimately easier to work with, although more complicated to state; let us call it (*) for the moment. (Precisely, (*) is (5.2), and Theorem 5.2 proves the analogue of Theorem 1.8 under (*)). To recover Theorem 1.2 in full, we will use the properties of $n$ -genuine polynomials in order to reduce any instance of Theorem 1.2 to a special case where (*) holds and the original proof of [Coh81, Thm. 2.1] can proceed. More precisely, given a linear transformation $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ , let $F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,\sigma(\mathbf{X}))$ . We will show that for any $F$ considered by Theorem 1.2 there is a linear transformation $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ (with small norm) such that the minimal polynomial $M_{F_{\sigma}}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ (of the splitting field of $F_{\sigma}$ ) acquires property (*), so that $F_{\sigma}$ lies in a special case for which the outcome of Theorem 1.2 is already known (by Theorem 5.2). We will then bound the number of $\|\mathbf{x}\|$ counted by Theorem 1.2 for $F$ , by a related count for $F_{\sigma}$ . The fact that the linear transformation $\sigma$ has small norm will allow Theorem 1.2 to inherit the (at most) polynomial dependence on $\|F\|$ from the special case we apply to $F_{\sigma}$ . (For further remarks on dependence on $\|F\|$ , see §2.2 and in particular Remark 2.1.)

### 1.3. Outline of the paper

In §2 we briefly describe some relevant previous literature, and record several standard lemmas. In §3 we outline the gap for $n\geq 2$ in the original proof of Theorem 1.2, illustrate its relation to Noether’s lemma, and show how to fill the gap if we assume an additional hypothesis in a key lemma. In §4 we describe the general theory of strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials, characterize their essential properties, and prove Theorem 1.6 (also over any number field). In §5 we briefly show how this theory allows the original method of [Coh81] to proceed (under an additional hypothesis), resulting in the special case of Theorem 1.8, as well as the special case Theorem 5.2 with condition (*). To complete the recovery of Theorem 1.2 in full, we also require the larger class of $n$ -genuine polynomials. Thus in §6 we describe the general theory of $n$ -genuine polynomials, characterize their essential properties, and prove Theorem 1.5 (also over any number field). Finally, in §7 we employ $n$ -genuine and strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials to complete the proof of Theorem 1.2.

### 1.4. Notation and terminology

For clarity, we reserve $K$ to denote the number field considered in Theorem 1.2. We will also let $k$ denote any fixed number field. When we consider an arbitrary field (finite or infinite) our generic notation will be $\mathcal{K}$ .

For a given subset $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , denote $\mathbf{X}_{I}=(X_{i})_{i\in I}$ . For example, if $I=\{2,\ldots,n\}$ then $\mathbf{X}_{I}=(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})$ , so that as a function field $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})=k(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})$ , and a polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ can depend on $Y$ and $X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}$ but not $X_{1}$ . Denote $I^{c}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus I$ . With a slight abuse of notation with respect to the ordering of variables, we define $G_{\mathbf{x}_{I}}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}}):=G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{I})$ so that $X_{i}$ is specialized to $x_{i}$ for each $i\in I$ for a given $\mathbf{x}_{I}\in k^{|I|}$ , while $Y$ and $X_{i}$ for $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus I$ are indeterminates. Given a polynomial $G(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , we let $\deg G$ denote the total degree of $G$ while $\deg_{Y}G$ denotes the degree of $G$ as a polynomial in $Y$ . Additionally we may specify the total degree of $G$ as a polynomial in a subset of the variables; for example, $\deg_{Y,X_{1}}G(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ denotes the total degree of $G$ as a polynomial in $Y,X_{1}$ . We say $G(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is monic in $Y$ if

$$ G(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{D_{Y}}+Y^{D_{Y}-1}f_{D_{Y}-1}(\mathbf{x})+\cdots+Yf_{1}(\mathbf{X})+f_{0}(\mathbf{X}) $$

for polynomials $f_{j}(\mathbf{X})$ .

Given an extension of fields $\mathcal{L}/\mathcal{K}$ , $\mathcal{L}$ is said to be a regular extension of $\mathcal{K}$ if the extension is separable, and moreover $\mathcal{K}$ is integrally closed in $\mathcal{L}$ , that is, $\overline{\mathcal{K}}\cap\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{K}$ . One of the outcomes of the present work is that the notion of being strongly $n$ -genuine is equivalent to certain extensions being regular. Precisely, let $k$ be a number field, let $H(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathcal{O}_{k}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be irreducible over $k(\mathbf{X})=k(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , and define $\mathcal{L}_{H}=k(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(H(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ . In the case $n=1$ for example, $H(Y,X_{1})$ is a strongly $1$ -genuine polynomial if and only if $\mathcal{L}_{H}$ is a regular extension of $k$ , namely $\overline{k}\cap\mathcal{L}_{H}=k$ . (This is proved in Theorem 4.1; see also Lemma 5.4.) More generally, $H(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial if and only if for each subset $I^{\prime}\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$ that omits one index, $\mathcal{L}_{H}$ is a regular extension of $L(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ (Theorem 4.2).

#### 1.4.1. Comparison to original notation

For clarity, we distinguish once and for all between the notation of Cohen [Coh81] and Serre [Ser97], and the notation we employ. In Cohen’s work, for a polynomial $F$ with coefficients in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , recall that Theorem 1.2 uses $\|F\|$ to denote the maximum absolute norm of any coefficient of $F$ . This agrees conceptually with Cohen’s work, but the notation is different. In the original paper, Cohen uses the notation $|F|$ to denote the maximum absolute norm of the coefficients of $F$ , and the notation $\|F\|=\log|F|$ . (Cohen’s statement of Theorem 1.2 also allows the more general setting that $K/k$ is a finite extension of number fields, and $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{O}_{k}^{n}$ varies in the ring of integers of the smaller field, but we do not pursue that variant here.)

The height $\|\mathbf{x}\|$ we have defined for $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n}$ agrees with Cohen’s notation. In Serre’s original discussion [Ser97, §13], a slightly different height is considered: for $x\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , temporarily define

$$ |x|:=\max_{\sigma:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}}|\sigma(x)|. $$

For a vector $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n}$ , then Serre takes $\|x\|_{\mathrm{Serre}}=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_{i}|.$ In comparison with Cohen’s choice of height, note that for our fixed integral basis $w_{1},\ldots,w_{h}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ and any embedding $\sigma:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ , we have that

$$ |\sigma(x)|\leq|a_{1}||\sigma(w_{1})|+\dots+|a_{h}||\sigma(w_{h})|. $$

Hence, $|x|\ll_{w_{1},\dots,w_{h},K}H_{K}(x)^{1/h}.$ On the other hand, note that for any embedding $\sigma:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ we have that

$$ \sigma(x)=a_{1}\sigma(w_{1})+\dots+a_{h}\sigma(w_{h}), $$

and hence

$$ \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{1}(x)\\
\sigma_{2}(x)\\
\vdots\\
\sigma_{h}(x)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{1}(w_{1})&\sigma_{1}(w_{2})&\dots&\sigma_{1}(w_{h})\\
\sigma_{2}(w_{1})&\sigma_{2}(w_{2})&\dots&\sigma_{2}(w_{n})\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
\sigma_{h}(w_{1})&\sigma_{h}(w_{2})&\dots&\sigma_{h}(w_{h})\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}\\
a_{2}\\
\vdots\\
a_{h}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Since $w_{1},\dots,w_{h}$ is an integral basis, the above matrix is invertible and thus we also have that

$$ H_{K}(x)^{1/h}=\max_{1\leq i\leq h}|a_{i}|\ll_{w_{1},\dots,w_{h},K}|x|. $$

Thus, Cohen’s choice of height (and hence our choice) is comparable to Serre’s height in the sense that $\|x\|\ll_{K,w_{1},\dots,w_{n}}\|x\|_{\mathrm{Serre}}^{h}\ll_{K,w_{1},\dots,w_{n}}\|x\|.$

#### Remark 1.9 (Arbitrary fields).

In this paper, we develop the theory of $n$ -genuine and strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials in the setting of number fields, but the definitions are valid over an arbitrary field $\mathcal{K}$ . To our knowledge, the only proofs in the characterization theorems of §4 and §6 which would require modification when working over an arbitrary field rather than a number field would be Lemma 4.4 (which is used to show (II) for $i_{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ (IV) for $i_{0}$ in Theorem 4.2), and Lemma 6.9 (which is used to prove (II) for $i_{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ (III) for $i_{0}$ in Theorem 6.7).

## 2. Previous literature and preliminaries

### 2.1. Recent literature beyond Theorem 1.2

Let $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , and of degree $d$ in $Y$ . Considering $F$ as a polynomial over the function field $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , let $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d}$ denote its roots in an algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})}$ ; the roots are distinct, under the condition that $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is irreducible. The Galois group $G$ of $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is a subgroup of the symmetric group $S_{d}$ ; that is, it acts on the roots by permutations, and there is an injective homomorphism $\rho:G\hookrightarrow S_{d}$ . If $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ is chosen such that $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ is also irreducible, then the Galois group $G(\mathbf{x})$ of $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is a subgroup of $G$ , determined up to conjugation. Indeed, let $\Delta(\mathbf{X})$ denote the discriminant of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ as a polynomial in $Y$ ; note that $\Delta(\mathbf{X})\not\equiv 0$ since $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ . (Indeed, by the Hilbert Irreducibility Theorem, there is some $\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}$ such that $F(Y,\mathbf{x}_{0})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , hence separable, and thus square-free, so that $\Delta(\mathbf{x}_{0})\neq 0.$ ) For all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ such that $\deg F(Y,\mathbf{x})=d$ and $\Delta(\mathbf{x})\neq 0$ , there exist injective homormorphisms $\rho_{\mathbf{x}}:G(\mathbf{x})\hookrightarrow S_{d}$ and $\iota:G(\mathbf{x})\hookrightarrow G$ such that $\rho_{\mathbf{x}}=\rho\circ\iota$ ; see [CD17, Lemma 1]. (By applying the trivial bound in Lemma 2.3, we can see that these two conditions on $\mathbf{x}$ are verified for all but $\ll_{n,\deg F}B^{n-1}$ values of $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cap[-B,B]^{n},$ for example.) Thus for any subgroup $K\subseteq G$ , one can ask for an upper bound on

$$ M(K,G;B):=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cap[-B,B]^{n}:\text{splitting field of $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ has Galois group $K$}\}. $$

In this setting, Castillo and Dietmann have proved that for any subgroup $K$ of $G$ ,

$$ M(K,G;B)\ll_{F,\varepsilon}B^{n-1+\delta_{K}+\varepsilon}\qquad\text{for any $\varepsilon>0$,} $$

in which $\delta_{K}:=[G:K]^{-1}$ , where $[G:K]$ denotes the index of $K$ in $G$ , so that $\delta_{K}\leq 1/2$ for any proper subgroup. For $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ irreducible, this implies a sharper result (for certain groups $G$ ) than Theorem 1.2 (over $\mathbb{Q}$ ), since it implies that

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cap[-B,B]^{n}:G(\mathbf{x})\not\simeq G\}\ll_{F,\varepsilon}B^{n-1+\gamma_{G}+\varepsilon}\qquad\text{for any $\varepsilon>0$}, $$

in which

$$ \gamma_{G}=\max\{[G:K]^{-1}:\text{$K$ is a proper subgroup of $G$}\}. $$

For $G=S_{d}$ , note that $\gamma_{G}=1/2$ , but $\gamma_{G}$ can be smaller for certain other groups. For example, if $G=A_{d}$ with $d\geq 5$ then $\delta_{G}=1/d$ ; see [CD17] for details. Castillo and Dietmann’s method employs Galois resolvents and results from the determinant method on bounding the number of integral points on curves; this strategy generalizes earlier work of Dietmann [Die12]. Zywina has also obtained (2.1) over any number field, as long as $K$ is any subset of $G$ that is stable under conjugation (for example, when $K$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ ); that method employed the larger sieve in place of the large sieve [Zyw10, unpublished]. Castillo and Dietmann remarked in [CD17] that in principle their method should allow the dependence on $F$ in the implicit constant to be quantified.

Our focus in this paper centers on $n\geq 2$ , but we remark that certain improvements have been achieved in the case $n=1$ ; most recently, Parades and Sasyk have achieved a quantification of the implicit constant in (2.1) for $n=1$ , and removed the $B^{\varepsilon}$ factor completely [PS24, Thm. 1.4]. This employs a version of the $p$ -adic determinant method on bounding the number of integral points on curves, and their work is also valid over any global field. If $K$ denotes the global field, the dependence on $F$ in the implicit constant is polylogarithmic in the so-called $K$ -relative height of $F$ , which in the case $K=\mathbb{Q}$ is simply $\|F\|$ , the maximum absolute value of any coefficient of $F$ .

An upper bound (such as Theorem 1.2) that explicitly controls the dependence on $\|F\|$ is interesting, for example, because it allows one to deduce an explicit estimate for the “smallest” specialization $\mathbf{x}$ such that $G(\mathbf{x})\simeq G$ . (We return to the question of dependence on $\|F\|$ in the next section, and in particular in Remark 2.1.)

### 2.2. Relation to thin sets of type II

Theorem 1.2 has frequently been cited in the study of thin sets. Any thin set in $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ is a finite union of two types of thin set, called Type I and Type II (see [Ser97, Ch. 9], [Ser92, §3.1] or [BPW26]).

Type I: A thin set $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ is of type I if there is a Zariski-closed subvariety $V\subsetneq\mathbb{A}^{n}$ such that $M\subset V(\mathbb{Q})$ .

Type II: A projective thin set $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ is of type II if there is an irreducible affine algebraic variety $Z$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $\dim Z=n$ , and a dominant morphism $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}$ with generically finite fibres, of degree $d\geq 2$ , with $M\subset\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q}))$ .

The types can also be defined analogously over any number field $K$ , and the discussion of this section applies in such generality, although we focus on $\mathbb{Q}$ for simplicity. There is a useful interpretation of the Type I/Type II dichotomy in terms of polynomials, following Serre [Ser97, §9.1]. If $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ is an affine thin set of type I, then there is a nonconstant polynomial $G\in\mathbb{Q}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ such that

$$ M\subset\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}:G(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0\}. $$

On the other hand, given an irreducible $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})[Y]$ , a polynomial in $Y$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ , then the following set is an affine thin set of type II:

$$ \{\bfx\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}:\text{$\bfx$ not a pole of any coefficient of $F$, $F(Y,\bfx)=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Q}$}\}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q}). $$

By replacing $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ by a multiple $\tilde{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ of $F$ by an appropriate polynomial in $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ so that $\tilde{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ , the set depicted above is contained in the set

$$ \{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}:\text{$\tilde{F}(Y,\mathbf{x})=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Q}$}\}. $$

Thus it is no loss of generality to assume that within (2.2), $F$ is a polynomial $Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ . Moreover, modulo a thin set of type I, every thin set of type II takes the form of (2.2); see [BPW26, Lemma 1.2].

For a quantitative statement, we now suppose $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ is a thin set, and for each integral point $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ define $\|\mathbf{x}\|=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_{i}|$ . Then define the counting function

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M,B):=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z}):\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B\}. $$

Certainly $N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M,B)\ll_{n}B^{n}$ is trivially true for all $B\geq 1$ . Serre established a baseline upper bound: for any thin set $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ , for some unspecified $C(M)\geq 1$ and $0<\gamma(M)<1$ ,

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M,B)\leq C(M)B^{n-1/2}(\log(B+2))^{\gamma(M)},\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$.} $$

Serre’s motivation in [Ser97, Ch. 13 Thm. 1] included questions of Hilbert irreducibility, and specialization of Galois groups, as well as hilbertian fields. (A field $k$ is hilbertian precisely when for all $n\geq 1$ , $\mathbb{P}^{n}(k)$ is not a thin set; $\mathbb{Q}$ and all number fields are hilbertian [Ser97, §9.5-9.6].) Serre observed that (2.4) is in fact sharp (up to the power of log), although he predicted a stronger upper bound in an analogous projective setting. We leave that broader discussion to the recent survey [BPW26], but remark here that if we define

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B):=\#\{\bfx\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{ $F(Y,\bfx)=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$}\}, $$

it can be shown that to prove (2.4) it suffices to prove that for all polynomials $F$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ that are absolutely irreducible (that is, irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ ),

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\leq C(F)B^{n-\frac{1}{2}}(\log(B+2))^{\gamma(F)}\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$,} $$

in which $C(F)$ and $\gamma(F)$ are positive constants that may depend on $F$ . Note that Theorem 1.2 also implies (2.4). Indeed, if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is irreducible and $F(Y,\mathbf{x})=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$ , then $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ is certainly reducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , so that $G(\mathbf{x})$ cannot be isomorphic to $G$ . Consequently Theorem 1.2 implies (2.6) (and hence also a version of (2.4)) in which $C(F)$ has at most polynomial dependence on $\|F\|$ , and $\gamma(F)=1$ .

As remarked above, (2.4) is sharp, as can be demonstrated by considering the polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=Y^{2}-(X_{1}+\cdots+X_{n})$ . For certain special shapes of polynomial $F$ , better bounds than (2.4) have been obtained, in works such as [Mun09, HBP12, Bon21, BP26] and most recently by Buggenhaut, Cluckers, Salberger, Santens, and Vermeulen [BCS+25] and by the present authors [BPW25]. The former paper [BCS+25] improves the main exponent in (2.4) to $n-1$ if $F$ has the special form $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=F_{\mathrm{top}}(Y,\mathbf{X})+F_{0}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ in which $F_{0}(Y^{e},\mathbf{X})$ has total degree strictly smaller than $de$ , and for some $d\geq 2$ ,

$$ F_{\mathrm{top}}(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{d}+Y^{d-1}f_{1}(\mathbf{X})+\cdots+Yf_{d-1}(\mathbf{X})+f_{d}(\mathbf{X}) $$

is an absolutely irreducible polynomial, in which each $f_{i}$ is homogeneous of degree $e\cdot i$ , so that $F_{\mathrm{top}}(Y^{e},\mathbf{X})$ is homogeneous of degree $de$ . The bound in [BCS+25] exhibits at most polynomial dependence on $\|F\|$ . The latter paper [BPW25] motivated the initial construction of the classes of $n$ -genuine and strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials. Its main theorem improves the main exponent in (2.4) to $n-1+1/(n+1)$ if for some integer $m\geq 2$ , $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is a polynomial in $Y^{m}$ , and $F$ has the property that for any linear transformation $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ , $F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ is strongly $n$ -genuine. (If $m=1$ , the same result is obtained, but conditional on GRH.) The bound in [BPW25] exhibits weaker dependence on $\|F\|$ , in the sense that it has at most polylogarithmic dependence on $\|F\|$ ; this is qualitatively the same order of dependence on $\|F\|$ as found by Parades and Sasyk [PS24] in their work on quantitative HIT, mentioned earlier.

#### Remark 2.1 (Dependence on $\|F\|$ ).

Can an upper bound for the number of integral points in an affine thin set be made uniform, that is, independent of the coefficients of the defining polynomial(s) of the thin set? For an affine thin set of type I, the answer is famously yes (the subject of the well-known Uniform Dimension Growth Conjecture, surveyed in [BPW26]). For an affine thin set of type II, the answer is not yet clear, and a subtlety has recently been raised. In particular, we have constructed examples in [BPW26, Thm. 1.6] that violate a putative uniform upper bound for integral points in affine thin sets of type II. Precisely, let $n\geq 1$ be given. As $k$ varies over positive integers, there is a family of thin sets $M_{k}\in\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ of type II, defined by polynomials $F_{k}(Y,X_{1},\dots,X_{n})$ with $\|F_{k}\|=k$ , for which the counting function defined in (2.3) (or in this case, equivalently (2.5)) has the following property: there is no constant $c>0$ such that

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M_{k},B)\ll_{n,\deg F_{k}}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{c} $$

can hold as $k\rightarrow\infty$ , with an implicit constant independent of $k$ . In particular for $n=1$ , there is no universal constant $C(n,d)$ (dependent only on dimension and degree) such that $N_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}(M,B)\leq C(n,d)$ for all thin sets $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{1}$ and $B\geq 1$ . The examples do not violate, however, a putative uniform upper bound of the form

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M_{k},B)\ll_{n,\deg F_{k},\varepsilon}B^{n-1+\varepsilon} $$

for a given $\varepsilon>0$ .

Such questions on uniformity are also relevant to studying quantitative Hilbert irreducibility theorems, by the inclusion properties recorded in Lemma 1.1. The question of uniformity, in this context, has been raised by Yasumoto [Yas88]. Let $K$ be a number field. Yasumoto proved that if $F(Y,X,T)\in K[Y,X,T]$ is irreducible, then there is a constant $C(F)$ such that for each $t\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , if $F(Y,X,t)$ is irreducible then $F(Y,x_{t},t)$ is irreducible for some natural number $x_{t}<C(F)$ [Yas88, Thm. 2]. This exhibits partial uniformity, in that $C(F)$ is independent of $t$ . Yasumoto furthermore asked Open Problem 1: For each $d\geq 1$ , is there a constant $C(d)$ such that for every irreducible polynomial $F(Y,T)\in K[Y,T]$ with $\deg F\leq d$ , there is a natural number $t<C(d)$ with $F(Y,t)$ irreducible? The observations above, for thin sets, suggest the answer may be no.

### 2.3. The qualitative result of Lemma 1.1

For clarity, we recapitulate the proof of [Ser97, Prop. 1, 2 §9.2] for Lemma 1.1; see also [Ser92, Prop. 3.3.1 and 3.3.5].

#### Proof.

We start by proving (ii): Let $\Omega_{F}$ be the Galois closure of $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})$ over $K(\bfX)$ , $L(Y,\bfX)\in\mathcal{O}_{K}[Y,\bfX]$ its minimal polynomial over $K(\bfX)$ , and $G=\Gal(\Omega_{F}/K(\bfX))$ . Consider $\mathcal{X}=\textbf{Spec}(K(\bfX)[Y]/L)=\textbf{Spec}(\Omega_{F})$ . Then the inclusion $K(\bfX)\hookrightarrow\Omega_{F}$ , induces a morphism $\pi:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}$ . Then for every proper subgroup $H\leq G$ , one can consider $\mathcal{X}/H=\textbf{Spec}((\Omega_{F})^{H})$ . Since $(\Omega_{F})^{G}=K(\bfX)$ , we get a dominant morphism

$$ \pi_{H}:\mathcal{X}/H\rightarrow\mathcal{X}/G=\textbf{Spec}((\Omega_{F})^{G})=\textbf{Spec}(K(\bfX))=\mathbb{A}^{n}, $$

of degree $[G:H]>1$ . Now the set $T\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(K)$ defined by

$$ T:=\bigcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}H\subset G\\
H\text{ proper subgroup}\end{subarray}}\pi_{H}((\mathcal{X}/H)(K)), $$

is a thin set.

It remains to show that if $\bfx\in K^{n}$ is such that $G(\bfx)$ , the Galois group of $F(Y,\bfx)$ over $K$ , is strictly smaller than $G$ , then $\bfx\in T$ . In what follows we are going to denote by $d=\deg L=[\Omega_{F}:K(\bfX)]$ , and for every $\bfx$ , $\Omega_{\bfx}$ will denote the Galois closure of $F(Y,\bfx)$ over $K$ , and $G(\bfx)=\Gal(\Omega_{\bfx}/K)$ . Let $\gamma$ be a root of $L(Y,\bfX)$ . Then we claim that if $G(\bfx)\not\simeq G$ , then

$$ R(Y):=\prod_{\sigma\in G(\bfx)}(Y-\sigma(\gamma))\not\in K(\bfX)[Y]. $$

Indeed, since $G(\bfx)\not\simeq G$ , then $\deg R=|G(\mathbf{x})|<|G|=\deg L$ , yet $L$ is the minimal polynomial of $\gamma$ over $K(\mathbf{X})$ ; hence $R$ cannot lie in $K(\mathbf{X})[Y]$ . On the other hand, if we denote $\gamma_{\bfx}=\gamma\mod\bfx$ , one gets

$$ r(Y):=\prod_{\sigma\in G(\bfx)}(Y-\sigma(\gamma_{\bfx}))\in K[Y]; $$

this is an element of $K[Y]$ since $r(Y)$ is certainly in $\Omega_{\bfx}[Y]$ and is invariant under the action of $G(\mathbf{x})=\Gal(\Omega_{\bfx}/K)$ .

Let $K(\bfX)\subset M\subset\Omega_{F}$ be the minimal extensions which contains all the coefficients of $R(Y)$ , i.e. $R(Y)\in M[Y]$ . Then since $M\supsetneq K(\bfX)$ , we have $\Gal(\Omega_{F}/M)=H\subsetneq G$ , and $M=(\Omega_{F})^{H}$ . Let $S(Y,\bfX)$ be the minimal polynomial of $M$ over $K(\bfX)$ , i.e. $K(\bfX)[Y]/S=M=(\Omega_{F})^{H}$ . Hence $\mathcal{X}/H=\textbf{Spec}(K(\bfX)[Y]/S)$ . On the other hand, since $r(Y)\in K[Y]$ (so that specializing to $\mathbf{x}$ collapses $M$ to $K$ ), then $S(Y,\bfx)$ is solvable over $K$ and hence $\bfx\in\pi_{H}((\mathcal{X}/H)(K))$ , as we wanted. Thus, if $\mathbf{x}\in K^{n}$ satisfies that $G(\mathbf{x})\not\simeq G$ , we must have that $\mathbf{x}\in T$ .

For part $(i)$ , it is enough to observe that if $\bfx\in K$ is such that $F(Y,\bfx)$ is reducible, then $G(\bfx)$ is strictly smaller than $G$ , hence one can apply part (ii). ∎

### 2.4. Useful lemmas

We recall a version of Hilbert’s Irreducibility Theorem from [FJ23, Ch. 13 and Ch. 14 §3] and [Lan83, Ch. 9, pp. 233-235].

#### Lemma 2.2 (Hilbert).

Let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be a number field and $F_{1},...,F_{s}\in K(X_{1},...,X_{n},T_{1},...,T_{r})$ be polynomials in $n+r$ variables, irreducible over $K$ . There exists a dense subset $U\subset\mathbb{A}^{r}_{K}$ such that for any $(t_{1},...,t_{r})\in U$ , $F_{1}(X_{1},...,X_{n},t_{1},...,t_{r}),...,F_{s}(X_{1},...,X_{n},t_{1},...,t_{r})$ are irreducible over $K$ .

We require a trivial bound:

#### Lemma 2.3 (Trivial bound, Schwartz-Zippel).
