Since $f(Y,Z)$ is irreducible over $\mathcal{K}(Z)$ , the automorphisms of $\mathcal{K}(Z)[Y]/(f(Y,Z))$ act transitively on the roots of $f(Y,Z)$ . Since $f(Y,Z)$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathcal{K}}$ ,

$$ f(Y,Z)=\prod_{\sigma_{j}}(Y-\sigma_{j}(Q(Z))) $$

for some polynomial $Q(Z)\in\overline{\mathcal{K}}[Z],$ and $\sigma_{j}$ varying over the group of embeddings of the extension $\mathcal{K}(Z)[Y]/(f(Y,Z))$ in its Galois closure. We observe that $\sigma_{j}(Q(Z))\in\overline{\mathcal{K}}[Z]$ to complete the proof. ∎

We will later call upon the following equivalence:

#### Lemma 6.4.

Let $\mathcal{K}$ be a field. If $f(Y,Z)\in\mathcal{K}[Y,Z]$ is irreducible over $\mathcal{K}(Z)$ , then $f(Y,Z)$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathcal{K}}$ if and only if

$$ (\mathcal{K}(Z)[Y]/f(Y,Z)\cap\overline{\mathcal{K}})(Z)=\mathcal{K}(Z)[Y]/f(Y,Z). $$

#### Proof.

If $f$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathcal{K}}$ then by Lemma 6.3, all the roots of $f$ lie in $\overline{\mathcal{K}}[Z]$ , so that (6.5) holds. In the other direction, since $f$ is irreducible over $\mathcal{K}(Z)$ then for any root $W$ of $f$ , $\mathcal{K}(Z)[Y]/f(Y,Z)\simeq\mathcal{K}(Z)[W]$ . Thus if (6.5) holds then $(\mathcal{K}(Z)[Y]/f(Y,Z)\cap\overline{\mathcal{K}})(Z)\simeq\mathcal{K}(Z)[W]$ , so that $W$ must lie in $\mathcal{K}^{\prime}(Z)$ for some finite extension $\mathcal{K}^{\prime}/\mathcal{K}$ . That is to say, $W\in\overline{\mathcal{K}}(Z)$ , and then this implies that a factorization of the form (6.1) holds, so that $f$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathcal{K}}$ . ∎

#### Remark 6.5.

Lemma 6.4 plays a similar role in the proof of our classification theorem for $n$ -genuine polynomials to the role that Lemma 4.3 plays in Theorem 4.2 for the classification of strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials. They are related in the following way. Over a number field $k$ , Lemma 4.3 gives that if $f(Y,Z)$ is absolutely irreducible, then $M_{f}:=\overline{k}\cap(k(Z)[Y]/f(Y,Z))$ satisfies $M_{f}=k$ . Lemma 6.4 states that if $f(Y,Z)$ does not have a linear factor over $\overline{k}$ (a strictly weaker condition than being absolutely irreducible), then $M_{f}(Z)\subsetneq k(Z)[Y]/f(Y,Z)$ . The latter is a strictly weaker requirement than $M_{f}=k$ .

Next we characterize the key properties of $n$ -genuine polynomials. For clarity, we separate the cases $n=1$ and $n\geq 2$ .

#### Theorem 6.6 ( $1$ -Genuine).

Let $k/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite extension. Let $H\in\mathcal{O}_{k}(X_{1})[Y]$ be irreducible over $k(X_{1})$ , monic in $Y$ , and of total degree $D$ . Define $\mathcal{L}_{H}=k(X_{1})[Y]/(H(Y,X_{1}))$ . The following are equivalent:

(I) $H$ is a $1$ -genuine polynomial, that is to say, $k(X_{1})[Y]/H(Y,X_{1})$ is a $1$ -genuine extension of $k(X_{1})$ .

(II) $(\overline{k}\cap\mathcal{L}_{H})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{H}.$

(III) $H(Y,X_{1})$ does not have a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ .

(IV) Expanding the polynomial as $H(Y,X_{1})=\sum_{\ell+m\leq D}a_{\ell,m}Y^{\ell}X_{1}^{m},$ the form $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(a_{\ell,m})_{\ell,m})$ defined as in (6.4), when evaluated at the coefficients $a_{\ell,m}$ , is a nonzero integer.

#### Theorem 6.7 ( $n$ -Genuine).

Let $k/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite extension. Let $I$ be an index set of cardinality $n\geq 1$ . Let $H\in\mathcal{O}_{k}(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]$ be irreducible over $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ , monic in $Y$ , and of total degree $D$ . Define $\mathcal{L}_{H}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/(H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}))$ . Consider the following conditions.

(I) $H$ is an $n$ -genuine polynomial, that is to say, $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is an $n$ -genuine extension of $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ .

(II) Given any index $i_{0}$ , upon defining $I^{\prime}:=I\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ , the following inclusion of fields is strict:

$$ (\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{H})(X_{i_{0}})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{H}. $$

(III) Given any index $i_{0}$ , upon defining $I^{\prime}:=I\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ , there exists a point $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in k^{n-1}$ such that $H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ , as a polynomial in $Y,X_{i_{0}}$ , does not have a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , and $\deg H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})=\deg_{Y,X_{i_{0}}}H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ .

(IV) Given any index $i_{0}$ , upon defining $I^{\prime}:=I\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ , upon expanding the polynomial $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ in $Y$ and $X_{i_{0}}$ as

$$ H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell,m\\
\ell+m\leq D\end{subarray}}a_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})Y^{\ell}X_{i_{0}}^{m}, $$

the form $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(a_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))$ defined as in (6.4) is not identically zero as a polynomial in $\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}$ .

The following are equivalent:

$$ \Leftrightarrow \Leftrightarrow \Leftrightarrow $$

Furthermore, for any fixed index $i_{0}\in I$ , the following are equivalent:

$$ \text{(II) for $i_{0}$ $\Leftrightarrow$ (III) for $i_{0}$ $\Leftrightarrow$ (IV) for $i_{0}$}. $$

### 6.1. Proof of Theorem 6.6 for $n=1$

(I) is the statement that we cannot write $\mathcal{L}_{H}=k(X_{1})[Y]/R(Y)$ for any polynomial $R$ independent of $X_{1}$ ; equivalently, if $L^{\prime}$ is some extension with $k\subset L^{\prime}\subset(\overline{k}\cap\mathcal{L}_{H})$ , then $L^{\prime}(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{H}$ ; this confirms (I) $\Leftrightarrow$ (II). The equivalence (II) $\Leftrightarrow$ (III) holds by Lemma 6.4, which shows $H(Y,X_{1})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{k}$ if and only if $(\mathcal{L}_{H}\cap\overline{k})(X_{1})=\mathcal{L}_{H}$ . By Noether’s Lemma 3.3 and Lemma 6.2, (III) $\Leftrightarrow$ (IV), since $H$ is monic in $Y$ .

### 6.2. Proof of Theorem 6.7 for $n\geq 2$

We prove all of the more elementary relations, before extracting a more subtle relation (II) $\Rightarrow$ (III) as a lemma. Throughout, for any index set $I$ , we say that a polynomial $f(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\in k[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{k}$ if

$$ f(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})=(Y-Q(\mathbf{X}_{I}))\tilde{H}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}), $$

in which $Q(\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\overline{k}[\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ and $\tilde{H}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\overline{k}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}].$

#### Lemma 6.8.

Given $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\mathcal{O}_{k}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ that is irreducible over $k[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ and monic in $Y$ , define $\mathcal{L}_{H}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/(H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}))$ . Suppose that for some set $J\subsetneq I$ , there is a polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{J})\in k[Y,\mathbf{X}_{J}]$ , irreducible over $k[Y,\mathbf{X}_{J}]$ , such that

$$ (k(\mathbf{X}_{J})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{J}))(\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J})=\mathcal{L}_{H}. $$

Then for all $\mathbf{x}_{J}\in k^{|J|}$ , $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J},\mathbf{x}_{J})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{k}$ .

In particular, the lemma applies if $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is not $|I|$ -genuine.

#### Proof.

Let $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ and $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{J})$ be given as in the lemma, so that $J\subsetneq I$ and

$$ (k(\mathbf{X}_{J})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{J}))(\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J})=\mathcal{L}_{H}. $$

Let $W_{G}$ be a root of $G$ so that $k(\mathbf{X}_{J})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{J})=k(\mathbf{X}_{J})(W_{G})$ ; hence $\mathcal{L}_{H}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I})(W_{G})$ . Let $W_{H}$ denote a root of $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ such that $\mathcal{L}_{H}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I})(W_{H})$ ; then we can decompose

$$ H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})=(Y-W_{H})\tilde{H}(Y) $$

over $\mathcal{L}_{H}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I})(W_{H})=k(\mathbf{X}_{I})(W_{G})$ , that is to say $\tilde{H}(Y)\in\mathcal{L}_{H}[Y]$ . Note that as a polynomial in $Y$ , $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is monic and has coefficients that are elements in $k[\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ (that is, are polynomials in $\mathbf{X}_{I}$ ); thus its root $W_{H}$ in $\mathcal{L}_{H}$ must lie in the ring of integers of that field. Since this ring of integers is contained in $k(W_{G})[\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ , this implies that the root $W_{H}$ lies in $k(W_{G})[\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ , and since $W_{G}$ only depends on $\mathbf{X}_{J}$ , we finally conclude that $W_{H}$ is a polynomial (rather than algebraic function) of $\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J}$ . That is, we may write $W_{H}=Q(\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J},\mathbf{X}_{J})$ as a function that is a polynomial function of the variables $\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J}$ and an algebraic function of the variables $\mathbf{X}_{J}$ . A similar argument shows that $\tilde{H}(Y)\in k(W_{G})[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ , so that it also depends only polynomially on $\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J}$ . That is to say, we may write $\tilde{H}(Y)=H^{\sharp}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J},\mathbf{X}_{J})$ as a function that is a polynomial function of $Y$ and the variables $\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J}$ and an algebraic function of the variables $\mathbf{X}_{J}$ .

Consequently, when specialized to any $\bfx_{J}\in k^{|J|}$ , we see that

$$ H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J},\mathbf{x}_{J})=(Y-Q(\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J},\mathbf{x}_{J}))H^{\sharp}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J},\mathbf{x}_{J}) $$

for $Q(\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J},\mathbf{x}_{J})\in\overline{k}[\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J}]$ and $H^{\sharp}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J},\mathbf{x}_{J})\in\overline{k}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J}]$ , which are polynomials in the variables $Y$ and $\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J}$ with coefficients in $\overline{k}$ . In particular, for any $\mathbf{x}_{J}\in k^{|J|}$ , $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J},\mathbf{x}_{J})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{k}$ , and the proof is complete. ∎

With this lemma in hand, we can prove several relations within Theorem 6.7.

((I) $\Rightarrow$ (II)) Suppose $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is $n$ -genuine. Fix any $i_{0}\in I$ and set $I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ . Let $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})\in k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]$ be a polynomial such $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ is the integral closure of $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ in $\mathcal{L}_{H}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/H(Y,\mathbf{X})$ , that is,

$$ (k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))\simeq(\mathcal{L}_{H}\cap\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}). $$

Since $H$ is $n$ -genuine, it has $\deg_{X_{i_{0}}}H\geq 1$ , whereas $G$ does not depend on $X_{i_{0}}$ . Thus the hypothesis that $\mathcal{L}_{H}$ is an $n$ -genuine field implies

$$ (k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))(X_{i_{0}})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{H}. $$

Combining these two facts shows that (II) holds.

((II) $\Rightarrow$ (I)) We will prove the contrapositive. Suppose that $\mathcal{L}_{H}$ is not $n$ -genuine, so there exists some polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{J})\in k[Y,\mathbf{X}_{J}]$ with an index set $J\subsetneq I$ such that

$$ (k(\mathbf{X}_{J})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{J}))(\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J})=\mathcal{L}_{H}. $$

Fix any index $i_{0}\in I\setminus J$ ; then by writing $G$ nominally as a polynomial in $Y$ and $X_{i}$ with $i\neq i_{0}$ , without loss of generality the above property holds in particular for the set $J=I^{\prime}$ with $I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ . That is,

$$ (k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))(X_{i_{0}})=\mathcal{L}_{H}. $$

Note that $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})\subset\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}$ , and certainly $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})\subset\mathcal{L}_{H}$ , so the above relation implies that $(\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{H})(X_{i_{0}})=\mathcal{L}_{H}$ . This argument confirms (II) $\Rightarrow$ (I).

((III) $\Rightarrow$ (I)) We will prove the contrapositive, namely that if $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is not $n$ -genuine, then for some $i_{0}\in I,$ $H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ for all $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in k^{n-1}$ . This follows from Lemma 6.8: since $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is not $n$ -genuine, there exists a non-empty subset $J\subsetneq I$ and polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{J})$ such that

$$ (k(\mathbf{X}_{J})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{J}))(\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J})=\mathcal{L}_{H}. $$

By the lemma, it follows that for every $\bfx_{J}\in k^{|J|}$ , the polynomial $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus J},\mathbf{x}_{J})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Then the desired conclusion is certainly true for any index $i_{0}\in I\setminus J$ .

((III) for $i_{0}$ $\Leftrightarrow$ (IV) for $i_{0}$ ) For a fixed index $i_{0}$ , the condition in (III) for the index $i_{0}$ is equivalent to the condition in (IV) for the index in $i_{0}$ , by (6.4) of Lemma 6.2. Indeed, for each point $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in k^{n-1}$ , the property

$$ H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}) Y \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \deg H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})=\deg_{Y,X_{i_{0}}}H $$

occurs if and only if $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(a_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}))\neq 0.$

((III) for $i_{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ (II) for $i_{0}$ ) We will prove the contrapositive, namely that if

$$ (\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{H})(X_{i_{0}})=\mathcal{L}_{H}, $$

then for all $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in k^{n-1}$ , $H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{k}$ . There exists a polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})\in k[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}]$ , irreducible over $k[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}]$ , such that

$$ \overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{H}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}). $$

Under the hypothesis (6.7),

$$ \mathcal{L}_{H}=(k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))(X_{i_{0}}), $$

so we may apply Lemma 6.8 with subset $J=I^{\prime}$ , and obtain the desired conclusion.

This completes the proof of the theorem, except for the relation that (II) for $i_{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ (III) for $i_{0}$ ; this will be obtained in Lemma 6.10, via the following lemma.

#### Lemma 6.9.

Let $k/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite extension. Let $I$ be an index set of cardinality $n\geq 1$ . Let $H\in\mathcal{O}_{k}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ be irreducible over $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ , monic in $Y$ , and of total degree $D$ , and let $\mathcal{L}_{H}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/H(Y,\mathbf{X})$ . For any $i_{0}\in I$ , and $I^{\prime}:=I\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ , let $G$ be a polynomial in $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]$ , irreducible over $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ , such that $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ is the integral closure of $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ in $\mathcal{L}_{H}$ , that is,

$$ k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})\simeq(\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{H}). $$

Then there exists an open set $V\subset k^{n-1}$ such that for every $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in V$ , $k[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ is integrally closed in $k(X_{i_{0}})[Y]/H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ .

#### Proof.

Consider

$$ W_{H}=\textbf{Spec}(k(X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})),\qquad W_{G}=\textbf{Spec}(k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})). $$

The inclusion of fields gives us a morphism

$$ \pi:W_{H}\rightarrow W_{G}. $$

Let $V^{\prime\prime}$ be the set of points $u\in W_{G}$ where the fiber

$$ \pi_{u}:W_{H,\pi^{-1}(u)}\rightarrow W_{G,u} $$

is geometrically integral. We first claim that this contains a nonempty open set. By [Gro66, EGA IV part 3, Theorem 9.7.7], $V^{\prime\prime}$ is locally constructible. Since $G$ is defined so that $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ is integrally closed in $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ , the generic fiber is geometrically integral and therefore contained in $V^{\prime\prime}$ . Hence, $V^{\prime\prime}$ contains a nonempty open subset $V^{\prime}$ such that for all $u\in V^{\prime}$ , $K(W_{G,u})$ is integrally closed in $K(W_{H,\pi^{-1}(u)})$ . (Here we use the notation that $K(W_{u})$ is the field of rational functions on $W_{u}$ .)

Finally, let $\rho:W_{G}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}_{k}^{|I^{\prime}|}$ and $\rho\circ\pi:W_{H}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}_{k}^{|I^{\prime}|}$ be the morphisms induced by the maps

$$ k(\bfX_{I^{\prime}})\hookrightarrow k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})\hookrightarrow k(X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}). $$

Since $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ is a finite extension of $k(\bfX_{I^{\prime}})$ , it follows that $\rho$ is a dominant and finite morphism, in particular $\rho$ is surjective, and closed (closed since $\rho$ is finite, and surjective because it is closed and dominant). Hence for the open set $V^{\prime}\subset V^{\prime\prime}\subset W_{G}$ constructed above, $\rho(V^{\prime})$ contains an open subset of $\mathbb{A}_{k}^{|I^{\prime}|}$ , say $V$ . Notice that for every $\bfx_{I^{\prime}}\in V$ , one has that

$$ \pi_{\bfx_{I^{\prime}}}:W_{H,(\rho\circ\pi)^{-1}(\bfx_{I^{\prime}})}\rightarrow W_{G,\rho^{-1}(\bfx_{I^{\prime}})}, $$

is geometrically integral, since $\rho^{-1}(\bfx_{I^{\prime}})\subset V^{\prime}$ , and

$$ W_{H,(\rho\circ\pi)^{-1}(\bfx_{I^{\prime}})}=\bigcup_{u\in\rho^{-1}(\bfx_{I^{\prime}})}W_{H,\pi^{-1}(u)}. $$

That is to say, $K(W_{G,\rho^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})})=k[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ is integrally closed in $K(W_{H,(\rho\circ\pi)^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})})=k(X_{i_{0}})[Y]/(H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}))$ . ∎

The following lemma confirms that (II for $i_{0}$ ) $\Rightarrow$ (III for $i_{0}$ ) and thereby finishes the proof of Theorem 6.7.

#### Lemma 6.10 (II for $i_{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ III for $i_{0}$ ).

Let $k/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite extension. Let $I$ be an index set of cardinality $n\geq 1$ . Let $H\in\mathcal{O}_{k}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ be irreducible over $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ , monic in $Y$ , and of total degree $D$ , and let $\mathcal{L}_{H}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/H(Y,\mathbf{X})$ .

Suppose that for some $i_{0}\in I$ and $I^{\prime}:=I\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ ,

$$ (\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{H})(X_{i_{0}})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{H}. $$

Then for this index $i_{0}$ , there exists a point $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in k^{n-1}$ such that $H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ , as a polynomial in $Y,X_{i_{0}}$ , does not have a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , and has $\deg H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})=\deg_{Y,X_{i_{0}}}H(Y,\mathbf{X})$ .

#### Proof.

Under the hypotheses, let $G$ be a polynomial in $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]$ , irreducible over $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ , such that $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ is the integral closure of $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ in $\mathcal{L}_{H}$ , that is,

$$ k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})\simeq(\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{H}). $$

Without loss of generality, we may assume $G$ is monic in $Y$ . Then by hypothesis,

$$ (k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))(X_{i_{0}})\subsetneq k(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/(H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})). $$

Since both $G$ and $H$ are irreducible over $k$ , so that

$$ [(k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))(X_{i_{0}}):k(\bfX)]=\deg_{Y}G,\quad[\mathcal{L}_{H}:k(\bfX)]=\deg_{Y}H, $$

this implies that

$$ \deg_{Y}G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})<\deg_{Y}H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}). $$

By Hilbert’s Irreducibility Theorem (Lemma 2.2), there is a dense set $U^{\prime}\subset k^{|I^{\prime}|}=\mathbb{A}^{|I^{\prime}|}_{k}$ such that for all $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in U^{\prime}$ , $H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ and $G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ are irreducible over $k$ . Observe that there is a subset $U\subset U^{\prime}$ , also dense in $\mathbb{A}^{|I^{\prime}|}_{k}$ , such that for all $x_{I^{\prime}}\in U$ , $\deg_{Y}H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})=\deg_{Y}H$ , $\deg_{X_{i_{0}}}H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})=\deg_{X_{i_{0}}}H$ and $\deg_{Y}G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})=\deg_{Y}G$ . The degree of each polynomial with respect to $Y$ does not change upon specialization since $H$ and $G$ are monic in $Y$ . For the degree of $X_{i_{0}}$ , if we let $V_{0}$ denote the subset of $U^{\prime}$ where $\deg_{X_{i_{0}}}H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})<\deg_{X_{i_{0}}}H$ for $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in V_{0}$ , then $V_{0}$ is nowhere dense, and $U=U^{\prime}\setminus V_{0}$ is the desired dense set. (For $V_{0}$ is contained in a finite union of sets, each of which is defined as the vanishing set of a polynomial (a nonzero polynomial in $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}$ , that defines the coefficient of a certain monomial in ${X_{i_{0}}}$ in $H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ , so $V_{0}$ is a proper closed subset of lower dimension, and is nowhere dense.)

Let $V\subset\mathbb{A}_{k}^{|I^{\prime}|}$ denote the open set produced by Lemma 6.9. Since $V$ is open and $U$ is dense, we can find a point $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in V\cap U$ , and then $H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ and $G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ are irreducible over $k$ , with $\deg H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})=\deg_{Y,X_{i_{0}}}H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ . Moreover $k[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ is integrally closed in $k(X_{i_{0}})[Y]/(H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}))$ , which we record as

$$ k(X_{i_{0}})[Y]/(H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}))\cap\overline{k}=k[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}), $$

also using the fact that $\overline{k[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})}\simeq\overline{k}$ . By our choice of $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}$ , we know that

$$ \deg_{Y}H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})=\deg_{Y}H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}),\qquad\deg_{Y}G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})=\deg_{Y}G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}), $$

and that both $H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ and $G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ are irreducible over $k$ . Thus, an application of (6.9) shows that $\deg_{Y}G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})<\deg_{Y}H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ , and from the irreducibility it follows that we maintain the strict inclusion of fields:

$$ k[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}))(X_{i_{0}})\subsetneq k(X_{i_{0}})[Y]/(H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})). $$

We claim this implies that $H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ does not have a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{k}$ . Suppose on the contrary that $H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{k}$ ; then it splits completely by Lemma 6.3, so that

$$ H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})=\prod_{j}(Y-Q_{j}(X_{i_{0}})) $$

for certain $Q_{j}(X_{i_{0}})\in\overline{k}[X_{i_{0}}]$ . But this implies (as in Lemma 6.4) that

$$ (k(X_{i_{0}})[Y]/(H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}))\cap\overline{k})(X_{i_{0}})=k(X_{{i}_{0}})[Y]/(H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})). $$

By applying the identity (6.10) in the left-hand side, this is the statement

$$ (k[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}))(X_{i_{0}})=k(X_{{i}_{0}})[Y]/(H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})), $$

in contradiction to (6.11). Thus $H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ does not have a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , and the lemma is proved. ∎

### 6.3. Natural consequence of being $n$ -genuine

#### Theorem 6.11.

Let $n\geq 2$ . Let $k/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite extension of degree $m$ , with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_{k}$ . Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathcal{O}_{k}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be an $n$ -genuine polynomial of total degree $D$ . Then for all $B\gg 1$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{O}_{k}^{n-1},\|\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|\leq B:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ splits completely over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$}\}\ll_{m,n,D}B^{n-2}(\log B)^{(n-2)(m-1)}. $$

Also, there exists a finite set $\mathcal{E}$ of exceptional prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}\in\mathcal{O}_{k}$ , with $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{m,n,D}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ , such that for all $\mathfrak{p}\not\in\mathcal{E}$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in k_{\mathfrak{p}}^{n-1}:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ splits completely over $\overline{k_{\mathfrak{p}}}$}\}\ll_{n,D}|k_{\mathfrak{p}}|^{n-2}. $$

#### Proof of Theorem 1.5.

Theorem 1.5 is simply the special case when $k=\mathbb{Q}$ , $k_{\mathfrak{p}}=\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , so that $|k_{\mathfrak{p}}|=|\mathbb{F}_{p}|=p$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 6.11.

Since $F$ is $n$ -genuine, by Theorem 6.7 (IV), for each $i_{0}\in I$ , the polynomial $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(a_{\ell,j}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}]$ that detects whether $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ has a linear factor over $\overline{k}=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ is not identically zero. In particular this is true for $i_{0}=1$ , and then we denote $\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}$ by $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}$ . Thus to prove the first claim, it suffices to observe that by Lemma 6.3, then Lemma 6.2, and then the trivial bound in Lemma 2.3 followed by Lemma 2.4,

$$ \displaystyle\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime} \displaystyle\in\mathcal{O}_{k}^{n-1},\|\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|\leq B:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ splits completely over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$}\} \displaystyle=\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{O}_{k}^{n-1},\|\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|\leq B:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$}\} \displaystyle\leq\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{O}_{k}^{n-1},\|\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|\leq B:B_{\mathrm{lin}}(a_{\ell,j}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime}))=0\}\ll_{m,n,D}B^{n-2}(\log B)^{(n-2)(m-1)}. $$

For the second claim, we define $\mathcal{E}$ to be the set of all prime ideals that divide the gcd, call it $g$ , of the coefficients of $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(a_{\ell,j}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime}))\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}^{\prime}]$ . Note that $g\leq\|B_{\mathrm{lin}}\|$ and by Lemma 3.3, $\log\|B_{\mathrm{lin}}\|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|$ . Consequently by Lemma 2.4, $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{m,n,D}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ . Then for $\mathfrak{p}\not\in\mathcal{E}$ , $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(a_{\ell,j}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime}))$ is not identically zero over $k_{\mathfrak{p}}$ . To prove the second claim, it suffices again to apply Lemma 6.3, followed by Lemma 6.2 and the trivial bound in Lemma 2.3:

$$ \displaystyle\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime} \displaystyle\in k_{\mathfrak{p}}^{n-1}:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ splits completely over $\overline{k_{\mathfrak{p}}}$}\} \displaystyle=\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in k_{\mathfrak{p}}^{n-1}:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{k_{\mathfrak{p}}}$}\} \displaystyle\leq\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in k_{\mathfrak{p}}^{n-1}:B_{\mathrm{lin}}(a_{\ell,j}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime}))=0\}\leq\deg B_{\mathrm{lin}}|k_{\mathfrak{p}}|^{n-2}. $$

Since $\deg B_{\mathrm{lin}}\ll_{n,D}1$ , this suffices. ∎

#### Remark 6.12.

As the method of proof showed, Theorem 6.11 (and analogously Theorem 1.5) is still true under the following weaker hypothesis: that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is irreducible over $k(\mathbf{X})$ , and monic in $Y$ , and that for $i_{0}=1$ and $I^{\prime}=\{2,\ldots,n\}$ ,

$$ (\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{F}. $$

For then by Theorem 6.7 ((II) for $i_{0}=1$ $\Rightarrow$ (IV) for $i_{0}=1$ ), the polynomial $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(a_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}]$ that detects whether $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ has a linear factor over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ is not identically zero, and the above proof can proceed.

## 7. Shifting polynomials to prove Theorem 5.7

The remaining task to prove Theorem 1.2 is to prove Theorem 5.7. Recall from (5.3) that for any $\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ we define the shift (with respect to $X_{1}$ ) by

$$ F_{\bfa}(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})=F(Y,X_{1},X_{2}+a_{2}X_{1},...,X_{n}+a_{n}X_{1}). $$

We wish to show that for some shift $F_{\mathbf{a}}$ of the polynomial $F$ , the associated minimal polynomial $M_{F_{\mathbf{a}}}$ satisfies condition (II) of Theorem 4.2 for the particular index $i_{0}=1$ . (We have distinguished the variable $X_{1}$ , for notational simplicity, but we could in fact work with any fixed index $i_{0}$ and achieve an analogous outcome.) We first show that it suffices to prove the following result about shifting polynomials.

#### Proposition 7.1.

Let $L/K/\mathbb{Q}$ be finite extensions. Let $R\in\mathcal{O}_{L}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]$ be a polynomial of total degree $D$ , irreducible over $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , such that

$$ \mathcal{L}_{R}:=L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/R(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}) $$

is a strongly $1$ -genuine extension of $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ . Then there exists a choice of $\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ with $\|\bfa\|\ll_{n,D,[L:\mathbb{Q}]}1$ such that for the shifted polynomial $R_{\mathbf{a}}$ ,

$$ \mathcal{L}_{R_{\bf{a}}}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})}=L(X_{2},...,X_{n}). $$

#### Deduction of Theorem 5.7.

Suppose this proposition is true, and let us deduce Theorem 5.7. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 5.7, let $\Omega_{F}$ denote the splitting field of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ over $K(\mathbf{X})$ , with minimal polynomial $M_{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ of $\Omega_{F}$ over $L_{F}(\mathbf{X})$ , in which $L_{F}=\Omega_{F}\cap\overline{K}$ . Since $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ , note that $\deg_{Y}M_{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})\geq 2$ . Additionally, since $M_{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is a minimal polynomial it must be irreducible over $L_{F}(\mathbf{X})$ . Furthermore Corollary 5.5 shows that $M_{F}$ is strongly $1$ -genuine over $L_{F}$ , or equivalently $\Omega_{F}$ is a strongly $1$ -genuine extension of $L_{F}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , by construction.

Apply Proposition 7.1 with $L=L_{F}$ , $K=K$ , and the polynomial $R=M_{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})\in L(\mathbf{X})[Y]$ . The proposition produces a choice of $\bfa\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ such that the shifted polynomial, which we denote by

$$ (M_{F})_{\bfa}(Y,\mathbf{X})=M_{F}(Y,X_{1},X_{2}+a_{2}X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}+a_{n}X_{1}), $$

satisfies $\mathcal{L}_{(M_{F})_{\bfa}}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})}=L(X_{2},...,X_{n})$ . By the proposition, $\|\bfa\|\ll_{n,D,[L:\mathbb{Q}]}1$ , and $[L:\mathbb{Q}]\ll_{D,[K:\mathbb{Q}]}1$ , so that $\|\bfa\|\ll_{n,D,[K:\mathbb{Q}]}1$ . By Lemma 5.6, $(M_{F})_{\bfa}(Y,\mathbf{X})=M_{F_{\mathbf{a}}}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ . Thus $\mathcal{L}_{(M_{F_{\bfa}})}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})}=L(X_{2},...,X_{n})$ , and since $\mathcal{L}_{{(M_{F_{\mathbf{a}}}})}=\Omega_{\mathbf{a}}$ in the notation of Theorem 5.7, the proof of that theorem is complete. ∎

For orientation, here is an overview of the strategy to prove Proposition 7.1. If

$$ \mathcal{L}_{R}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})}=L(X_{2},...,X_{n}), $$

so that $L(X_{2},...,X_{n})$ is integrally closed in $\mathcal{L}_{R}$ , then the proposition is already true, with the zero shift $\bfa=0$ . If this does not hold, then since strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials are generic (recall Remark 1.7), we hope that by shifting $R$ we can produce a polynomial for which the relation (7.2) does hold. So suppose

$$ N_{R}:=\mathcal{L}_{R}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})}\supsetneq L(X_{2},...,X_{n}). $$

Enumerate all the intermediate extensions $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\subsetneq K_{j}\subseteq\mathcal{L}_{R}$ (including $\mathcal{L}_{R}$ ) by $K_{1},\ldots,K_{e}$ , say. (Each of these fields is $\ell$ -genuine for some $\ell\geq 1$ , by Lemma 5.4.) If it were true that for all $j=1,\ldots,e$ , $K_{j}\not\subset N_{R}(X_{1})$ then we could conclude that $N_{R}(X_{1})=L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , since the $K_{j}$ exhaust the nontrivial intermediate fields. This would imply that $N_{R}=L(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})$ , so that (7.2) holds. Presently we are not in this case, but the strategy is to shift $R$ to $R_{\bfa}$ , and again enumerate the intermediate fields $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\subsetneq K_{j,\bfa}\subseteq\mathcal{L}_{R_{\bfa}}$ , now denoted by $K_{1,\bfa},\ldots,K_{e,\bfa}$ , and hope in particular to find a choice of shift $\bfa$ such that for all $j=1,\ldots,e$ , $K_{j}\not\subset N_{R_{\bfa}}(X_{1})$ , thus forcing $N_{R_{\bfa}}=L(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})$ .

The property $K_{j,\bfa}\not\subset N_{R_{\bfa}}(X_{1})$ will hold if $K_{j,\bfa}\not\subset(K_{j,\bfa}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1})$ , that is to say,

$$ (K_{j,\bfa}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1})\subsetneq K_{j,\bfa}, $$

or in other words, if $K_{j,\bfa}$ requires some nontrivial algebraic expression in $X_{1}$ . (For indeed, the property $K_{j,\bfa}\subset N_{R_{\bfa}}(X_{1})$ would imply $K_{j,\bfa}\subset\overline{L(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})}(X_{1})$ , which would imply $K_{j,\bfa}\subset(K_{j,\bfa}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1})$ .) Since the original polynomial $R(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is strongly $1$ -genuine, each of the intermediate fields $K_{1},\ldots,K_{e}$ depends in a nondegenerate way on at least one variable, say $X_{j}$ , and so by shifting $X_{j}\mapsto X_{j}+a_{j}X_{1}$ we aim to introduce nondegenerate dependence on $X_{1}$ , to result in (7.4). For a given field, say $F$ , (that is $\ell$ -genuine for some $\ell\geq 1$ ), we perform such a shift in one variable to produce a property like (7.4) in Lemma 7.2, and by shifting in multiple coordinates in Lemma 7.4. Moreover, since being $n$ -genuine is a generic property, we would expect most shifts $\bfa$ accomplish this. We quantify this in Lemma 7.4 by showing that for a given field $F$ , there exists a polynomial $g^{F}$ such that for every $\bfa$ such that $g^{F}(\bfa)\neq 0$ , we do obtain (7.4). With this result in hand, we can apply it to each of $K_{1},\ldots,K_{e}$ in turn, generate the corresponding polynomials $g^{1},\ldots,g^{e}$ , and find a shift $\bfa$ that is not a root of any of them. For this shift $\bfa$ , we achieve (7.4) simultaneously for all $j=1,\ldots,e$ , and this is the key step to prove the proposition. We now turn to carrying out this strategy rigorously.

### 7.1. Step 1: shifting one variable

The main goal of this section is the following lemma:

#### Lemma 7.2.

Let $L/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite extension. Let $R\in\mathcal{O}_{L}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]$ be a polynomial of total degree $D$ , irreducible over $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ . Assume that $\mathcal{L}_{R}:=L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/R$ is an $\ell$ -genuine extension for some $\ell\geq 1$ . Then for every $i\in I$ , for all but $O_{n,D}(1)$ choices of $\alpha_{i}\in L$ , the following is true: if one considers the polynomial $R_{\alpha_{i},i}=R(Y,X_{1},...,X_{i}+\alpha_{i}X_{1},...,X_{n})$ , and the extension $\mathcal{L}_{R_{\alpha_{i},i}}:=L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/R_{\alpha_{i},i}$ then the total degree of $R_{\alpha_{i},i}$ is $D$ , and

$$ (\mathcal{L}_{R_{\alpha_{i},i}}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{R_{\alpha_{i},i}}. $$

Consider such a polynomial $R(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ that is $\ell$ -genuine. For some $I\subset\{1,...,n\}$ with $|I|\geq\ell$ there exists a polynomial $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\mathcal{O}_{L}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ such that $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is $|I|$ -genuine (and in particular monic in $Y$ ) and

$$ \mathcal{L}_{R}=(L(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/H)(\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}}). $$

If we shift a variable $X_{i}$ with $i\in I$ , $i\neq 1$ , by a multiple of $X_{1}$ , it will be useful to show that property (IV) for $i_{0}=1$ of Theorem 6.7 still holds for the shifted polynomial; this is the subject of the next lemma, for which we establish the following notation.

Fix an index $i\in I$ with $i\neq 1$ , and consider for any $\alpha_{i}\in L$ the polynomial $H(Y,X_{i}+\alpha_{i}X_{1},\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus\{i\}})$ , in which this notation implies $X_{i}+\alpha_{i}X_{1}$ appears in the place of $X_{i}$ . Note that this is a polynomial in $X_{1}$ and $\mathbf{X}_{I}$ . We expand this polynomial in terms of $Y$ and $X_{1}$ as

$$ H(Y,\alpha_{i}X_{1}+X_{i},\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus\{i\}})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell,m\\
\ell+m\leq D\end{subarray}}b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i})Y^{\ell}X_{1}^{m}. $$

Here and throughout, we use the convention that $I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{1\}$ if $1\in I$ and $I^{\prime}=I$ if $1\not\in I$ . Consider also the detection polynomial $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))$ provided by Lemma 6.2, that vanishes if and only if: as a polynomial in $Y,X_{1}$ , the expression (7.5) has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (or has degree $<\deg_{Y,X_{1}}H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ ). Note $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))$ is a polynomial in $\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}$ and $\alpha_{i}$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}$ , and degree $\ll_{n,D}1$ .

#### Lemma 7.3.

In the above setting, suppose $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is $|I|$ -genuine. Suppose $|I|\geq 2$ or $1\not\in I$ , and define $I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{1\}$ if $1\in I$ or $I^{\prime}=I$ if $1\not\in I$ . Fix any $i\in I^{\prime}$ and expand the polynomial $H(Y,\alpha_{i}X_{1}+X_{i},\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus\{i\}})$ as in (7.5). Aside from $O_{n,D}(1)$ possible values of $\alpha_{i}\in L$ , the polynomial $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))$ is not identically zero as a polynomial in $\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}$ .

#### Proof.

First, since $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is $|I|$ -genuine, by Theorem 6.7 (I) $\Rightarrow$ (III) we see that for every $i_{0}\in I$ , there exists $\mathbf{x}_{I\setminus\{i_{0}\}}\in L^{|I|-1}$ such that

$$ \text{$H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I\setminus\{i_{0}\}})$ does not have a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, }\\
\text{and $\deg_{Y,X_{i_{0}}}H(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I\setminus\{i_{0}\}})$ $=\deg_{Y,X_{i_{0}}}H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$}. $$

(If $I=\{i_{0}\}$ , this states that $H(Y,X_{i_{0}})$ does not have a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ .)

We distinguish two cases, depending whether $1\in I$ or $1\not\in I$ . In the case when $1\in I$ (and so $|I|\geq 2$ ), fix any $i\in I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{1\}$ . Also fix a choice $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}$ as provided by (7.6) applied with $i_{0}=1$ , and for this choice consider $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))$ as a polynomial in $\alpha_{i}$ . For our choice of $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}$ , we claim when $\alpha_{i}=0$ , $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}},0))\neq 0$ . Indeed upon setting $\alpha_{i}=0$ in (7.5), by definition,

$$ \left.H(Y,X_{i},\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus\{i\}})\right|_{\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}=\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}}=H(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}). $$

By our choice of $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}$ , the right-hand side satisfies (7.6), so the left-hand side does too and the claim is proved. Thus as a polynomial in $\alpha_{i}$ , $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))$ is not identically zero, and consequently $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))\neq 0$ for all but possibly $O_{n,D}(1)$ exceptional values of $\alpha_{i}$ . Now consider any value $\alpha_{i}$ such that $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))\equiv 0$ as a polynomial in $\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}$ ; then certainly $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))=0$ . Thus aside from all but possibly $O_{n,D}(1)$ exceptional values of $\alpha_{i}$ , $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))\not\equiv 0$ , as desired.

In the second case, when $1\not\in I$ , let $I^{\prime}=I$ and fix any $i\in I^{\prime}$ . Suppose $\alpha_{i}\neq 0$ . Then taking a choice of $\mathbf{x}_{I\setminus\{i\}}$ with the property (7.6) (applied with the choice $i_{0}=i$ ), $H(Y,X_{i},\mathbf{x}_{I\setminus\{i\}})$ does not have a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (and has degree $=\deg_{Y,X_{i}}H$ ); therefore, the same properties hold for $H(Y,\alpha_{i}X_{i},\mathbf{x}_{I\setminus\{i\}})$ since $\alpha_{i}\neq 0$ . Since $1\not\in I$ , this is equivalent to the statement, with $\alpha_{i}X_{1}$ now in the place of $\alpha_{i}X_{i}$ , that $H(Y,\alpha_{i}X_{1},\mathbf{x}_{I\setminus\{i\}})$ does not have a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (and has total degree (as a function of $Y,X_{1}$ ) equal to $\deg_{Y,X_{i}}H$ ). On the other hand, in the notation of (7.5) (recalling $I^{\prime}=I$ in the present case),

$$ H(Y,\alpha_{i}X_{1},\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus\{i\}})=H(Y,\alpha_{i}X_{1}+0,\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus\{i\}})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell,m\\
\ell+m\leq D\end{subarray}}\left.b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i})\right|_{X_{i}=0}Y^{\ell}X_{1}^{m}. $$

From these two facts we may conclude that for any nonzero $\alpha_{i}$ , $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))$ evaluates to a nonzero value when specialized to $X_{i}=0$ and $\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus\{i\}}=\mathbf{x}_{I\setminus\{i\}}.$ Consequently, for any nonzero $\alpha_{i}$ we conclude $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))\not\equiv 0$ as a polynomial in $\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}$ .

∎

#### Proof of Lemma 7.2.

Let the polynomial $R$ be given as in the lemma, with an $|I|$ -genuine polynomial $H$ such that

$$ \mathcal{L}_{R}=(L(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}))(\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}}). $$

We first claim that for every $i\in I$ , for all but $O_{n,D}(1)$ values of $\alpha_{i}$ , the polynomial $R_{\alpha_{i},i}=R(Y,X_{1},...,X_{i}+\alpha_{i}X_{1},...,X_{n})$ has total degree $D$ . We can write the polynomial $R_{\alpha_{i},i}$ as

$$ R_{\alpha_{i},i}=\sum_{\bfj,\ell}p_{\bfj,\ell}(\alpha_{i})\bfX^{\bfj}Y^{\ell}, $$

where for every $\bfj=(j_{1},...,j_{n})$ and for every $\ell$ , $p_{\bfj,\ell}(A_{i})$ is a polynomial of degree $\leq D$ , whose coefficients depend on the coefficients of $R$ . Note that $p_{\bfj,\ell}(A_{i})\equiv 0$ if $\ell+j_{1}+\cdots+j_{n}>D$ so the decomposition (7.8) has $O_{n,D}(1)$ summands. Each (nonzero) polynomial $p_{\bfj,\ell}(A_{i})$ vanishes for at most $D$ values of $\alpha_{i}$ . Thus, for all but $O_{n,D}(1)$ values of $\alpha_{i}$ , $p_{\bfj,\ell}(\alpha_{i})\neq 0$ , for all $p_{\bfj,\ell}$ appearing in $(\ref{eq : nolossdegree})$ , in which case the total degree of $R_{\alpha_{i},i}$ is $D$ , and the claim is proved.

We now prove that for all but $O_{n,D}(1)$ choices of $\alpha_{i}\in L$ ,

$$ (\mathcal{L}_{R_{\alpha_{i},i}}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{R_{\alpha_{i},i}}. $$

First, we deal separately with the case in which $1\in I$ and the distinguished index considered in the lemma is $i=1$ . If $I=\{1\}$ then we already have that $(\mathcal{L}_{H}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{H}$ . This then implies that $(\mathcal{L}_{R}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{R}$ via (7.7). Moreover the desired conclusion of the lemma is true for all $\alpha_{1}$ such that $\alpha_{1}+1\neq 0$ (we can see this by a change of variable $X_{1}^{\prime}=(1+\alpha_{1})X_{1}$ ). An analogous argument also works if $|I|\geq 2$ and $i=1\in I$ . Henceforward we may suppose that either $1\not\in I$ or $|I|\geq 2$ , and in the latter case we only need to prove the lemma in the case when the distinguished index $i\neq 1$ .

Let $I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{1\}$ if $1\in I$ and $I^{\prime}=I$ if $1\not\in I$ . Now we fix $i\in I^{\prime}$ and apply Lemma 7.3: thus aside from $O_{n,D}(1)$ possible values of $\alpha_{i}\in L$ , the polynomial $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))\not\equiv 0$ as a polynomial in $\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}$ . For each $\alpha_{i}$ with the property $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))\not\equiv 0$ , there is an open set $U\in L^{|I^{\prime}|}$ such that for all $\bfx_{I^{\prime}}\in U$ , $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))\neq 0$ . Note that $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}},\alpha_{i}))\neq 0$ occurs if and only if $H(Y,\alpha_{i}X_{1}+x_{i},\bfx_{I^{\prime}\setminus\{i\}})$ has no linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}=\overline{L}$ and has total degree $=\deg_{Y,X_{1}}H(Y,X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})$ .

On the other hand, note that since by hypothesis $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is irreducible over $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ then so is $H(Y,\alpha_{i}X_{1}+X_{i},\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus\{i\}})$ , since it is obtained by a linear transformation. Thus by the Hilbert Irreducibility Theorem (Lemma 2.2), there is a dense set $V\subset L^{|I^{\prime}|}$ such that for all $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in V$ , $H(Y,\alpha_{i}X_{1}+x_{i},\bfx_{I^{\prime}\setminus\{i\}})$ is irreducible over $L$ . Since $U$ is open and $V$ is dense, we may choose $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in U\cap V$ . For this choice, by Theorem 6.7 (III for $i_{0}=1$ ) $\Rightarrow$ (II for $i_{0}=1$ ) applied over the field $L$ , we learn that

$$ (L(\bfX)[Y]/H(Y,\alpha_{i}X_{1}+X_{i},\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus\{i\}})\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1})\\
\subsetneq L(\bfX)[Y]/H(Y,\alpha_{i}X_{1}+X_{i},\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus\{i\}}). $$

The final step is to note that

$$ \mathcal{L}_{R_{\alpha_{i},i}}:=L(\mathbf{X})[Y]/R_{\alpha_{i},i}=L(\mathbf{X})[Y]/H(Y,\alpha_{i}X_{1}+X_{i},\mathbf{X}_{I\setminus\{i\}}), $$

so that the previous identity is the conclusion of Lemma 7.2, as desired.

∎

### 7.2. Step 2: shifting multiple variables

For our second step we iterate the shifting process $X_{i}\mapsto a_{i}X_{1}+X_{i}$ for each index $i\neq 1$ , $i\in I$ . The main goal of this section is the following lemma:

#### Lemma 7.4.

Let $L/K/\mathbb{Q}$ be finite extensions. Let $R\in\mathcal{O}_{L}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]$ be a polynomial of total degree $D$ such that $\mathcal{L}_{R}=L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/R$ is an $\ell$ -genuine extension of $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ for some $\ell\geq 1$ . For any $\bfa\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ define the polynomial

$$ R_{\bfa}(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}):=R(Y,X_{1},X_{2}+a_{2}X_{1},...,X_{n}+a_{n}X_{1}) $$

and correspondingly set

$$ \mathcal{L}_{R_{\mathbf{a}}}:=L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/R_{\mathbf{a}}. $$

There exists a nonzero polynomial $g^{R}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}[A_{2},...,A_{n}]$ , such that for every $\bfa\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ with $g^{R}(\bfa)\neq 0$ ,

$$ (\mathcal{L}_{R_{\bfa}}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{R_{\bfa}}. $$

Moreover $\deg g^{R}\ll_{n,D,[L:K]}1$ .

#### Remark 7.5.

Note that here we require the shifts $\mathbf{a}$ to lie in the lower ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ . This is because later we will apply this to $R=M_{F}$ the minimal polynomial for some $F\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , where $M_{F}\in\mathcal{O}_{L_{F}}$ . Then we will use the relation $(M_{F})_{\mathbf{a}}=M_{F_{\mathbf{a}}}$ from Lemma 5.6, and we want $F_{\mathbf{a}}$ also to have coefficients in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ .

To prepare for the proof, we suppose that $R$ is given, so that $\mathcal{L}_{R}$ is an $\ell$ -genuine extension of $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ for some $\ell\geq 1$ . Let $I\subset\{1,...,n\}$ be a set with $|I|\geq\ell$ such that there exists a polynomial $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\mathcal{O}_{L}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ of total degree $d$ , irreducible over $L(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ and $|I|$ -genuine such that

$$ \mathcal{L}_{R}=(L(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}))(\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}}). $$

In the proof of the lemma, we will immediately reduce to the case where $1\not\in I$ or $|I|\geq 2$ . We establish some notational conventions so that we can treat both the cases together. If $1\not\in I$ , then $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ does not depend on $X_{1}$ ; we will set $I^{\prime}=I$ and our principal study will be the polynomial $H(Y,X_{i}+A_{i}X_{1})_{i\in I^{\prime}}$ , which is a polynomial in $Y,X_{1},\mathbf{X}_{I}$ . If $1\in I$ , we will set $I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{1\}$ and our principal study will be the polynomial $H(Y,X_{1},X_{i}+A_{i}X_{1})_{i\in I^{\prime}}$ , which is again a polynomial in $Y,X_{1},\mathbf{X}_{I}$ . With an abuse of notation, we will unify both of these cases by studying a polynomial we denote as $H(Y,X_{1},X_{i}+A_{i}X_{1})_{i\in I^{\prime}}$ in either case.

With the convention $I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{1\}$ if $1\in I$ and $I^{\prime}=I$ if $1\not\in I$ , expand as a polynomial in $Y$ and $X_{1}$ the polynomial $H$ after shifting each $X_{i}$ with $i\neq 1$ :

$$ H(Y,X_{1},X_{i}+A_{i}X_{1})_{i\in I^{\prime}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell,m\\
\ell+m\leq D\end{subarray}}b_{\ell,m}(\bfX_{I^{\prime}},\bfA_{I^{\prime}})Y^{\ell}X_{1}^{m}. $$

Consider the detection polynomial $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\bfX_{I^{\prime}},\bfA_{I^{\prime}}))$ that detects if this polynomial, as a polynomial in $Y,X_{1}$ , has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (or degree $<\deg_{Y,X_{1}}H$ ), as provided by Lemma 6.2. Note that $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\bfX_{I^{\prime}},\bfA_{I^{\prime}}))$ is a polynomial in $(\bfX_{I^{\prime}},\bfA_{I^{\prime}})$ , with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}$ and degree $\ll_{n,D}1$ . Then upon specializing $\bfA_{I^{\prime}}=\bfa_{I^{\prime}}\in L^{|I^{\prime}|}$ , $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\bfX_{I^{\prime}},\bfa_{I^{\prime}}))=0$ if and only if $H(Y,X_{1},X_{i}+a_{i}X_{1})_{i\in I^{\prime}}$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (or the degree drops, as a polynomial in $Y$ and $X_{1}$ ). We claim:

#### Lemma 7.6.

In the above setting, suppose $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is $|I|$ -genuine. Suppose $|I|\geq 2$ or $1\not\in I$ , and define $I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{1\}$ if $1\in I$ or $I^{\prime}=I$ if $1\not\in I$ . Expand the polynomial $H(Y,X_{1},X_{i}+A_{i}X_{1})_{i\in I^{\prime}}$ as in (7.11). As a polynomial in $(\bfX_{I^{\prime}},\bfA_{I^{\prime}})$ , $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\bfX_{I^{\prime}},\bfA_{I^{\prime}}))\not\equiv 0$ .

#### Proof.

Fix any index $i_{k}\in I^{\prime}$ , and fix a choice of $a_{i}\in L$ for each $i\in I^{\prime}\setminus\{i_{k}\},$ and then consider the polynomial $H(Y,X_{1},X_{i}+a_{i}X_{1},X_{i_{k}})_{i\in I^{\prime}\setminus\{i_{k}\}}$ . This polynomial defines an $\ell$ -genuine extension for some $\ell\geq 1$ since it certainly has nontrivial degree with respect to $X_{i_{k}}$ , for example. Moreover, it is irreducible over $L(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ , since by hypothesis $L(\bfX_{I})/H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is a field; hence $H(Y,X_{1},X_{i}+a_{i}X_{1},X_{i_{k}})_{i\in I^{\prime}\setminus\{i_{k}\}}$ is irreducible since it is obtained by a linear transformation. Now, apply Lemma 7.2 with $R=H(Y,X_{1},X_{i}+a_{i}X_{1},X_{i_{k}})_{i\in I^{\prime}\setminus\{i_{k}\}}$ in the variables $Y,X_{1},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}$ , and with the distinguished index $i_{k}$ . The outcome is that for all but $O_{n,D}(1)$ choices of $a_{i_{k}}\in L$ , the tuple $\bfa_{I^{\prime}}:=(a_{i})_{i\in I^{\prime}}=(a_{i},a_{i_{k}})_{i\in I^{\prime}\setminus\{i_{k}\}}$ and the definition

$$ H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}):=H(Y,X_{1},X_{i}+a_{i}X_{1},X_{i_{k}}+a_{i_{k}}X_{1})_{i\in I^{\prime}\setminus\{i_{k}\}}, $$

we have $\deg H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}=\deg H$ , and moreover the field

$$ \mathcal{L}_{H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}}:=L(X_{1},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/(H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})) $$

has the property

$$ (\mathcal{L}_{H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}}\cap\overline{L(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}}. $$

Now by an application of Lemma 6.10 (Theorem 6.7 (II) for $i_{0}=1$ $\Rightarrow$ (III) for $i_{0}=1$ ), this implies that there exists a point $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in L^{|I^{\prime}|}$ such that $H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ , as a polynomial in $Y,X_{1}$ , does not have a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , and has $\deg H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})=\deg_{Y,X_{1}}H_{\mathbf{a}_{I^{\prime}}}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ . Hence for this $\bfa_{I^{\prime}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}$ , $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\bfx_{I^{\prime}},\bfa_{I^{\prime}}))\neq 0$ . Consequently, $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\bfX_{I^{\prime}},\bfA_{I^{\prime}}))\not\equiv 0$ as a polynomial in $\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}$ , and the lemma is proved. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 7.4.

We suppose that $R$ is given, so that $\mathcal{L}_{R}$ is an $\ell$ -genuine extension of $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ for some $\ell\geq 1$ . As in (7.10), let $I\subset\{1,...,n\}$ be a set with $|I|=\ell$ such that there exists an $|I|$ -genuine polynomial $H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\mathcal{O}_{L}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ of total degree $D$ such that

$$ \mathcal{L}_{R}=(L(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/H(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}))(\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}}). $$

If $I=\{1\}$ , then observe that $(\mathcal{L}_{H}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{H}$ . Since $I=\{1\}$ , for each index $j\neq 1$ , then $\deg_{X_{j}}H=0$ so that shifts $X_{j}\mapsto X_{j}+a_{j}X_{1}$ do not change $H$ . Hence $\mathcal{L}_{R_{\bfa}}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{R_{\bfa}}$ for all $\bfa\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ , so we may simply define the polynomial $g^{R}(\bfa)=c_{0}$ for some $c_{0}\neq 0$ . Henceforward we may assume $1\not\in I$ or $|I|\geq 2$ .

Let $I^{\prime}=I$ if $1\not\in I$ and $I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{1\}$ if $1\in I$ . Recall from the convention above that in both cases, we denote the polynomial we study by $H(Y,X_{1},X_{i}+A_{i}X_{1})_{i\in I^{\prime}}$ . Note that it suffices to construct a nonzero polynomial $g_{I^{\prime}}$ with coefficients in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , in $|I^{\prime}|$ variables, and of degree $\deg g_{I^{\prime}}\ll_{n,D,[L:K]}1$ with the following property: for all $\bfa_{I^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{|I^{\prime}|}$ with $g_{I^{\prime}}(\bfa_{I^{\prime}})\neq 0$ , the polynomial

$$ H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}):=H(Y,X_{1},X_{i}+a_{i}X_{1})_{i\in I^{\prime}}, $$

has associated field

$$ \mathcal{L}_{H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}}:=L(X_{1},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})[Y]/(H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})) $$

with the property

$$ (\mathcal{L}_{H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}}\cap\overline{L(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}}. $$

From this it would follow that

$$ R_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}):=R(Y,X_{1},X_{i}+a_{i}X_{1},X_{j})_{i\in I^{\prime},j\not\in I^{\prime}\cup\{1\}}, $$

is such that

$$ (\mathcal{L}_{R_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}}\cap\overline{k(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{R_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}}. $$

The final step is then to observe that for each index $j\not\in I^{\prime}\cup\{1\}$ , then $\deg_{X_{j}}H=0$ , so that shifts of the form $X_{j}\mapsto X_{j}+a_{j}X_{1}$ do not change $H$ . Thus we may consider $g_{I^{\prime}}$ as a polynomial in $\mathcal{O}_{K}[A_{2},\ldots,A_{n}]$ (i.e. in $n-1$ variables), which we call $g^{R}$ , and the desired conclusion of the lemma holds for all $\bfa\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ such that $g^{R}(\bfa)\neq 0$ .

To construct the desired polynomial $g_{I^{\prime}}$ in variables $A_{i}$ for $i\in I^{\prime}$ that leads to (7.13), we will apply Lemma 7.6. Expand

$$ B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\bfX_{I^{\prime}},\bfA_{I^{\prime}}))=\sum_{|\bfk|\leq D^{\prime}}g_{\bfk}(\bfA_{I^{\prime}})\bfX_{I^{\prime}}^{\bfk}, $$

in which $D^{\prime}\ll_{n,\deg R}1$ , and $\deg g_{\bfk}\ll_{n,\deg R}1$ for each $\bfk$ . By Lemma 7.6, $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\bfX_{I^{\prime}},\bfA_{I^{\prime}}))\not\equiv 0$ so we can find $\bfk$ such that $g_{\bfk}(\bfA_{I^{\prime}})\not\equiv 0$ . Note that while $B_{\mathrm{lin}}$ has coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}$ (as a function of $b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\bfA_{I^{\prime}})$ ), in the expansion above, a priori $g_{\bfk}(\bfA_{I^{\prime}})\in\mathcal{O}_{L}[\bfA_{I^{\prime}}]$ . To construct our desired polynomial $g_{I^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}[\bfA_{I^{\prime}}]$ , define

$$ g_{I^{\prime}}(\bfA_{I^{\prime}}):=\prod_{\sigma\in\Aut(L/K)}\sigma(g_{\bfk}(\bfA_{I^{\prime}})), $$

where $\sigma\in\Aut(L/K)$ act on the coefficients of $g_{\bfk}$ ; observe that all the coefficients of $g_{I^{\prime}}$ lie in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ as desired. Also, $\deg{g_{I^{\prime}}}\ll_{n,\deg R,[L:K]}1$ . It remains to check that when $g_{I^{\prime}}(\bfa_{I^{\prime}})\neq 0$ , then $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\bfa_{I^{\prime}}))\not\equiv 0$ . This follows from the fact that $g_{I^{\prime}}(\bfa_{I^{\prime}})\neq 0$ implies that $g_{\bfk}(\bfa_{I^{\prime}})\neq 0$ and hence $B_{\mathrm{lin}}(b_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}},\bfa_{I^{\prime}}))\not\equiv 0$ . That is, when $g_{I^{\prime}}(\bfa_{I^{\prime}})\neq 0$ , then the property in (IV) of Theorem 6.7 holds for the index $i_{0}=1$ . By Theorem 6.7 ((IV) for $i_{0}=1$ $\Rightarrow$ (II) for $i_{0}=1$ ), it follows that when $g_{I^{\prime}}(\bfa_{I^{\prime}})\neq 0$ , then

$$ (\mathcal{L}_{H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1})\subsetneq\mathcal{L}_{H_{\bfa_{I^{\prime}}}}, $$

verifying (7.13). This suffices to complete the proof of the lemma. ∎

### 7.3. Step 3: Proof of Proposition 7.1

By convention, let $\mathcal{L}_{R}$ denote $\mathcal{L}_{R_{\mathbf{a}}}$ when $\mathbf{a}=\boldsymbol{0}.$ If $R$ has the property that

$$ \mathcal{L}_{R}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})}=L(X_{2},...,X_{n}), $$

then the conclusion of the proposition is true for $\bfa=0$ , and we are finished. Thus we reduce consideration to the case in which $\mathcal{L}_{R}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})}\supsetneq L(X_{2},...,X_{n}).$ In this case, let $K_{1},...,K_{e}$ denote all the nontrivial extensions of $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ contained in $\mathcal{L}_{R}$ (including $\mathcal{L}_{R}$ itself). Under the hypotheses of the proposition, an application of Lemma 5.4 shows that for each $j=1,\ldots,e$ , $K_{j}$ is an $\ell_{j}$ -genuine extension of $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ for some $\ell_{j}\geq 1$ . For each $j$ , let $P_{j}(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ be a polynomial, irreducible over $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , and monic in $Y$ , such that $K_{j}=L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/P_{j}$ . Define the field $K_{j,\bfa}=L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/(P_{j})_{\bfa}$ generated by the shifted polynomial $(P_{j})_{\bfa}$ , for each $\bfa\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ . We claim that for a fixed $\bfa$ , the fields $K_{1,\bfa},...,K_{e,\bfa}$ also enumerate all the nontrivial intermediate extensions of $L(X_{1},...,X_{n})$ contained in $\mathcal{L}_{R_{\bfa}}$ . To see this, first observe that, for every polynomial $G$ and every $\bfa$ ,

$$ \begin{split}(G_{-\bfa})_{\bfa}&=G_{-\bfa}(X_{1},X_{2}+a_{2}X_{1},...,X_{n}+a_{n}X_{1})\\
&=G_{\bfa}(X_{1},(X_{2}-a_{2}X_{1})+a_{2}X_{1},...,(X_{n}-a_{n}X_{1})+a_{n}X_{1})\\
&=G.\end{split} $$

Now let $L(\bfX)\subsetneq\mathcal{K}\subset\mathcal{L}_{R_{\bfa}}$ be a nontrivial intermediate extension and let $G(Y,\bfX)$ be monic in $Y$ and irreducible over $L$ such that $\mathcal{K}=L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/G$ ; in the nomenclature above, $\mathcal{K}_{-\bfa}=L(\mathbf{X})[Y]/G_{-\bfa}$ . Then $k(\bfX)\subsetneq\mathcal{K}_{-\bfa}\subset\mathcal{L}_{R}$ , hence $\mathcal{K}_{-\bfa}=K_{j}$ for some $j\in\{1,...,e\}$ which implies that $K_{j,\bfa}=(\mathcal{K}_{-\bfa})_{\bfa}=L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/(G_{-\bfa})_{\bfa}=L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/G=\mathcal{K}$ . This verifies the claim.

We claim that Lemma 7.4 proves the existence of a vector $\bfa\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ such that for every $j=1,\ldots,e$ ,

$$ K_{j,\bfa}\supsetneq(K_{j,\bfa}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1}). $$

Indeed, in the notation above, for each $j$ we can apply that lemma with $R$ chosen to be the polynomial $P_{j}$ such that $K_{j}=L(\mathbf{X})[Y]/P_{j}$ , which as remarked above is $\ell_{j}$ -genuine over $L$ for some $\ell_{j}\geq 1$ . Then upon taking the polynomials $g^{P_{1}},\ldots,g^{P_{e}}$ provided by that lemma, it suffices to choose $\bfa\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ that is a root of none of these polynomials.

By Lemma 2.4, for any $M\geq 1$

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}:\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq M\}\asymp_{m}M^{n-1}, $$

in which $m=[K:\mathbb{Q}]\ll_{D}1$ . On the other hand, by the trivial bound in Lemma 2.3, for a fixed $j$ and any $M\gg 1$ ,

$$ \{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}:\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq M,g^{P_{j}}(\mathbf{x})=0\}\ll_{n,m}(\deg g^{P_{j}})M^{n-2}. $$

For each $j$ , $\deg g^{P_{j}}\ll_{n,D,[L:\mathbb{Q}]}1$ . Thus in total the union over $j=1,\ldots,e$ of the roots of $g^{P_{j}}$ contains at most $\ll_{n,D,[L:\mathbb{Q}]}M^{n-2}$ points. By applying this for any $M\gg_{n,D,[L:\mathbb{Q}]}1$ , there must be some element $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ with $\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq M$ for which none of the $g^{P_{j}}$ vanishes; hence, taking $M\asymp_{n,D,[L:\mathbb{Q}]}1$ , there exists a suitable $\bfa$ with $\|\bfa\|\ll_{n,D,[L:\mathbb{Q}]}1$ .

As a consequence of (7.14), we claim that for every $j=1,\ldots,e$ ,

$$ K_{j,\bfa}\not\subset(\mathcal{L}_{R_{\mathbf{a}}}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1}). $$

Indeed, if not, then $K_{j,\bfa}\subset\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})}(X_{1})$ , and hence

$$ K_{j,\bfa}=(K_{j,\bfa}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})})(X_{1}), $$

which contradicts (7.14). Now denote $N_{R_{\mathbf{a}}}:=\mathcal{L}_{R_{\mathbf{a}}}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})}$ so that the right-hand side in (7.15) is $N_{R_{\mathbf{a}}}(X_{1})$ . Since $K_{1,\bfa},...,K_{e,\bfa}$ enumerate all nontrivial intermediate extensions of $L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ contained in $\mathcal{L}_{R_{\mathbf{a}}}$ , yet $K_{j,\mathbf{a}}\not\subset N_{R_{\mathbf{a}}}(X_{1})$ for every $j=1,\ldots,e$ , it follows that $N_{R_{\mathbf{a}}}(X_{1})=L(X_{1},...,X_{n})$ , i.e. $\mathcal{L}_{R_{\mathbf{a}}}\cap\overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})}=N_{R_{\mathbf{a}}}=L(X_{2},...,X_{n})$ . This completes the proof of Proposition 7.1, and hence also the proof of Theorem 5.7.

#### Remark 7.7.

It is reasonable to ask whether this strategy of shifting $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ by a choice of “short” $\bfa\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ with $\|\bfa\|\ll_{n,D}1$ could allow the methods of [BPW25] to apply to a broader class of polynomials than presently achieved in that paper. In order to apply the methods leading to [BPW25, Theorem 6.4] and hence to [BPW25, Theorems 1.1-1.3], it suffices for $F$ to be strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable; this is the requirement that $F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ is strongly $n$ -genuine for all $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ . Proposition 7.1 can shift a polynomial $R(Y,\mathbf{X})$ by a vector $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ with $\|\mathbf{a}\|\ll_{n,D,[L:\mathbb{Q}]}1$ to a polynomial satisfying (7.1) (weaker than being strongly $n$ -genuine, by Theorem 4.2 (I) $\Rightarrow$ (II)), but it is not clear that such a “short” shift can produce a strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomial. On the other hand, the methods leading to [BPW25, Theorem 6.4] only require a weaker property that for every $L$ belonging to a finite set $\mathscr{L}$ of linear transformations, $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ satisfies $\mathcal{L}_{F_{L}}\cap\overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})$ for all $L\in\mathscr{L}$ ; the linear transformations in $\mathscr{L}$ may themselves have large norms.
